5  Beta Regression

When to Use and Not Use Beta Regression

Beta regression is a likelihood-based regression model for modelling continuous outcomes that are bounded between two finite limits and, after any meaningful rescaling, take values strictly inside the open unit interval \((0,1)\) (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto 2004; Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010). Examples include a continuous proportion of land covered by vegetation, the fraction of a budget allocated to a particular activity, or a continuous performance measure recorded as a proportion. Unlike Binary Logistic regression, the response is not an event indicator: each observational unit contributes a continuous bounded measurement rather than a \(0/1\) outcome.

Use Beta regression when the following conditions are reasonable for the data and the modelling inquiry:

  • The response is continuous and bounded, with values that lie strictly inside \((0,1)\) after any scientifically meaningful rescaling. A response recorded on another finite interval, such as a percentage from \(0\) to \(100\), can often be rescaled to the unit interval when the underlying quantity is genuinely continuous.
  • The response is not simply a binary event indicator or a count of successes out of a known number of trials. The Beta likelihood models a continuous bounded response rather than Bernoulli or Binomial sampling.
  • The scientific or data-science inquiry concerns how the conditional mean of the bounded response is associated with a set of regressors, how its conditional dispersion changes across observations, or how accurately the fitted model can predict bounded responses and their predictive distributions for new or held-out observational units.
  • The observations can be treated as statistically independent, or any remaining dependence is negligible for the modelling purpose. Repeated, clustered, or longitudinal bounded responses require a model that accounts explicitly for that dependence.
  • The chosen mean submodel is reasonable. With the logit mean link used in this chapter, continuous regressors should be related adequately to the logit of the conditional mean through linear terms, suitable transformations, or explicitly modelled nonlinear terms.
  • The chosen precision submodel is also reasonable. Beta regression can use a common precision parameter or allow precision to depend on regressors (Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010; Smithson and Verkuilen 2006). A constant-precision model should not be retained automatically when the conditional spread changes systematically in a way that the fitted Beta variance structure cannot represent.
  • The data contain enough observations across the relevant regressor values and categories to estimate both the mean and, when used, precision components without severe numerical instability.
  • For the standard Beta regression likelihood developed in this chapter, the response contains no exact \(0\) or \(1\) values at the modelling stage. Exact boundary observations require an explicitly justified preprocessing strategy or a model designed to accommodate boundary mass.

Beta regression should not be the default choice merely because a response is reported as a percentage, proportion, fraction, or number between zero and one. The data-generating structure matters. Other response structures require different modelling choices:

  • Binary outcomes: use Binary Logistic regression, such as whether a student passes or fails or whether a customer clicks or does not click.
  • Grouped successes and trials: when each row records a number of successes out of a known number of trials, use a Binomial generalized linear model for grouped data rather than treating the observed success fraction as an ordinary continuous Beta response. See Agresti (2013) for a deeper treatment of Binomial response models.
  • More than two unordered categorical outcomes: use Multinomial Logistic regression.
  • More than two ordered categorical outcomes: use Ordinal Logistic regression. An ordinal score should not be converted automatically to a proportion merely because its numerical coding is bounded.
  • Continuous outcomes that are not naturally bounded: use a model appropriate to their support and distribution, such as Ordinary Least-squares regression when its assumptions are reasonable or Gamma regression for suitable positive, right-skewed responses.
  • Non-negative integer counts: use a count-regression model such as Classical Poisson regression, Negative Binomial regression, Zero-Inflated Poisson regression, or Generalized Poisson regression.
  • Genuine boundary observations at \(0\) and/or \(1\): standard Beta regression is not designed for boundary mass. Depending on the scientific meaning of those values, alternatives include models that explicitly accommodate boundaries, such as extended-support Beta regression (Kosmidis and Zeileis 2026), or another model tailored to the data-generating process.
  • Repeated, clustered, or longitudinal bounded outcomes: use a dependence-aware extension, such as a mixed-effects Beta regression or another model that accounts explicitly for within-cluster association.

Ordinary maximum likelihood estimation also requires caution when the model contains very sparse factor levels, strong redundancy among regressors, observations extremely close to the boundaries, influential observations, or a mean or precision specification that is too restrictive. Successful numerical convergence does not by itself establish that the fitted Beta distribution is adequate. Mean structure, precision structure, residual behaviour, influence, and the agreement between observed and fitted conditional distributions must still be checked.

Beta regression also does not automatically make a coefficient causal, nor does a satisfactory in-sample fit guarantee accurate out-of-sample prediction. Inferential conclusions must respect the study design, while predictive claims require evaluation on held-out data. When probabilistic prediction is part of the inquiry, the fitted conditional Beta distribution should be assessed in addition to point-prediction error.

In this chapter, we begin with a Beta regression model for the conditional mean and a common precision parameter, diagnose whether that distributional structure is adequate, and then allow the precision to vary when the training data provide a concrete reason to do so. This progression supports both inferential and predictive inquiries while keeping model refinement tied to evidence rather than added complexity for its own sake.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Identify when Beta regression is an appropriate model for a continuous response bounded inside the open unit interval \((0,1)\), and distinguish this setting from binary, grouped-Binomial, count, unbounded continuous, and boundary-mass response structures.
  • Explain the Beta distribution using both its shape-parameter form and its mean–precision parameterization, including how the conditional mean \(\mu_i\) and precision \(\phi_i\) determine the response variance.
  • Specify a Beta regression model by combining a conditional Beta distribution with a regression submodel for the conditional mean and, when needed, a separate regression submodel for the precision.
  • Explain how Beta regression parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood, how likelihood curvature leads to model-based standard errors, and why reliable inference depends on an adequate mean structure, precision structure, and conditional distribution.
  • Fit equivalent Beta regression models in R and Python, using explicit response preparation, category reference levels, mean and precision links, and matched model specifications.
  • Assess model adequacy using observed-versus-fitted comparisons, quantile residuals, precision-structure checks, and influence diagnostics, and use training-stage evidence to justify model refinement rather than adding complexity automatically.
  • Interpret Beta regression coefficients on the logit-mean scale, distinguish exponentiated mean-submodel coefficients from event odds ratios, and communicate results using fitted conditional means and percentage-point contrasts on the original response scale.
  • Distinguish an inferential inquiry from a predictive inquiry, freeze the final model specification before using testing outcomes, and use the testing data appropriately for each goal.
  • Generate point predictions and full predictive Beta distributions for new or held-out observations, construct predictive intervals, and distinguish predictive intervals from confidence intervals for the conditional mean.
  • Evaluate held-out predictive performance using a training-derived baseline, point-prediction metrics, and a probabilistic predictive score, and synthesize inferential and predictive conclusions without making unsupported causal claims.

5.1 Introduction

Many regression problems involve numerical responses that are continuous but bounded rather than free to vary across the entire real line. Examples include the proportion of household income spent on food, the proportion of crude oil converted to gasoline, coral cover measured as a proportion, and performance measures reported on a percentage scale. These responses can vary continuously within a finite range, yet values outside that range are impossible.

This boundedness changes the modelling problem in an important way. A regression model should not only describe how the conditional mean of the response changes across observational units; its probability model should also be compatible with the values the response can actually take. For a proportion, a fitted conditional mean below \(0\) or above \(1\) is not merely unusual (it lies outside the response scale). Moreover, responses near the middle of the unit interval can exhibit a different amount of variability from responses whose means lie close to either boundary.

Definition of bounded continuous response

A bounded continuous response is a response variable that can, in principle, take any value within a continuous interval but is constrained by finite lower and upper limits. For the standard Beta regression model developed in this chapter, the response for observational unit \(i\), denoted by \(Y_i\), is represented on the open unit interval:

\[ 0 < Y_i < 1. \]

A response measured on another finite scale, such as a percentage from \(0\) to \(100\), can sometimes be rescaled to \((0,1)\) when that transformation is scientifically meaningful. Exact boundary values require additional consideration because the standard Beta probability distribution assigns positive density only to values strictly between \(0\) and \(1\).

The word proportion needs some care here. A response taking values between \(0\) and \(1\) is not automatically a Beta-regression response. A binary response records one of two outcomes, typically \(0\) or \(1\), for each observational unit. On the other hand, a grouped Binomial response arises when a row records a number of successes out of a known number of trials, so an observed proportion such as \(8/10\) comes from an underlying count. By contrast, Beta regression treats the response itself as a continuous bounded measurement. Hence, choosing among these models requires understanding how the response was generated, not merely inspecting its numerical range.

As Figure 5.1 emphasizes, Beta regression belongs to the continuous-response part of our regression toolkit. Even though Beta regression and Binary Logistic regression can both use a logit link, this continuous distinction is critical. In Binary Logistic regression, the model targets the probability of an event for a Bernoulli response. In Beta regression, the logit link can instead connect regressors to the conditional mean of a continuous bounded response. Therefore, the same mathematical transformation appears in two different probability models with different interpretations.

At first glance, Ordinary Least-squares (OLS) regression may seem like a natural starting point for any continuous response. However, the usual linear model does not constrain fitted means to remain within a bounded response range, and its classical constant-variance Normal-error formulation may not reflect the skewness or mean-dependent variability that bounded responses can exhibit. This does not mean that OLS must perform poorly whenever a response is bounded. In some datasets, it can provide a useful approximation. Instead, the motivation for Beta regression is that it provides a probability model whose support and distributional structure are designed explicitly for a continuous response inside \((0,1)\) (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto 2004; Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010).

Beta regression accomplishes this by modelling the response with a Beta conditional distribution. A convenient parameterization describes that distribution using a conditional mean, \(\mu_i\), and a precision parameter, \(\phi_i\). The mean submodel relates \(\mu_i\) to regressors through a link function, while the precision submodel describes how concentrated the conditional response distribution is around that mean. The model can begin with one common precision parameter and, when the data provide evidence that this structure is too restrictive, allow precision to vary across observations. This separation between mean and precision is one of the features that makes Beta regression particularly flexible.

That separation is also important for prediction. A single fitted conditional mean tells us where the model expects a response to be centred, but it does not by itself describe how uncertain a future bounded response may be around that value. By estimating a full conditional Beta distribution, we can obtain both a point prediction and a distribution of plausible response values. Later in the chapter, this will let us evaluate not only how close held-out point predictions are to observed responses, but also whether the model’s predictive distributions represent uncertainty reasonably well.

The running case in this chapter uses a synthetic student dataset in which final grade percentage is the bounded continuous response and study time is the primary regressor. The example is intentionally used as a teaching case rather than evidence about real student behaviour. It gives us a sufficiently clear bounded-response setting in which we can follow the complete modelling workflow (from response preparation and training-stage diagnostics to final inference and held-out prediction).

We will use the fitted Beta-regression framework to answer two related but distinct questions:

  • Our inferential inquiry asks how the conditional mean final-grade proportion differs across study time categories.
  • Our predictive inquiry asks how accurately the developed model predicts held-out final-grade proportions and how well its fitted conditional Beta distributions represent predictive uncertainty.

These questions share the same model-development stage, but they do not use the testing data in the same way. For final inference, we will eventually refit a frozen model specification on the testing data. For prediction, we will instead preserve the model fitted on the training data and evaluate how well it predicts the untouched testing responses. Keeping those roles distinct prevents the predictive evaluation from becoming another model-fitting exercise.

The rest of the chapter develops this workflow section by section:

  • Section 5.2 explains why bounded continuous responses require careful model selection, including the support of the response, the limitations of OLS as a general bounded-response model, and the distinction between continuous proportions and Binomial proportions.
  • Section 5.3 introduces the student final-grade case, defines the observational unit and the regressor called study time, and formalizes the inferential and predictive inquiries.
  • Section 5.4 documents the dataset’s provenance, defines the variables and mathematical notation used throughout the chapter, and performs the initial data-integrity checks.
  • Section 5.5 prepares the response for standard Beta regression by rescaling grades, addressing exact boundary observations, fixing the boundary-handling strategy, and establishing categorical reference levels.
  • Section 5.6 creates the shared training and testing sets for R and Python, explains how the split protects against double dipping, and distinguishes the testing-data roles for inference and prediction.
  • Section 5.7 uses only the training data to explore the bounded response, its relationship with study time, the remaining variables, and the descriptive patterns that inform (but do not determine) the model specification.
  • Section 5.8 develops the Beta probability distribution, including its shape-parameter form, mean–precision parameterization, mean, variance, and the role of the precision parameter.
  • Section 5.9 builds the Beta regression model by combining the conditional Beta distribution with the mean and precision submodels and the logit mean link.
  • Section 5.10 develops maximum likelihood estimation for Beta regression, including the conditional probability density function, likelihood, log-likelihood, score structure, model-based covariance and standard errors, and the way the model is fitted in software.
  • Section 5.11 fits the initial study-time Beta regression model with a common precision parameter and introduces its fitted coefficient output without treating the training results as final inference.
  • Section 5.12 assesses the adequacy of that constant-precision model using convergence checks, observed-versus-fitted conditional means, quantile residuals, precision-structure diagnostics, and influence screening.
  • Section 5.13 responds to the training-stage diagnostic evidence by allowing precision to vary with study time, formally compares the nested precision specifications, and considers whether any additional mean-model complexity is justified.
  • Section 5.14 repeats the adequacy checks after the precision refinement and determines whether the resulting model is suitable to freeze for the two final inquiries.
  • Section 5.15 records the final response definition, category coding, mean and precision submodels, links, predictive baseline, and evaluation criteria before any testing outcomes are used.
  • Section 5.16 explains how to interpret mean-submodel coefficients on the logit-mean scale and translates the fitted associations into more intuitive conditional-mean grade percentages and percentage-point contrasts.
  • Section 5.17 develops prediction with the frozen training model, moving from conditional-mean point predictions to full predictive Beta distributions and predictive intervals.
  • Section 5.18 answers the two guiding inquiries by separating the fixed-specification testing-data refit used for inference from the held-out predictive evaluation based on the training-fitted model.
  • Section 5.19 brings the inferential and predictive evidence together while emphasizing that statistical association, predictive usefulness, and causal effects are different claims.
  • Section 5.20 translates the results into stakeholder-facing language while preserving the uncertainty, study-design limitations, and synthetic nature of the running case.
  • Section 5.21 discusses the main limitations of standard Beta regression and the running analysis, along with natural extensions such as alternative links, richer precision structures, boundary-aware models, and dependence-aware approaches.
  • Section 5.22 reviews the main statistical and workflow ideas developed throughout the chapter.
  • Section 5.23 provides conceptual questions and a second coding case that transfer the complete workflow to another bounded continuous response.

By the end of the chapter, the goal is not simply to know how to call a Beta-regression function. The broader goal is to recognize when a Beta probability model matches the response structure, understand how its mean and precision components work together, diagnose when the initial specification is too restrictive, separate model development from final evaluation, and communicate both inferential and predictive conclusions on scales that make sense for the applied question.

Heads-up on further documented use-cases!

Beta regression is not only a teaching model. Table 5.1 summarizes documented applications involving bounded continuous responses in industrial processes, household economics, ecological monitoring, and marine oceanography. Although the substantive questions differ, each application starts from the same modelling principle: identify a genuinely continuous bounded response, relate its conditional distribution to scientifically meaningful regressors, and assess whether the resulting model is adequate for its inferential or predictive purpose.

The applications in Table 5.1 are substantively different, but they share a common response structure: the outcome is a continuous quantity constrained to a finite interval and represented on \((0,1)\). Then, Beta regression provides a conditional distribution whose mean can depend on regressors and whose precision can be modelled when the spread itself changes systematically. Recognizing that shared structure is the first step toward deciding whether Beta regression is appropriate (and toward recognizing when a binary, grouped-Binomial, count, or other continuous-response model is the better choice).

5.2 Why a Dedicated Model for Bounded Continuous Responses?

The numerical range of a response is an important clue when choosing a regression model, but it is not enough by itself. We also need to ask:

What values could the response meaningfully take?

How was each observed value generated?

What aspect of its conditional distribution is the analysis intended to describe or predict?

These questions are especially critical for proportions and percentages because the same number, such as \(0.80\), can arise from very different data-generating structures.

For example, \(0.80\) could represent a continuously measured fraction of an area covered by vegetation, a score of \(80\%\) on a continuously treated performance scale, or \(8\) successes out of \(10\) trials. Those responses share a numerical scale but not the same probability structure. Beta regression is designed for the first type of problem: a continuous bounded response whose conditional distribution is modelled directly inside the unit interval (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto 2004; Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010). This section sharpens that distinction before we introduce the running case. We first examine the support required by standard Beta regression, then compare its probability-modelling perspective with OLS, and finally distinguish continuous proportions from binary and grouped-Binomial responses.

5.2.1 Response Support

For the standard Beta regression model developed in this chapter, the response for observational unit \(i\) satisfies

\[ 0 < Y_i < 1. \]

This is an open interval: values arbitrarily close to \(0\) or \(1\) are permitted, but exact boundary values are not part of the support of the standard Beta distribution. This requirement concerns the probability model itself, not merely the smallest and largest observations that happen to appear in one dataset.

A continuously measured response on another finite interval can often be expressed on the unit interval through a meaningful rescaling. For instance, if a response is recorded as a percentage between \(0\) and \(100\), dividing by \(100\) maps an interior percentage to an interior proportion. More generally, a continuous response \(Y_i\) bounded between finite constants \(a\) and \(b\), where \(a<b\), can be represented on the unit interval as

\[ Y_i^* = \frac{Y_i-a}{b-a}, \]

where \(Y_i^*\) denotes the rescaled response for observational unit \(i\). This transformation changes the scale but preserves the relative position of an observation between its lower and upper bounds.

Nevertheless, rescaling does not solve a boundary problem. If the original response can equal its lower or upper bound exactly, the transformation above maps those observations to exactly \(0\) or \(1\). Standard Beta regression still cannot assign them positive density. Whether those boundary values should be transformed, modelled through a boundary-aware extension, or handled using a different probability model depends on what the endpoints mean scientifically. We will make that decision explicitly for the running dataset in Section 5.5.

Support also matters for prediction. A fitted probability distribution should assign probability only to values that could plausibly occur. When the response is genuinely continuous and bounded, the Beta distribution provides a natural way to keep the entire fitted conditional distribution inside \((0,1)\) rather than constraining only a point prediction.

5.2.2 Why Ordinary Linear Regression Can Be Problematic

OLS regression is often the first regression method considered for a continuous response. Its conditional mean has the familiar linear form

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i,1} + \cdots + \beta_kx_{i,k}, \]

where \(\mathbf{x}_i=(x_{i,1},\ldots,x_{i,k})^\mathsf{T}\) denotes the regressor vector for observational unit \(i\), and \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k\) are regression parameters. Nothing in this linear predictor, by itself, forces the fitted conditional mean to remain between \(0\) and \(1\).

That lack of a built-in support constraint does not imply that an OLS fit must produce impossible fitted values in every bounded dataset. If the observed responses occupy a relatively narrow interior range and the fitted relationship is mild, all fitted means may remain within the bounds. The concern is more fundamental: the classical OLS probability model was not constructed specifically for a bounded response.

Several features of bounded continuous data can make that distinction important:

  • Fitted means can leave the response range. A linear conditional mean can, in principle, fall below \(0\) or above \(1\), particularly when the model extrapolates beyond the regressor values well represented in the data.
  • A Normal conditional distribution extends beyond the bounds. Even when an OLS fitted mean lies inside \((0,1)\), a Normal-error model assigns positive probability to values below \(0\) and above \(1\). This matters when the goal includes a full predictive distribution rather than only a point prediction.
  • Conditional variability can depend on the conditional mean. For bounded responses, the amount of available variation is naturally restricted near the boundaries. Thus, a model with one constant response variance may be too rigid in some applications.
  • Conditional distributions can be asymmetric. A bounded response can be left-skewed, right-skewed, approximately symmetric, or concentrated near different parts of the unit interval. The Beta family can represent a wide range of such shapes.
  • Point prediction and probabilistic prediction are different goals. Two models can produce very similar conditional-mean predictions while implying different amounts and shapes of predictive uncertainty.

These considerations do not imply that OLS must perform poorly whenever a response is bounded. In some applications, an OLS model may still provide reasonable fitted means or point predictions, particularly when the observed responses remain well inside the boundaries and the fitted relationship is modest. The motivation for Beta regression is therefore not that it must always outperform OLS. Rather, Beta regression provides a probability model whose support matches a continuous response in \((0,1)\), whose conditional variability can depend naturally on the conditional mean, and whose fitted distribution can be used to describe predictive uncertainty as well as a conditional mean.

At the same time, choosing a probability distribution with the correct support does not guarantee that a particular Beta regression specification is adequate. The conditional mean may be misspecified, the assumed precision structure may be too restrictive, or individual observations may have an unusual influence on the fitted model. For this reason, model adequacy remains an essential part of our regression workflow: after fitting a Beta regression model, we will examine its mean structure, precision structure, residual behaviour, influence, and fitted conditional distributions before using it for final inference or prediction.

5.2.3 Proportions Are Not All the Same Kind of Data

A value written as a proportion or percentage does not, by itself, determine the appropriate probability model. The key questions are what one row of the dataset represents and how the observed proportion was generated. The same numerical value can arise from very different stochastic mechanisms. For instance, an observed value of \(0.80\) could mean that one observational unit has a continuously measured response equal to \(0.80\), that \(8\) successes were observed out of \(10\) trials, or that a binary event was encoded using \(0\) and \(1\). These situations may look similar numerically, but they carry different information and require different modelling assumptions. The distinction is summarized in Table 5.2.

The grouped-Binomial case deserves particular attention. Suppose two observational units both have an observed proportion of \(0.80\), but one arises from \(8\) successes out of \(10\) trials and the other from \(800\) successes out of \(1000\) trials. The observed proportions are identical, but the second observation contains much more trial information. A Binomial model uses the success count together with the number of trials, whereas treating both rows simply as the continuous value \(0.80\) would discard that denominator information.

A binary response is different again. If \(Y_i\) can take only the values \(0\) and \(1\), those two values represent the outcomes of a Bernoulli random variable. They are not interior observations from a Beta distribution. Consequently, a binary response should be modelled through a Bernoulli probability model rather than by treating its numerical coding as a continuous proportion.

Continuous bounded responses with genuine boundary values require separate consideration. If exact \(0\) or \(1\) values can occur as meaningful outcomes of the measurement process, standard Beta regression does not represent the full response distribution because its support is the open interval \((0,1)\). The appropriate strategy depends on what those endpoints represent. In some settings, an explicitly justified transformation may be reasonable; in others, a model that directly accommodates boundary mass is more appropriate. We return to this issue for the running case in Section 5.5.2 and Section 5.5.3.

Heads-up on why a percentage is a scale, not a probability model!

Seeing a percentage sign in a dataset does not tell us which regression model to use given the following:

  • A continuously measured percentage whose scientifically meaningful values lie inside the bounds may be suitable for Beta regression after appropriate rescaling.
  • A percentage calculated from a known number of successes and trials is fundamentally a Binomial response, and the numerator and denominator carry information that should generally be retained.
  • A response recorded only as \(0\%\) or \(100\%\) may simply be a recoded binary outcome.
  • A genuinely continuous response that can attain exact \(0\%\) or \(100\%\) values is not fully described by the standard Beta distribution without additional treatment.

Always identify the observational unit and the process that generated the response before choosing the probability model.

The central principle is therefore simple: match the probability model to the response structure, not merely to the way the response is formatted. In Section 5.3, we apply this principle to the student final-grade response and formalize the inferential and predictive questions that will guide the analysis.

5.3 Case Study: Student Final Grades

The remainder of the chapter develops Beta regression through a single running case so that the statistical ideas, computational workflow, diagnostics, inference, and prediction remain connected. The dataset is a toy/synthetic teaching dataset supplied through the {cookbook} R package. Its accompanying dataset documentation describes the variables included in the object. Note that this dataset is designed for practicing regression methods rather than for drawing substantive conclusions about a real student population.

Having said all this, we will treat the variables as a coherent modelling example, but we will not invent a school, course, sampling scheme, intervention, or data-collection process that is not documented in the dataset. Likewise, any associations we estimate should be understood as features of this teaching dataset rather than causal evidence about how students would perform in a real educational setting.

5.3.1 Practical Scenario

Each row in the running dataset represents one student. The response is the student’s final grade percentage, and the primary substantive regressor is study time, recorded in four weekly categories. This creates a natural bounded-response setting: grades are expressed on a finite percentage scale, and after the response preparation developed later in Section 5.5, the modelling response will lie strictly inside the open unit interval required by standard Beta regression.

The case is useful pedagogically for more than boundedness alone. It lets us study how the conditional mean of a bounded response changes across categories, while also considering whether the conditional spread of that response is adequately represented. This distinction will eventually motivate separate mean and precision components in the Beta regression model.

The same case also supports two complementary goals:

  • From an inferential perspective, we can ask how the conditional mean final-grade proportion differs across study time categories.
  • From a predictive perspective, we can ask how accurately a model developed on one part of the data predicts grades for held-out students and how well its fitted Beta distributions represent predictive uncertainty.

These are related questions, but they require different forms of evidence and different uses of the testing data.

5.3.2 Study Design

Before fitting a model, we need to state clearly what one observation represents, which response is being modelled, which regressor is central to the inferential question, and how the inferential and predictive goals differ. Doing so prevents the model formula from determining the scientific question after the fact.

Observational Unit and Response

The observational unit is one student. Let

\[ Y_i \]

denote the modelling-scale final-grade proportion for student \(i\), where \(i=1,\ldots,n\) indexes the students included in the relevant analysis set. After the response is rescaled and the approved boundary-handling procedure is applied in Section 5.5,

\[ 0<Y_i<1. \]

The corresponding observed realization is denoted by \(y_i\). Thus, \(Y_i\) is the random response used in the Beta regression model, whereas \(y_i\) is the final-grade proportion actually observed for student \(i\) on the modelling scale.

The original grade is recorded as a percentage. We will retain that original percentage scale whenever it improves interpretation (for example, when reporting fitted conditional means, prediction errors, or percentage-point contrasts) while using the interior \((0,1)\) scale required by the Beta likelihood for model fitting.

Primary Inferential Regressor

The primary inferential regressor is study time, recorded using four categories:

  • <1 hour;
  • 1–3 hours;
  • 3–5 hours;
  • 5+ hours.

Although the labels have a natural ordering, they do not provide equally spaced numerical measurements of weekly study time. For example, the distance from <1 hour to 1–3 hours is not the same kind of numerical quantity as the distance from 3–5 hours to the open-ended 5+ hours category. Therefore, we treat study time as a categorical regressor rather than imposing a linear numerical score. Moreover, the chapter uses treatment coding with <1 hour as the reference category. The remaining three categories are therefore compared with the <1 hour group without assuming that the category effects follow a straight-line trend or are equally spaced. The resulting coefficient comparisons will later be translated from the link scale to fitted conditional means and percentage-point contrasts on the grade scale.

Mean-model Scope

The running analysis is intentionally organized around a focused mean structure:

\[ \text{conditional mean of final grade} \quad\sim\quad \text{study time}. \]

This is a modelling choice tied to the chapter’s primary inferential question. The goal is not to place every available column into the mean submodel simply because it appears in the dataset, nor to turn the chapter into a search for which student characteristics appear statistically significant. Other available variables may still be useful during data understanding and exploratory analysis. If a larger candidate mean model is considered during model development, its role will be limited: it will provide a training-stage check of whether additional mean-model complexity is warranted. Additional regressors will not be retained automatically merely because they are available.

This focused mean-model scope also keeps a later distinction clear. The mean submodel addresses systematic differences in the centre of the conditional grade distribution, whereas the precision submodel addresses systematic differences in its concentration or spread. Evidence that the spread changes across study time categories is therefore a question about the precision structure, not a reason to add unrelated variables to the mean submodel.

Inferential Inquiry

The primary inferential inquiry is:

How does the conditional mean final-grade proportion differ across weekly study time categories?

The final inferential analysis will examine study time as a categorical regressor rather than reducing the question to a single linear trend. Evidence will include a joint test for study time, category-versus-reference coefficient estimates with model-based standard errors (SEs) and confidence intervals (CIs), and fitted conditional means translated back to the original grade scale.

Because the dataset is synthetic and no causal design is supplied, these results will be interpreted associationally. A difference in fitted mean grade between study time categories describes a difference represented by the model; it should not be described as the causal effect of changing a student’s study time.

For communication, the link-scale coefficients are not the endpoint of the analysis. We will also report fitted conditional mean grades and percentage-point contrasts, which express the modelled differences in units that are easier to connect to the original response.

Predictive Inquiry

The primary predictive inquiry is:

How accurately can the developed Beta regression model predict held-out final-grade proportions, and how well does its fitted conditional Beta distribution represent predictive uncertainty?

This question has two components:

  • First, the fitted conditional mean provides a point prediction for each held-out student. We can evaluate how close those predictions are to the observed held-out grades using prediction-error measures on the grade scale.
  • Second, Beta regression provides more than a conditional mean. Once both the fitted mean and precision are available, each held-out student has a fitted conditional Beta distribution. That distribution can be evaluated using a proper probabilistic predictive score, predictive intervals, and a held-out distributional assessment.

The final predictive analysis will therefore compare the developed model with a simple intercept-only Beta regression baseline fitted on the training data. The comparison will consider both point-prediction accuracy and the quality of the fitted predictive distributions. A model that changes the precision structure may improve probabilistic prediction even when its conditional-mean predictions change only modestly.

Connecting the Two Inquiries

The two inquiries use the same model-development workflow, but they ask different questions and require different final evidence. Table 5.3 summarizes that distinction.

The same frozen model specification will ultimately support both inquiries, but the testing data will not play the same role. For inference, the frozen specification will be refitted to the testing data so that the final coefficient-level inferential evidence is obtained without using those outcomes to choose the model. For prediction, the model fitted on the training data will remain fixed and will generate predictions for the untouched testing responses. Refitting the predictive model to those responses before evaluating it would no longer constitute held-out prediction.

This distinction will be developed operationally in Section 5.6. For now, the important point is that inference and prediction can share a model without sharing the same evaluation procedure. Keeping their roles explicit from the beginning helps prevent model development, inferential assessment, and predictive evaluation from being blended together.

5.4 Data Provenance and Understanding

A regression workflow should begin from the dataset as it is actually supplied rather than from a model-ready object whose provenance and preprocessing are hidden. In this section, we document the source of the student dataset, connect its software variables to the mathematical notation used throughout the chapter, and perform basic integrity checks before rescaling the response, creating the training/testing split, or carrying out exploratory analysis.

5.4.1 Data Source and Provenance

The running dataset is the Beta teaching dataset supplied through the {cookbook} R package, which accompanies this Regression Cookbook. Let us recall that this repository describes the package as a source of toy datasets used in the book. Accordingly, these observations are treated as synthetic teaching data, not as measurements collected from a documented population of university students. Note that keeping the package object as the common source also gives the R and Python analyses the same starting point. Hence, R loads the dataset directly from the running Beta dataset supplied through the {cookbook} package, whereas Python downloads the corresponding .rda file from the package repository and reads the same Beta object with {pyreadr}.

5.4.2 Variable Definitions and Mathematical Notation

The dataset contains the final-grade response together with ten recorded student characteristics. Nevertheless, for the regression equation modelling, a categorical variable with more than two levels cannot generally be represented by a single numerical regressor when treatment coding is used. Instead, as shown in Table 1.8, a variable with \(u\) levels contributes \(u-1\) indicator regressors after one level is chosen as the reference category.

Accordingly, we use \(x_{i,j}\) to denote the numerical regressors that can appear as columns of a design matrix, rather than using one \(x\)-symbol for each raw data column. Moreover, let \(\mathbb{1}{\cdot}\) denote the indicator function, which equals \(1\) when the condition inside braces is true and \(0\) otherwise. Indicator functions let us convert category membership into numerical regressors that can enter the design matrix. For example, \(\mathbb{1}{\text{Study Time is 1-3 hours}}=1\) for a student in the 1–3 hours category and equals \(0\) for a student in any of the other study time categories. Using one such indicator for each non-reference category allows a categorical regressor to be represented numerically without imposing an artificial numerical spacing among its levels.

Now, for student \(i\), define the full candidate regressor vector

\[ \mathbf{x}_i = \left( x_{i,1}, x_{i,2}, \ldots, x_{i,21} \right)^\top, \]

where \(i=1,\ldots,n\). The 21 entries correspond to the treatment-coded categorical regressors and the numerical regressors listed in Table 5.6. This indexing is fixed for the remainder of the chapter.

The first three entries, \(x_{i,1}\), \(x_{i,2}\), and \(x_{i,3}\), encode study time because study time is the primary inferential and predictive regressor. With <1 hour as the reference category,

\[ \begin{aligned} x_{i,1} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 1-3 hours}\} \\ x_{i,2} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 3-5 hours}\} \\ x_{i,3} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 5+ hours}\}. \end{aligned} \]

Thus, a student in the <1 hour reference category has \(x_{i,1}=x_{i,2}=x_{i,3}=0\). This treatment coding respects the ordering of the study time categories without imposing equally spaced numerical scores.

The remaining categorical variables are encoded using the same reference-category (treatment) coding principle. When a categorical variable has no scientifically chosen baseline, we select one fixed level. Hence, every non-reference indicator shares a common comparison category, and the resulting coefficients have a consistent interpretation.

Tip on why we use a common reference category!

Categorical regressors can be represented in several mathematically equivalent full-rank ways, but the resulting coefficients answer different comparison questions. In this chapter, we use reference-category (treatment) coding because each non-reference coefficient compares one category with the same baseline. This makes the coefficient interpretation transparent and aligns directly with the category-versus-reference comparisons used in the inferential workflow (Fox and Weisberg 2019).

This choice is especially useful for ordinal regressors such as study time. An ordering of categories does not, by itself, imply that the distances between adjacent levels are equal. The study time categories <1 hour, 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours are not equally spaced numerical measurements, and the final category is open-ended. We therefore do not encode study time using a numerical score or an orthogonal-polynomial trend.

Other coding systems can be appropriate when the scientific question is different. For example, Helmert, sum-to-zero, successive-difference, or polynomial coding can target comparisons with averages, adjacent levels, or structured trends. In fact, treatment coding is itself one type of contrast coding in the general statistical sense. Here, the important distinction is that we deliberately use a common baseline rather than polynomial or other structured contrasts. The official R documentation for contr.treatment() and contr.poly() summarizes these different constructions.

With the reference-category coding fixed, we also need to distinguish the 21 non-intercept regressor columns from the intercept that will appear in the fitted design matrix.

Heads-up on regressor columns and the intercept!

The vector \(\mathbf{x}_i\) contains the 21 numerical, non-intercept regressor columns defined for student \(i\). Therefore, a multi-level categorical variable contributes several entries to \(\mathbf{x}_i\), not one.

The intercept is still kept separate. When we later write a model in matrix form, the design matrix will prepend a column of \(1\)s to the selected columns of \(\mathbf{x}_i\), so the intercept coefficient \(\beta_0\) is represented explicitly. For example, the core study time mean model will use an intercept together with \(x_{i,1}\), \(x_{i,2}\), and \(x_{i,3}\), whereas a larger candidate mean model can use additional columns from the same fixed 21-regressor design basis.

Keeping this distinction explicit ensures that the \(x_{i,j}\) notation introduced here remains consistent with the design matrix used later for estimation.

Table 5.6 records the raw variables, their roles, and the exact design-matrix columns they generate.

For the multi-level categorical variables in Table 5.6, each listed \(x_{i,j}\) is an indicator for membership in the corresponding non-reference category. Consequently, the complete candidate design basis contains 21 non-intercept columns, but the core running model does not use all 21. Its mean structure is intentionally based on study time and therefore uses only \(x_{i,1}\), \(x_{i,2}\), and \(x_{i,3}\) together with an intercept. The larger set of columns is available only for explicitly motivated training-stage model-complexity checks.

5.4.3 Initial Data-integrity Checks

Before transforming the response or creating the training/testing split, we check the dimensions of the imported object, exact duplicate rows, missing or blank entries, the raw response range, the occurrence of boundary grades, and the categorical levels needed for the design coding in Table 5.6. We also verify whether Primary Sport contains any blank or missing entries that would need to be represented explicitly as None. No response transformation or model-specific filtering is performed at this stage.

  • R
  • Python
count_missing_or_blank <- function(data) {
  missing <- sum(is.na(data))
  blanks <- sum(vapply(data, function(column) {
    if (!(is.character(column) || is.factor(column))) return(0L)
    sum(trimws(as.character(column)) == "", na.rm = TRUE)
  }, integer(1)))
  missing + blanks
}

primary_sport_values <- trimws(as.character(academic_raw$`Primary Sport`))
primary_sport_none <- is.na(academic_raw$`Primary Sport`) | primary_sport_values == ""

academic_raw_missing_or_blank <- count_missing_or_blank(academic_raw)
primary_sport_none_n <- sum(primary_sport_none, na.rm = TRUE)

academic_data <- academic_raw |>
  mutate(`Primary Sport` = if_else(primary_sport_none, "None", primary_sport_values))

academic_missing_or_blank <- count_missing_or_blank(academic_data)

expected_levels <- list(
  `Study Time` = c("<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours"),
  `Café Location` = c("AMS Nest", "Bean Around the World", "Ike's Café",
    "Koerner's Pub", "The Loop Café"),
  `Year in School` = c("1st Year", "2nd Year", "3rd Year", "4th Year"),
  Hobbies = c("Gaming", "Music", "Reading", "Sports"),
  `Primary Sport` = c("None", "Basketball", "Soccer"),
  `Living Arrangement` = c("Alone", "At Home", "With Friends"),
  `Study Group Participation` = c("No", "Yes"),
  `Has a Tutor` = c("No", "Yes")
)

categorical_levels_ok <- all(vapply(names(expected_levels), function(variable) {
  setequal(unique(as.character(academic_data[[variable]])), expected_levels[[variable]])
}, logical(1)))

academic_integrity <- tibble(
  Check = c("Number of observations", "Number of variables", "Exact duplicate rows",
    "Raw missing/blank entries", "Entries recoded as no primary sport",
    "Remaining missing/blank entries", "Categorical level check",
    "Minimum final grade (%)", "Maximum final grade (%)", "Exact 100% grades",
    "Exact 0% grades"),
  Value = c(format(nrow(academic_data), big.mark = ","), ncol(academic_data),
    sum(duplicated(academic_raw)), academic_raw_missing_or_blank, primary_sport_none_n,
    academic_missing_or_blank, if_else(categorical_levels_ok, "Passed", "Failed"),
    sprintf("%.4f", min(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)`)),
    sprintf("%.4f", max(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)`)),
    sum(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)` == 100),
    sum(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)` == 0))
)

stopifnot(
  academic_raw_missing_or_blank == primary_sport_none_n,
  academic_missing_or_blank == 0,
  categorical_levels_ok
)

academic_integrity |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c"))
import pandas as pd

def count_missing_or_blank(data):
    missing = int(data.isna().sum().sum())
    text_data = data.select_dtypes(include=["object", "string", "category"])
    blanks = sum(int(text_data[column].astype("string").str.strip().eq("")
                     .fillna(False).sum()) for column in text_data.columns)
    return missing + blanks


primary_sport_values = academic_raw["Primary Sport"].astype("string").str.strip()
primary_sport_none = primary_sport_values.isna() | primary_sport_values.eq("")

academic_raw_missing_or_blank = count_missing_or_blank(academic_raw)
primary_sport_none_n = int(primary_sport_none.sum())

academic_data = academic_raw.copy()
academic_data["Primary Sport"] = primary_sport_values.mask(primary_sport_none, "None")
academic_missing_or_blank = count_missing_or_blank(academic_data)

expected_levels = {
    "Study Time": ["<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours"],
    "Café Location": ["AMS Nest", "Bean Around the World", "Ike's Café",
                      "Koerner's Pub", "The Loop Café"],
    "Year in School": ["1st Year", "2nd Year", "3rd Year", "4th Year"],
    "Hobbies": ["Gaming", "Music", "Reading", "Sports"],
    "Primary Sport": ["None", "Basketball", "Soccer"],
    "Living Arrangement": ["Alone", "At Home", "With Friends"],
    "Study Group Participation": ["No", "Yes"],
    "Has a Tutor": ["No", "Yes"],
}

categorical_levels_ok = all(
    set(academic_data[variable].dropna().astype(str)) == set(levels)
    for variable, levels in expected_levels.items()
)

response = academic_data["Final Grade (%)"]

academic_integrity = pd.DataFrame([
    ["Number of observations", f"{academic_data.shape[0]:,}"],
    ["Number of variables", academic_data.shape[1]],
    ["Exact duplicate rows", int(academic_raw.duplicated().sum())],
    ["Raw missing/blank entries", academic_raw_missing_or_blank],
    ["Entries recoded as no primary sport", primary_sport_none_n],
    ["Remaining missing/blank entries", academic_missing_or_blank],
    ["Categorical level check", "Passed" if categorical_levels_ok else "Failed"],
    ["Minimum final grade (%)", f"{response.min():.4f}"],
    ["Maximum final grade (%)", f"{response.max():.4f}"],
    ["Exact 100% grades", int(response.eq(100).sum())],
    ["Exact 0% grades", int(response.eq(0).sum())],
], columns=["Check", "Value"])

assert academic_raw_missing_or_blank == primary_sport_none_n
assert academic_missing_or_blank == 0
assert categorical_levels_ok

academic_integrity_html = scrollable_table_html(academic_integrity)

As shown in Table 5.7, the dataset contains 1,000 students measured on 11 variables, with 0 exact duplicate rows. The package object is also complete: it contains 0 missing or blank entries, and 0 observations require recoding to the explicit None level for Primary Sport. Consequently, no observations need to be removed or imputed before modelling. The categorical-level check also passes, confirming that the levels used to define the reference categories and the 21 design-matrix regressors in Table 5.6 are all represented as expected in the imported data.

The final-grade response requires more attention. Its observed values range from 50.2981% to 100.0000%, so all students have positive grades and the upper boundary of the grading scale is actually attained. Specifically, 6 students received exactly 100%, while 0 students received exactly 0%. This distinction is critical because simply dividing the percentages by \(100\) would place the six perfect grades exactly at \(y_i=1\), whereas a standard Beta distribution has support only on \(0<y_i<1\). Therefore, rescaling alone is not sufficient for this dataset. In Section 5.5, we will distinguish the percentage-to-proportion rescaling from the additional boundary-handling step required before fitting the Beta regression model.

Finally, we verify the representation of the study time categories that generate \(x_{i,1}\), \(x_{i,2}\), and \(x_{i,3}\).

  mutate(`Study Time` = factor(`Study Time`, levels = study_time_order)) |>

As Table 5.9 shows, the four study time categories are quite evenly represented. The <1 hour reference category contains 266 students, followed by 255 in 1–3 hours, 247 in 3–5 hours, and 232 in 5+ hours. These correspond to approximately 26.6%, 25.5%, 24.7%, and 23.2% of the full dataset, respectively. The largest and smallest categories differ by only 34 students, so none of the study time indicators is being defined from a sparsely represented category. In particular, the <1 hour baseline itself has ample representation for the category-versus-reference comparisons encoded by \(x_{i,1}\), \(x_{i,2}\), and \(x_{i,3}\).

Checking these counts before the training/testing split does not use the response \(Y_i\) and therefore does not constitute outcome-based EDA. Instead, it verifies that the categorical structure we intend to preserve is present in the full dataset. This is particularly useful because the split in Section 5.6 will be stratified by study time: maintaining these four categories in similar proportions across the training and testing sets will ensure that each part of the analysis contains observations from every study time level.

At this stage, the integrity checks do not indicate a need to remove observations, collapse study time categories, or alter the fixed 21-column design basis. The feature that does require additional preparation is the response itself: six students have an exact grade of 100%, which would become \(y_i=1\) after simple division by 100 and would fall outside the open support of the standard Beta distribution. We address precisely that issue next in Section 5.5.

5.5 Preparing the Response for Standard Beta Regression

The integrity checks in Section 5.4.3 identified one feature that must be resolved before a standard Beta likelihood can be fitted: although the final grade is naturally bounded, six observations occur exactly at the upper boundary of the grading scale. Hence, response preparation requires two distinct operations:

  • First, we rescale the original percentage to the unit interval.
  • Second, we apply one fixed boundary-handling rule that moves the modelling response strictly inside \((0,1)\).

These operations are deterministic preprocessing steps. They are defined before the training/testing split and then kept unchanged throughout model development, inference, and prediction. The original percentage variable is also retained so that fitted means, contrasts, and point-prediction errors can later be communicated on the familiar grade-percentage scale.

5.5.1 Rescaling to the Unit Interval

Let \(g_i\) denote the observed final-grade percentage for student \(i\). The first step converts this percentage to a proportion:

\[ y_i^{\mathrm{raw}} = \frac{g_i}{100}. \tag{5.1}\]

This transformation changes only the scale: a grade of \(75\%\) becomes \(0.75\), a grade of \(100\%\) becomes \(1\), and the ordering and relative positions of the observations are preserved. We use the superscript \(\mathrm{raw}\) here because this simple rescaling does not yet produce the final response used in the standard Beta likelihood.

In the code, we retain the original percentage column and create a separate proportion column.

  • R
  • Python

After this rescaling, the observed proportions range from 0.502981 to 1.000000. In particular, 6 observations equal exactly \(1\), so the rescaled response still does not satisfy the open-support requirement of standard Beta regression.

5.5.2 The Boundary Problem

The standard Beta distribution is defined for a continuous response whose possible values lie strictly inside the open unit interval. Thus, the modelling response must satisfy

\[ 0<Y_i<1. \]

The endpoints are excluded. Thus, a value of \(Y_i=0\) or \(Y_i=1\) cannot contribute an ordinary Beta density value under the standard likelihood developed in this chapter (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto 2004; Smithson and Verkuilen 2006).

For the student dataset, simple division by \(100\) leaves 6 perfect grades at \(y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=1\) and 0 observations at \(y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=0\). The issue is consequently concentrated at the upper boundary, but even one exact endpoint would be enough to prevent us from fitting the standard Beta likelihood directly to the rescaled response.

Heads-up on why rescaling is not the same as handling the boundaries!

Dividing a percentage by \(100\) maps the interval from \([0,100]\) to \([0,1]\); it does not change whether an observation lies on a boundary. Therefore, \(100\%\) becomes exactly \(1\), not a value just below \(1\).

This distinction is crucial because the standard Beta model requires an interior response. Hence, boundary handling is a separate modelling decision from ordinary percentage-to-proportion rescaling.

A different model would be appropriate if exact boundary values represented a scientifically distinct outcome-generating mechanism that we wanted to model directly (as discussed in Section 5.21). Nevertheless, in this synthetic teaching case, we use a fixed literature-supported transformation so that the standard Beta-regression workflow can be developed consistently.

5.5.3 Boundary-handling Strategy

For this case study, we adopt the transformation proposed by Smithson and Verkuilen (2006) for bounded responses containing endpoint observations. Let \(n\) denote the size of the full dataset before splitting, and let \(y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}\) denote the simply rescaled proportion as in Equation 5.1. We define the modelling-scale observation as

\[ y_i = \frac{ y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1)+0.5 }{ n }. \tag{5.2}\]

This transformation sends every observation to the open unit interval. In particular,

\[ y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_i=\frac{0.5}{n}>0, \]

and

\[ y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_i=1-\frac{0.5}{n}<1. \]

It is important that Equation 5.2 is applied to every observation, not only to the observations at \(0\) or \(1\). The same transformation can be written as

\[ y_i = y_i^{\mathrm{raw}} + \frac{0.5-y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}}{n}, \]

which shows that each rescaled proportion is moved slightly toward \(0.5\). For a large sample size \(n\), this movement is small for interior observations while still moving exact endpoints away from \(0\) and \(1\).

For this chapter, we calculate \(n\) once from the full imported dataset and then freeze that value for the entire workflow. We do not recompute the transformation separately within the training and testing sets. Consequently, a testing observation and a training observation with the same original grade receive exactly the same modelling-scale value.

  • R
  • Python

With 1000 observations as the overall sample size \(n\), an exact rescaled value of \(1\) is mapped to 0.999500. The transformed response therefore ranges from 0.502978 to 0.999500, with no observations remaining at either endpoint.

Tip on what we should consider before moving boundary values!

The Smithson–Verkuilen adjustment should not be interpreted merely as a mechanical trick for replacing \(0\)s and \(1\)s. Smithson and Verkuilen first distinguish the theoretical bounds of the response scale from the smallest and largest values that happen to appear in a particular sample. For a response defined on a bounded interval \([a,b]\), they recommend rescaling using those known theoretical bounds and then modifying the rescaled values slightly when necessary to avoid exact \(0\)s and \(1\)s (Smithson and Verkuilen 2006). This distinction is straightforward for the student-grade response. Its grading scale has known theoretical bounds of \(0\%\) and \(100\%\), regardless of whether both endpoints appear in the observed dataset. Hence, dividing by \(100\) uses the bounds of the measurement scale itself rather than the observed sample minimum and maximum.

The authors also emphasize that the meaning of the boundaries is important when choosing a model. A standard Beta distribution is defined on the open interval \((0,1)\). By contrast, if a response genuinely lives on the closed interval \([0,1]\) and observations at \(0\) or \(1\) represent genuine probability masses, Smithson and Verkuilen argue that the response may be better viewed as a mixed discrete–continuous process. They discuss Tobit regression as one possible alternative when boundary observations arise through censoring and note that such models treat boundary cases as qualitatively distinct from interior observations (Smithson and Verkuilen 2006). Therefore, their broader recommendation is to consider how the response is generated, whether its bounds are fixed or censoring limits, whether its domain is naturally open or closed, and whether boundary observations have a distinct substantive meaning before deciding that standard Beta regression is appropriate.

For this synthetic teaching case, we adopt the Smithson–Verkuilen transformation as a fixed preprocessing rule so that all observations can be represented on the open interval required by the standard Beta model. This is a decision for the workflow developed in this chapter. Once chosen, we keep the transformation unchanged throughout the subsequent training/testing analysis and retain the original grade percentage separately for later interpretation on the familiar grading scale.

5.5.4 Categorical Coding and Reference Levels

Response preparation also gives us an appropriate place to lock the categorical coding that will be used by software implementations. The mathematical design basis was defined in Section 5.4.2; here we ensure that the software uses the same category order and common reference levels. That said, for the primary study time regressor, <1 hour remains the reference category. Using the indicator-function convention introduced in Section 5.4.2,

\[ \begin{aligned} x_{i,1} &= \mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 1-3 hours per week}\}}, \\ x_{i,2} &= \mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 3-5 hours per week}\}}, \\ x_{i,3} &= \mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 5+ hours per week}\}}. \end{aligned} \]

Hence, a student in the <1 hour category has

\[ x_{i,1}=x_{i,2}=x_{i,3}=0. \]

Although study time and year in school have a natural ordering, we do not ask the software to treat either variable as a numerical score or as an ordered factor with polynomial contrasts. Their ordering is substantive, but it does not establish equally spaced levels. Hence, we store them as ordinary categorical factors with an explicitly chosen level order and use reference-category treatment coding, consistent with the discussion in Section 5.4.2.

As shown in Listing 5.7 (or Listing 5.8), the first level listed for each categorical variable below is its common reference category. These are the same reference levels used to define the 21-column candidate design basis in Table 5.6.

  • R
  • Python

The two implementations, in R and Python, now use the same category order and the same common baselines. In particular, the three study time indicators represented mathematically by \(x_{i,1}\), \(x_{i,2}\), and \(x_{i,3}\) have the same meaning. Later model-fitting formulas will preserve these reference choices rather than allowing software defaults to redefine the coefficient comparisons.

At the end of response preparation, academic_prepared therefore contains three versions of the grade information with distinct roles: the untouched percentage for interpretation, the simply rescaled proportion for documenting the original support, and the boundary-adjusted interior response used by the standard Beta likelihood. The categorical levels are also frozen. Now, we can create the training/testing split without changing either the response transformation or the design coding.

5.6 Training and Testing Sets

The response transformation and categorical coding are now fixed, so we can divide academic_prepared into the subsets that will support the remaining workflow. As established in Section 1.4.3, the purpose of a split depends on the inquiry. In this chapter, one shared split supports both inferential and predictive goals, but the two branches will use the testing data differently.

5.6.1 Why Split the Data?

The student dataset contains 1,000 observations, which is large enough to reserve a meaningful testing set while retaining substantial data for model development. Hence, we allocate 70% of the observations to training and 30% to testing. Note that the split is stratified by the variable study time. Stratification does not force the grade distributions to be the same in the two subsets. Instead, it protects the representation of the four study time categories so that each subset contains approximately the same category proportions as the full dataset. This is especially useful here because study time is the primary regressor in both the inferential and predictive inquiries.

The training data will be used for:

  • exploratory data analysis (EDA);
  • fitting the initial constant-precision Beta regression model;
  • model-adequacy and diagnostic checks;
  • the pre-specified precision-model refinement;
  • any pre-specified candidate mean-model comparison;
  • fitting the intercept-only predictive baseline; and
  • freezing the final model specification before testing outcomes are examined.

The testing data are then reserved for the results stage. Apart from structural sanity checks, such as the number of rows and the study time allocation created by the stratified split, we do not inspect the testing response values during model development. Furthermore, we do not create a separate validation set for this running case. The chapter is not conducting broad predictive tuning across many competing algorithms or hyperparameter choices. Instead, the limited model refinements are motivated and assessed within the training data, after which the final specification is frozen.

5.6.2 Canonical R/Python Split

For the side-by-side workflow to be genuinely comparable, R and Python must ultimately use the same students in their training and testing sets. Using the same nominal split proportion and the same seed in two different software ecosystems does not guarantee the same sampled observations. Thus, we create the canonical split in R and later import those exact subsets into Python.

Because the four study time strata do not all divide into exact 70/30 integer counts, the R code first determines an exact proportional allocation for the 700 training places. Within each study time category, it begins with the integer part of 70% of that category count, then assigns any remaining training places to the categories with the largest fractional remainders. This preserves the study time distribution as closely as possible while ensuring that the overall split contains exactly 70% training observations and 30% testing observations.

Listing 5.9 implements that allocation, randomly samples the required number of students within each study time category using seed 123, and stores the resulting indices in an {rsample} split object.

  • R
  • Python

The Python split, in Listing 5.10, is conceptually equivalent, but it is only a demonstration of how stratified splitting is carried out with train_test_split() from {scikit-learn}. It is not the split used for the downstream Python analysis.

Heads-up on using the same seed in R and Python!

A seed makes a random procedure reproducible within a software implementation. It does not create a universal sequence of sampled observations across different random-number generators and splitting algorithms. Therefore, seed 123 in R and random_state=123 in Python can both be perfectly reproducible while still selecting different students.

For the remainder of this chapter, the R-generated split is the canonical one. This prevents apparently equivalent R and Python analyses from disagreeing merely because they were fitted to different observations.

We now transfer the exact R training and testing subsets into Python through {reticulate}. After transfer, the categorical levels are restored explicitly so that study time and the other categorical variables retain the same category ordering and reference levels fixed in Section 5.5.4.

  • Python

The canonical split contains 700 training observations and 300 testing observations. Table 5.11 and Table 5.12 verify that every study time category remains well represented in both subsets.

testing_counts <- testing_data |>

    .rename_axis("Study Time")

    testing_data["Study Time"]
