Table 5.11 and Table 5.12 are split-integrity checks, not analyses of the testing outcomes. Specifically, they verify that the canonical split contains 700 training observations and 300 testing observations, and show how those observations are distributed across the 4 study time categories. The within-category training/testing counts and percentages confirm that the stratified procedure has preserved the study time composition of the full dataset as closely as possible. Note that the table does not summarize, plot, compare, or otherwise use the final grade response (or either of its rescaled modelling versions) in the testing set. Thus, inspecting these allocation summaries does not expose the testing outcomes or influence subsequent model development. The testing grade responses remain uninspected until the results stage.

5.6.3 Protecting Against Double Dipping

The split also protects the inferential workflow from double dipping. As discussed in Section 1.4.3, double dipping can arise when the same observations are used to discover or refine a statistical claim and then to provide the formal inferential evidence for that claim. If hypotheses or model specifications are shaped by exploratory patterns in the same data used for the final test, nominal error rates can become misleading.

Data splitting is not a universal requirement for valid statistical inference. Here, it is an intentional workflow choice because the training data will be used for EDA, model fitting, diagnostics, and a planned check of whether the precision structure should be extended. Those activities can affect the final model specification. Accordingly, the chapter uses the two subsets as follows:

  • Training stage: explore the data, fit the candidate Beta models, diagnose the mean and precision structures, carry out the pre-specified training-stage model comparisons, fit the predictive baseline, and freeze the final specification.
  • Testing stage: only after that specification is frozen, use the testing data for the final coefficient-level inferential analysis and for the held-out predictive evaluation described in Section 5.6.4.

The term frozen specification is crucial. Before the testing outcomes are examined, we commit to the response definition and boundary transformation, mean and precision regressors, links, category/reference coding, and the model-refinement decisions supported by the training analysis. A surprising testing result does not send us back to modify those choices and then reuse the same testing observations as if the revised analysis had been pre-specified.

5.6.4 Different Testing-set Roles for Inference and Prediction

The same testing set supports both guiding inquiries in this chapter, but inference and prediction ask different questions. Consequently, they do not use the testing observations in the same way. Simply saying that the testing data are “used at the end” is not precise enough: we must distinguish whether the model is being estimated using those observations or whether an already fitted model is being evaluated against them.

For the inferential inquiry, our goal is to obtain final evidence about how the conditional mean final-grade proportion differs across study time categories. The training data are used to explore this relationship, assess the Beta regression model, diagnose the precision structure, carry out the planned model comparisons, and determine the final model specification. Once that specification has been frozen, we fit that same model structure to the testing data. The resulting testing-set fit will provide the joint study time test, coefficient estimates, model-based SEs, CIs, and original-scale conditional-mean contrasts used for the chapter’s final inferential conclusions. Importantly, this testing-set refit is not another model-development stage. The testing results cannot be used to add or remove regressors, change the precision structure, alter the mean or precision links, redefine the study time coding, reconsider the boundary transformation, or otherwise modify the specification selected from the training analysis.

For the predictive inquiry, the goal is different: we want to assess how well the model developed from the training sample predicts grades for students whose response values were not used to fit that model. Therefore, the final training-fitted Beta regression model is not refitted on the testing responses. Instead, the testing regressors are supplied to the frozen training model to obtain held-out conditional-mean predictions, fitted precision values, predictive Beta distributions, and predictive intervals. Only after these predictive quantities have been generated are the observed testing grades brought into the analysis to evaluate predictive performance using the pre-specified point and probabilistic metrics.

The distinction between these two uses of the testing set is summarized in Table 5.13.

The intercept-only Beta regression model used as the predictive baseline follows the same predictive principle. It is estimated using the training data and then applied unchanged to the testing observations. Therefore, both the study time model and its baseline are evaluated against the same genuinely held-out responses without allowing those responses to influence model fitting.

Heads-up on the two roles of the testing set!

“Using the testing set” does not mean the same operation in the two branches of the workflow:

  • Inference: refit the already frozen specification on the testing data and use that fit for final inferential evidence.
  • Prediction: keep the training-fitted model fixed and use the testing responses only for final out-of-sample evaluation.

The critical rule is that both branches begin only after the model specification has been frozen. Results obtained from the testing data must not be used to revise the mean model, precision model, links, category coding, boundary treatment, or predictive evaluation plan and then be presented as though those revised choices had been made beforehand.

Likewise, results from one testing-set branch must not be used to modify the other. For example, an unexpectedly weak held-out prediction metric does not justify changing the model and then repeating the inferential analysis on the same testing data, just as a testing-set coefficient or \(p\)-value does not justify revising the model before reporting its predictive performance.

With the split and its two roles established, the next stage is EDA using the training data only. From this point until the results stage, the testing grade responses remain outside the model-development workflow. We will first use the training data to understand the response and its relationship with study time, and later to fit, diagnose, and refine the Beta regression model before its final specification is frozen.

5.7 Exploratory Data Analysis

The EDA now uses only the training data. This restriction is critical for both guiding inquiries: the training observations can inform our understanding of the response, the initial mean structure, and the aspects of model adequacy that will later need attention, whereas the testing grade outcomes remain protected until the results stage. This EDA has three specific goals:

  • First, we examine the distribution and support of the final-grade response on both the familiar percentage scale and the interior Beta-modelling scale.
  • Second, we study the relationship between study time and final grade because study time is the primary regressor for both inference and prediction.
  • Third, we conduct a deliberately concise screen of the remaining variables to determine whether any of them show descriptive mean-grade structure comparable with study time. These are exploratory summaries, not fitted Beta regression results, formal tests, or causal evidence.

5.7.1 Exploring the Response

We begin with the response itself. Two versions of the grade are relevant:

  • Final Grade (%) preserves the original percentage scale and is the most natural scale for describing the students’ grades.
  • grade_beta is the boundary-adjusted response from Section 5.5.3 and is the version that will enter the standard Beta likelihood.

The two scales contain essentially the same ordering and distributional information, but they serve different purposes. The original percentage scale is easier to interpret, while the transformed scale verifies that every modelling observation lies strictly inside \((0,1)\).

Table 5.14 and Table 5.15 summarize the centre, spread, and observed range of both response versions in the training data.

The training grades range from 50.30% to 100.00%, a span of 49.70 percentage points. Their mean is 78.77%, compared with a median of 79.37%, while the training-set standard deviation (SD) is 10.72 percentage points.

The upper end of the scale deserves particular attention. In the training set, 4 students have a grade of exactly 100%, and 36 students have grades of at least 95%, corresponding to 5.1% of the training observations. These counts quantify how much of the upper-boundary and near-boundary behaviour documented in the full dataset is actually present in the training sample that will drive model development.

The boundary transformation changes the support much more than it changes the substantive grade information. On the transformed scale, the training response ranges from 0.5030 to 0.9995, and the largest absolute movement induced by the transformation is only 0.050 percentage point when expressed back on the original grading scale. Hence, the transformed observations remain extremely close to their original grades while satisfying the open-support requirement of standard Beta regression.

Figure 5.2 (or Figure 5.3) shows the training grades on their original percentage scale. The orange vertical line marks the training-set mean.

The histogram in Figure 5.2 is a marginal description of final grades in the training data, not a diagnostic for a fitted Beta regression model. Most training-set grades lie roughly between 60% and 95%, with the overall mean near 80%. However, this plot pools students from all four Study Time categories—<1 hour, 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours. Thus, it does not show whether the conditional grade distributions differ across study-time groups. For example, differences in group-specific centres or spreads could be obscured when all observations are combined into a single histogram.

This distinction is critical for the modelling workflow. The bounded percentage scale, together with the absence of observations at 0% after the boundary adjustment described earlier, motivates modelling the transformed response with a Beta distribution. However, the marginal histogram does not tell us whether Study Time is associated with the conditional mean of final grades, nor whether the conditional spread is similar across its four categories. Those are features of the conditional distribution that must be investigated using the explanatory variables and, later, assessed through the fitted Beta regression model. Hence, we examine the relationship between final grades and Study Time next.

5.7.2 Response and Study Time

Study time is the primary regressor in both guiding inquiries, so this is the central relationship in the EDA. We want to determine whether the location of the grade distribution changes across study time categories, whether all four categories remain sufficiently represented in the training sample, how much their grade distributions overlap, and whether their within-category spread appears broadly similar or markedly different on the original percentage scale.

Table 5.16 reports the category sizes together with several summaries of the training-grade distribution.

  • R
  • Python
study_time_summary <- training_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(
    students = n(), mean_grade = mean(`Final Grade (%)`),
    median_grade = median(`Final Grade (%)`), sd_grade = sd(`Final Grade (%)`),
    q1_grade = quantile(`Final Grade (%)`, 0.25),
    q3_grade = quantile(`Final Grade (%)`, 0.75),
    min_grade = min(`Final Grade (%)`), max_grade = max(`Final Grade (%)`),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(iqr_grade = q3_grade - q1_grade)

study_time_sd_max <- max(study_time_summary$sd_grade)

    study_time_summary["q3_grade"] - study_time_summary["q1_grade"])

    - study_time_summary["mean_grade"].min())

The category summaries in Table 5.16 show a clear ordered shift in final grades across the four study-time groups. The mean final grade rises from 65.8% in the <1 hour reference category to 75.2% for 1–3 hours, 85.3% for 3–5 hours, and 90.6% for 5+ hours. These correspond to successive increases of 9.5, 10.0, and 5.3 percentage points. Overall, the mean differs by 24.8 percentage points between the lowest and highest study-time categories. The medians follow essentially the same ordering, ranging from 65.7% to 90.6%, so the pattern is not being created solely by a few unusually high or low grades. Descriptively, this strong separation in group location provides a direct reason for including Study Time in the initial conditional-mean submodel.

The within-category spread is much more stable than the group centres. The four standard deviations lie between 4.60 and 5.01 percentage points, a range of only 0.41 percentage points, compared with the 24.8-percentage-point span in the category means. The interquartile ranges (IQRs) tell the same story: they range from 5.87 to 6.68 percentage points. Thus, on the original grade scale, increasing study time is associated descriptively with a pronounced upward shift in the centre of the distribution, while the amount of within-group variation changes comparatively little. This distinction between location and spread will be especially relevant when we later assess whether the Beta regression requires only a study-time-dependent mean or also a study-time-dependent precision parameter.

Finally, the ordered pattern is not being driven by a sparsely represented category. The <1 hour, 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours groups contain 186, 179, 173, 162 students, respectively. All four categories therefore contribute substantial numbers of training observations to the comparisons above.

The distributional comparison is easier to inspect in Figure 5.4 and Figure 5.5. The boxplots summarize the centre and middle spread, the blue points retain the individual training observations, and the orange diamonds mark the category means.

Heads-up on the jittered grade points!

The individual observations in Figure 5.4 (or Figure 5.5) are jittered only in the horizontal direction. Their vertical positions remain the students’ actual final-grade percentages. Hence, the display separates overlapping points without altering the response values.

The horizontal jitter is only a visualization device. Neither the jittered positions nor the boxplots are components of the Beta regression model fitted later.

  • R
  • Python

The individual observations add two important details beyond the group means. First, the four distributions still overlap substantially: students in different study time categories can achieve similar final grades, so study time alone does not determine individual performance. Second, the within-group spread is fairly similar across categories, even as the centres shift upward with greater study time. The main EDA pattern is therefore a clear increase in the conditional mean of final grade across study time categories, with broadly comparable variability around those means.

These are still unadjusted descriptive differences. They do not account for other student characteristics, are not Beta regression effects, and should not be interpreted causally. Their purpose is to identify the dominant training-data pattern that the initial conditional-mean submodel should be able to capture.

5.7.3 Response and the Remaining Variables

The remaining variables should be examined without allowing the EDA to become a long catalogue of plots. The question relevant to the running analysis is narrower:

Does any other recorded variable show mean-grade structure comparable with the study time pattern?

There are nine remaining candidate variables: seven categorical variables and two numerical variables. To compare their exploratory relationships with final grade on a common practical scale, we summarize mean-grade contrasts in percentage points:

  • For a categorical variable, the raw contrast is the difference between the largest and smallest category-specific mean grades.
  • For a numerical variable, the raw contrast is the absolute difference between the mean grade among observations in the upper quartile of that regressor and the mean grade among observations in its lower quartile.

These definitions are deliberately simple because they do not pretend that categorical and numerical regressors have identical mathematical structures; instead, they provide a common percentage-point scale for judging whether another descriptive pattern is remotely comparable to the study time mean span.

We also compute a second, more targeted descriptive quantity. For each training observation, define its study-time-centred grade as the observed final grade minus the mean grade of its own study time category. Then, we repeat the same secondary-variable comparisons using these centred grades. This centring removes the four study time group means before asking whether a secondary variable still shows a sizeable location shift.

Heads-up on study-time-centred grades!

A study-time-centred grade is not a Beta regression residual, an adjusted coefficient, or a formal conditional effect. It is only an exploratory quantity:

\[ \text{centred grade} = \substack{ \text{observed}\\ \text{grade} } - \substack{ \text{training mean for the student's}\\ \text{study time category} }. \]

Therefore, the centred contrasts below help us assess whether noticeable mean-grade differences remain after removing the dominant four-group study time pattern. They do not replace the later regression model, a likelihood-ratio test, or any formal adjustment for the other regressors.

Table 5.18 reports this compact screen. The variables are ordered by the study-time-centred contrast so that the largest remaining descriptive differences appear first.

  • R
  • Python
secondary_categorical_variables <- c(
  "Café Location", "Year in School", "Hobbies", "Primary Sport",
  "Living Arrangement", "Study Group Participation", "Has a Tutor"
)

secondary_numeric_variables <- c(
  "Part-time Work Hours", "Hours of Sleep per Night"
)

training_secondary <- training_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  mutate(
    study_time_centered_grade =
      `Final Grade (%)` - mean(`Final Grade (%)`)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

categorical_secondary_screen <- bind_rows(lapply(
  secondary_categorical_variables,
  function(variable) {
    group_summary <- training_secondary |>
      group_by(category = .data[[variable]]) |>
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_grade = mean(`Final Grade (%)`),
        mean_centered_grade = mean(study_time_centered_grade),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    tibble(
      Variable = variable,
      Comparison = "Largest minus smallest category mean",
      raw_contrast = diff(range(group_summary$mean_grade)),
      centered_contrast = diff(range(group_summary$mean_centered_grade)),
      smallest_group_n = min(group_summary$n)
    )
  }
))

numeric_secondary_screen <- bind_rows(lapply(
  secondary_numeric_variables,
  function(variable) {
    q <- quantile(training_secondary[[variable]], c(0.25, 0.75))
    lower <- training_secondary |> filter(.data[[variable]] <= q[1])
    upper <- training_secondary |> filter(.data[[variable]] >= q[2])

    tibble(
      Variable = variable,
      Comparison = "Upper versus lower regressor quartile",
      raw_contrast = abs(
        mean(upper[["Final Grade (%)"]]) -
          mean(lower[["Final Grade (%)"]])
      ),
      centered_contrast = abs(
        mean(upper$study_time_centered_grade) -
          mean(lower$study_time_centered_grade)
      ),
      smallest_group_n = min(nrow(lower), nrow(upper))
    )
  }
))

secondary_screen <- bind_rows(
  categorical_secondary_screen,
  numeric_secondary_screen
) |>
  arrange(desc(centered_contrast), Variable)

secondary_raw_max <- secondary_screen |>
  slice_max(raw_contrast, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

secondary_centered_max <- secondary_screen |>
  slice_max(centered_contrast, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

secondary_centered_share <-
  100 * secondary_centered_max$centered_contrast / study_time_mean_span

secondary_screen |>
  transmute(
    Variable,
    `Descriptive comparison` = Comparison,
    `Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)` = round(raw_contrast, 2),
    `Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)` =
      round(centered_contrast, 2),
    `Smallest comparison group` = smallest_group_n
  ) |>
  kable(align = rep("c", 5))
secondary_categorical_variables = [
    "Café Location", "Year in School", "Hobbies", "Primary Sport",
    "Living Arrangement", "Study Group Participation", "Has a Tutor",
]

secondary_numeric_variables = [
    "Part-time Work Hours", "Hours of Sleep per Night",
]

training_secondary = training_data.copy()
training_secondary["study_time_centered_grade"] = (
    training_secondary["Final Grade (%)"]
    - training_secondary.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)[
        "Final Grade (%)"
    ].transform("mean")
)

def categorical_contrast(variable):
    summary = training_secondary.groupby(variable, observed=True).agg(
        n=("Final Grade (%)", "size"),
        mean_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "mean"),
        mean_centered_grade=("study_time_centered_grade", "mean"),
    )
    return {
        "Variable": variable,
        "Comparison": "Largest minus smallest category mean",
        "raw_contrast": summary["mean_grade"].max() - summary["mean_grade"].min(),
        "centered_contrast": (
            summary["mean_centered_grade"].max()
            - summary["mean_centered_grade"].min()
        ),
        "smallest_group_n": summary["n"].min(),
    }

def numeric_contrast(variable):
    q1, q3 = training_secondary[variable].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    lower = training_secondary.loc[training_secondary[variable] <= q1]
    upper = training_secondary.loc[training_secondary[variable] >= q3]

    return {
        "Variable": variable,
        "Comparison": "Upper versus lower regressor quartile",
        "raw_contrast": abs(
            upper["Final Grade (%)"].mean()
            - lower["Final Grade (%)"].mean()
        ),
        "centered_contrast": abs(
            upper["study_time_centered_grade"].mean()
            - lower["study_time_centered_grade"].mean()
        ),
        "smallest_group_n": min(len(lower), len(upper)),
    }

secondary_screen = pd.DataFrame(
    [categorical_contrast(v) for v in secondary_categorical_variables]
    + [numeric_contrast(v) for v in secondary_numeric_variables]
).sort_values(
    ["centered_contrast", "Variable"],
    ascending=[False, True],
).reset_index(drop=True)

secondary_raw_max = secondary_screen.loc[
    secondary_screen["raw_contrast"].idxmax()
]
secondary_centered_max = secondary_screen.loc[
    secondary_screen["centered_contrast"].idxmax()
]

secondary_centered_share = (
    100
    * secondary_centered_max["centered_contrast"]
    / study_time_mean_span
)

secondary_screen_display = secondary_screen.rename(columns={
    "Comparison": "Descriptive comparison",
    "raw_contrast": "Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)",
    "centered_contrast": "Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)",
    "smallest_group_n": "Smallest comparison group",
})[
    [
        "Variable",
        "Descriptive comparison",
        "Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)",
        "Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)",
        "Smallest comparison group",
    ]
]

contrast_columns = [
    "Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)",
    "Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)",
]
secondary_screen_display[contrast_columns] = (
    secondary_screen_display[contrast_columns].round(2)
)

secondary_screen_html = scrollable_table_html(secondary_screen_display)

The raw screen reinforces why study time remains the focal relationship in the EDA. Using the pre-specified descriptive comparisons in Table 5.18, the largest unadjusted mean-grade contrast across the nine secondary variables is 2.13 percentage points for Hobbies. The remaining contrasts are similarly modest. By comparison, the four study time category means span 24.83 percentage points. Thus, before accounting for any overlap with study time, none of the secondary variables exhibits a mean-grade separation approaching the magnitude of the study time pattern identified earlier.

Nevertheless, the raw contrasts are not the most informative comparison for deciding whether the running mean model should immediately become more complex. A secondary variable may appear associated with final grade partly because its categories also differ in their composition across the four study time groups. The study-time-centred contrasts provide a more targeted exploratory check. For each observation, we first subtract the training mean for that student’s study time category and then repeat the same categorical or quartile-based comparisons. In effect, we ask whether a noticeable location shift remains after removing the dominant between-group study time pattern from the grades.

Under this centred comparison, the largest remaining contrast is only 0.80 percentage points, occurring for Hobbies. For scale, this is approximately 3.2% of the raw study time mean span observed earlier. The table also shows that this is not an isolated consequence of one unusual secondary variable: the centred contrasts are small across the full set of candidate regressors. Descriptively, once the broad study time structure has been removed, there is relatively little remaining separation in mean final grade under these simple comparisons.

Note that this screening exercise has an intentionally limited role. It does not imply that every coefficient associated with the secondary variables would equal zero in a Beta regression, nor does it account simultaneously for all regressors, interactions, nonlinear effects, or other possible model structures. It is also not a formal variable-selection procedure and should not be interpreted as one. Its narrower conclusion is that the training-stage EDA does not reveal another mean-grade pattern comparable in magnitude with the study time relationship.

That conclusion supports keeping the initial conditional-mean submodel focused and interpretable rather than adding regressors simply because they are available in the dataset. The study time structure is the dominant descriptive feature that the running Beta regression model should first be able to reproduce. Later, a pre-specified training-stage comparison of nested mean models can provide the formal likelihood-based assessment of whether adding secondary mean terms produces enough improvement in fit to justify the additional model complexity.

5.7.4 Exploratory Data Analysis Summary


The training-stage EDA has now established a focused set of empirical features that the subsequent Beta regression should address. Table 5.20 separates what the training data show descriptively from what those observations motivate for modelling. None of these summaries is itself a fitted-model result.

All together, the EDA identifies a clear location–variation structure for the running analysis. Study time is associated with a pronounced and ordered shift in the centre of the final-grade distribution, while students from different study-time categories still achieve overlapping grades and exhibit broadly comparable amounts of variation on the original percentage scale. The remaining recorded variables show much smaller descriptive mean-grade differences, particularly after the dominant study-time group means are removed.

This evidence motivates a deliberately focused starting model. The initial conditional-mean submodel should first capture the four-category study-time structure rather than incorporating every available regressor. At the same time, the similarity of the observed within-group spreads gives us a second feature that the fitted distribution will eventually need to reproduce. Importantly, the EDA alone cannot tell us what precision structure is required: raw percentage-scale SDs cannot be translated directly into conclusions about the Beta precision parameter.

Thus, we turn next to the Beta distribution and its mean–precision parameterization. Once we establish how the conditional mean and precision jointly determine the variance of a Beta response, we can ask a more precise modelling question:

Can a common precision parameter reproduce the amount of variation observed across study-time groups whose mean grades differ substantially, or will the precision structure need to change as well?

5.8 The Beta Distribution

The EDA left us with a specific modelling question. The centre of the final-grade distribution changes substantially across study time categories, while the within-category spread changes much less on the original percentage scale (see Table 5.16). Before deciding what mean and precision structure a Beta regression requires, we need to understand what the Beta distribution can represent and how its mean and variance are controlled.

After the response preparation in Section 5.5, the modelling response lies strictly inside \((0,1)\). A Beta distribution is a natural probability model for a continuous response on this open unit interval. Unlike a Normal distribution (see Section E.6), whose support extends over the entire real line, a Beta distribution assigns probability only to values between \(0\) and \(1\).

Just as importantly, the Beta distribution is not one fixed shape. It is a family of distributions capable of representing symmetric, asymmetric, centrally concentrated, nearly uniform, and boundary-concentrated responses. We begin with the traditional shape-parameter form and then re-express the same family using a mean–precision parameterization that is much more useful for regression.

5.8.1 Shape-parameter Form

Let

\[ Y \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta), \]

where

\[ \alpha>0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \beta>0. \]

The probability density function (PDF) is

\[ f(y;\alpha,\beta) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}, \quad 0<y<1, \tag{5.3}\]

where \(B(\alpha,\beta)\) is the Beta function,

\[ B(\alpha,\beta) = \int_0^1 t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}\,dt. \tag{5.4}\]

The Beta function can also be written using the Gamma function:

\[ B(\alpha,\beta) = \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }. \]

Therefore,

\[ \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} = \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) }, \]

and the probability density function (PDF) can equivalently be written as

\[ f(y;\alpha,\beta) = \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) } y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}, \qquad 0<y<1. \]

Heads-up on the Gamma function!

The Gamma function is a mathematical generalization of the factorial function, but applied to non-integer numbers. In many different probability distributions, this function appears as a normalizing constant. Moreover, it also appears as part of the expressions of expected values and variances.

That said, for a variable \(z\) in general, we can represent the Gamma function via the following integral:

\[ \Gamma(z) = \int_{t = 0}^{t = \infty} t^{z - 1} \exp{\left( -t \right)} \mathrm{d}t. \]

Weisstein (n.d.) provides further insights on this Gamma function along with some useful properties.

The role of the normalizing constant is worth making explicit. Starting from the kernel

\[ y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}, \]

we have (via Equation 5.4 with \(t = y\))

\[ \int_0^1 y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy = B(\alpha,\beta). \]

Hence,

\[ \begin{aligned} \int_0^1 f(y;\alpha,\beta)\,dy &= \int_0^1 \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy \\ &= \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} \int_0^1 y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy \\ &= \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} B(\alpha,\beta) \\ &= 1. \end{aligned} \]

Thus, dividing by \(B(\alpha,\beta)\) turns the positive kernel into a valid probability density on \((0,1)\).

Tip on a short history of the Beta distribution!

The mathematics behind the Beta distribution predates its modern statistical use. Integrals of the form

\[ \int_0^1 x^{p-1}(1-x)^{q-1}\,dx \]

were studied well before modern probability theory. Pietro Mengoli evaluated related integrals in the seventeenth century, and Leonhard Euler studied such integrals for non-integer exponents in 1730 while working on extensions of the factorial. This mathematical history is documented in detail by Massa Esteve and Delshams (2009).

The distribution also has an early connection to statistical inference. Thomas Bayes’ posthumously published 1763 essay contains a density with the mathematical form now recognized as a Beta distribution when reasoning about an unknown probability of success from repeated Bernoulli-type outcomes (Bayes 1763).

More than a century later, Karl Pearson developed a systematic family of flexible frequency curves for modelling non-Normal variation (Pearson 1895). The modern Beta family on \((0,1)\) is the standardized unit-interval form associated with Pearson’s Type I distribution. Pearson’s broader statistical programme and the historical setting in which these flexible distribution families emerged are discussed by Magnello (1996).

Thus, the Beta distribution connects several strands in the history of mathematics and statistics: the study of special integrals, early inverse-probability reasoning, and the development of flexible probability models beyond the Normal distribution.

Heads-up on Karl Pearson and Eugenics!

Karl Pearson made foundational contributions to modern statistics, including the development of flexible families of frequency distributions such as the Pearson Type I distribution discussed here. However, his scientific legacy cannot be separated from his substantial involvement in the eugenics movement.

Pearson was an enthusiastic supporter of Francis Galton’s eugenic ideas. He directed the Francis Galton Laboratory for National Eugenics at University College London (UCL) and, in 1911, became the first Galton Professor of Eugenics. His eugenic work included attempts to use quantitative methods to support claims about heredity, social class, disability, and supposed racial and national differences. Historical scholarship has also emphasized that Pearson’s development of biometry and statistics was closely connected to his broader programme of establishing eugenics as a scientific discipline (Norton 1978; Cain 2021).

These views and the eugenic programme they supported are now recognized as scientifically discredited and ethically unacceptable. UCL itself has undertaken a formal examination of this history, describing Pearson as one of the institution’s most influential eugenicists. In 2020, UCL removed Pearson’s name from buildings and spaces, and in 2021 the university formally apologized for its historical role in the development and promotion of eugenics (Cain, n.d.).

Acknowledging this history does not change the mathematical properties of the statistical methods discussed in this chapter. It does, however, place their development in its proper historical context and reminds us that statistical methods have always been developed and applied within broader scientific and social settings.

Now, the two shape parameters determine how the density is distributed across \((0,1)\). Figure 5.6 preserves the useful visual comparison of several Beta distributions while making an important point explicit: the relationship between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is important, but so do their magnitudes.

Figure 5.6 shows several qualitatively different members of the same Beta family:

  • \(\alpha=\beta=0.5\) produces a symmetric U-shaped density, with greater density near the two boundaries than near the middle.
  • \(\alpha=\beta=1\) produces the Uniform distribution on \((0,1)\).
  • \(\alpha=\beta=2\) produces a symmetric unimodal density centred at \(0.5\).
  • \(\alpha=\beta=5\) remains symmetric around \(0.5\) but is more concentrated near the centre than \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\).
  • \(\alpha=2,\ \beta=5\) produces an asymmetric density with more probability concentrated toward smaller values.
  • \(\alpha=5,\ \beta=2\) gives the reflected pattern, with more probability concentrated toward larger values.

More generally, when both shape parameters exceed \(1\), the density has an interior mode. To see where it occurs, consider the log-density (see Equation 5.3) up to an additive constant:

\[ \log f(y;\alpha,\beta) = C + (\alpha-1)\log(y) + (\beta-1)\log(1-y), \]

where \(C\) does not depend on \(y\). Differentiate with respect to \(y\):

\[ \frac{d}{dy}\log f(y;\alpha,\beta) = \frac{\alpha-1}{y} - \frac{\beta-1}{1-y}. \]

At an interior mode, this derivative equals zero:

\[ \frac{\alpha-1}{y} - \frac{\beta-1}{1-y} = 0. \]

Therefore,

\[ \frac{\alpha-1}{y} = \frac{\beta-1}{1-y}. \]

Cross-multiplying gives

\[ (\alpha-1)(1-y) = (\beta-1)y. \]

Expanding the left-hand side,

\[ (\alpha-1) - (\alpha-1)y = (\beta-1)y. \]

Move the two terms involving \(y\) to the right:

\[ \alpha-1 = (\alpha-1)y + (\beta-1)y. \]

Factor out \(y\):

\[ \alpha-1 = y(\alpha+\beta-2). \]

Hence, for \(\alpha>1\) and \(\beta>1\),

\[ \operatorname{mode}(Y) = \frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2} \]

This expression helps explain why increasing \(\alpha\) relative to \(\beta\) shifts the interior peak toward \(1\), while increasing \(\beta\) relative to \(\alpha\) shifts it toward \(0\).

A useful qualitative summary is shown in Table 5.21.

Heads-up on equal shape parameters!

The condition

\[ \alpha=\beta \]

implies that the Beta density is symmetric around \(0.5\), but it does not imply that observations are concentrated around \(0.5\).

To see why, compare three cases:

\[ \begin{array}{rcl} 0<\alpha=\beta<1 &\Longrightarrow& \text{symmetric and U-shaped},\\[4pt] \alpha=\beta=1 &\Longrightarrow& \text{Uniform on }(0,1),\\[4pt] \alpha=\beta>1 &\Longrightarrow& \text{symmetric and centrally peaked}. \end{array} \]

Therefore, symmetry and concentration are different properties. Equality of the two shape parameters determines symmetry; their common magnitude determines whether that symmetric density is boundary-concentrated, Uniform, or centrally concentrated.

The \((\alpha,\beta)\) representation is excellent for describing the shape of the Beta family, but it is less convenient for regression. In regression, we want one parameter to have a direct interpretation as the conditional mean and another to describe how concentrated the response distribution is around that mean. This motivates a reparameterization.

5.8.2 Mean-precision Parameterization

For Beta regression, we re-express the same distribution using a mean parameter \(\mu\) and a precision parameter \(\phi\) (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto 2004; Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010).

Start by defining

\[ \mu = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta} \]

and

\[ \phi = \alpha+\beta. \]

Because \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta>0\) in Equation 5.3,

\[ \alpha+\beta>0, \]

so

\[ \phi>0. \]

Also,

\[ 0<\alpha<\alpha+\beta, \]

and dividing all three parts by the positive quantity \(\alpha+\beta\) gives

\[ 0 < \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta} < 1. \]

Therefore,

\[ 0<\mu<1. \]

Now, we solve explicitly for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) in terms of \(\mu\) and \(\phi\). Since

\[ \phi=\alpha+\beta, \]

we have

\[ \alpha+\beta=\phi. \]

From the definition of \(\mu\),

\[ \mu = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}. \]

But \(\alpha+\beta=\phi\), so

\[ \mu = \frac{\alpha}{\phi}. \]

Multiplying both sides by \(\phi\) gives

\[ \alpha=\mu\phi. \]

Next, because

\[ \beta = \phi-\alpha, \]

substituting \(\alpha=\mu\phi\) gives

\[ \beta = \phi-\mu\phi. \]

Factor out \(\phi\):

\[ \beta=(1-\mu)\phi. \]

Thus, the two parameterizations are related by

\[ \mu=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}, \qquad \phi=\alpha+\beta \]

and

\[ \alpha=\mu\phi, \qquad \beta=(1-\mu)\phi. \]

This is a one-to-one reparameterization: every \(\alpha>0,\beta>0\) corresponds to exactly one pair \(0<\mu<1,\phi>0\), and every \(0<\mu<1,\phi>0\) produces positive shape parameters because

\[ \mu\phi>0 \]

and

\[ (1-\mu)\phi>0. \]

Substituting the new expressions for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) into the Beta PDF makes the relationship explicit. Begin with

\[ f(y;\alpha,\beta) = \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) } y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}. \]

Since

\[ \alpha=\mu\phi, \qquad \beta=(1-\mu)\phi, \]

their sum is

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha+\beta &= \mu\phi+(1-\mu)\phi \\ &= \mu\phi+\phi-\mu\phi \\ &= \phi. \end{aligned} \]

Therefore,

\[ f(y\mid\mu,\phi) = \frac{ \Gamma(\phi) }{ \Gamma(\mu\phi) \Gamma\left[(1-\mu)\phi\right] } y^{\mu\phi-1} (1-y)^{(1-\mu)\phi-1}, \quad 0<y<1. \]

Equivalently, we can write

\[ Y \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( \mu\phi,\, (1-\mu)\phi \right). \]

The probability distribution has not changed. We have only changed the coordinates used to describe it. For example, suppose

\[ \mu=0.70 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \phi=20. \]

Then

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha &= \mu\phi \\ &= (0.70)(20) \\ &= 14, \end{aligned} \]

while

\[ \begin{aligned} \beta &= (1-\mu)\phi \\ &= (1-0.70)(20) \\ &= (0.30)(20) \\ &= 6. \end{aligned} \]

Hence,

\[ Y \sim \operatorname{Beta}(14,6) \]

and

\[ Y \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( (0.70)(20),\, (1-0.70)(20) \right) \]

describe exactly the same distribution.

This parameterization is especially handy for regression because the two parameters answer two different modelling questions:

  1. \(\mu\) describes where the conditional distribution is centred.
  2. \(\phi\) describes how concentrated the conditional distribution is for a fixed value of \(\mu\).

Later, for observational unit \(i\), we will allow

\[ \mu_i = \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i) \]

to depend on \(k\) regressors in vector \(\mathbf{x}_i\) through a mean submodel. If the training data provide evidence that a common precision is inadequate, we can also allow

\[ \phi_i \]

to depend on regressors through a separate precision submodel. This separation is the main reason the \((\mu,\phi)\) form is so useful for Beta regression.

5.8.3 Mean and Variance

The interpretation of \(\mu\) and \(\phi\) becomes precise once we derive the mean and variance. Start from the shape-parameter form

\[ Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta). \]

We will use two identities:

\[ B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)} \]

and the Gamma-function recurrence

\[ \Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z). \]

Deriving the Mean

By definition,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \int_0^1 y f(y;\alpha,\beta)\,dy. \]

Substitute the Beta density:

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \int_0^1 y \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} y^{\alpha-1} (1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy. \]

Combine the powers of \(y\):

\[ y\cdot y^{\alpha-1} = y^\alpha. \]

Therefore,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} \int_0^1 y^\alpha (1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy. \]

The integral is another Beta function:

\[ \int_0^1 y^\alpha (1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy = B(\alpha+1,\beta). \]

Hence,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \frac{ B(\alpha+1,\beta) }{ B(\alpha,\beta) }. \]

Now use the Gamma representation of each Beta function:

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \frac{ \displaystyle \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1) } }{ \displaystyle \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) } }. \]

Dividing by a fraction is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal:

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \left[ \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1) } \right] \left[ \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) } \right]. \]

Use

\[ \Gamma(\alpha+1) = \alpha\Gamma(\alpha) \]

and

\[ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1) = (\alpha+\beta)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta). \]

Then

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \left[ \frac{ \alpha\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) }{ (\alpha+\beta)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta) } \right] \left[ \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) } \right]. \]

Cancel the common Gamma-function factors:

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y) = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}. \]

But by definition,

\[ \mu = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}. \]

Therefore,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y)=\mu. \]

This is why \(\mu\) is called the mean parameter.

Deriving the Variance

To obtain the variance, first derive the second moment. By definition,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y^2) = \int_0^1 y^2 f(y;\alpha,\beta)\,dy. \]

Substitute the Beta density:

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y^2) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)} \int_0^1 y^{\alpha+1} (1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy. \]

Recognize the integral as

\[ B(\alpha+2,\beta), \]

so

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y^2) = \frac{ B(\alpha+2,\beta) }{ B(\alpha,\beta) }. \]

Using the Gamma representation,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y^2) = \left[ \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+2)\Gamma(\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta+2) } \right] \left[ \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) } \right]. \]

Apply the recurrence twice:

\[ \Gamma(\alpha+2) = (\alpha+1)\Gamma(\alpha+1) = (\alpha+1)\alpha\Gamma(\alpha), \]

and

\[ \begin{aligned} \Gamma(\alpha+\beta+2) &= (\alpha+\beta+1) \Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1) \\ &= (\alpha+\beta+1) (\alpha+\beta) \Gamma(\alpha+\beta). \end{aligned} \]

Therefore,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y^2) = \left[ \frac{ \alpha(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) }{ (\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1) \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) } \right] \left[ \frac{ \Gamma(\alpha+\beta) }{ \Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta) } \right]. \]

Cancel the common factors:

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y^2) = \frac{ \alpha(\alpha+1) }{ (\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1) }. \]

Now use

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}(Y^2) - \left[\mathbb{E}(Y)\right]^2. \]

Substituting the expressions just derived,

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{ \alpha(\alpha+1) }{ (\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1) } - \left( \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta} \right)^2. \]

Let

\[ s=\alpha+\beta. \]

Then

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)}{s(s+1)} - \frac{\alpha^2}{s^2}. \]

Use the common denominator \(s^2(s+1)\):

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{ \alpha(\alpha+1)s - \alpha^2(s+1) }{ s^2(s+1) }. \]

Expand the numerator:

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha(\alpha+1)s - \alpha^2(s+1) &= \alpha(\alpha+1)s - \alpha^2s - \alpha^2 \\ &= \alpha \left[ (\alpha+1)s - \alpha s - \alpha \right] \\ &= \alpha(s-\alpha). \end{aligned} \]

Because

\[ s=\alpha+\beta, \]

we have

\[ s-\alpha = \alpha+\beta-\alpha = \beta. \]

Therefore,

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{ \alpha\beta }{ (\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1) }. \]

Now, substitute the mean–precision relationships:

\[ \alpha=\mu\phi, \qquad \beta=(1-\mu)\phi, \qquad \alpha+\beta=\phi. \]

The numerator becomes

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha\beta &= (\mu\phi) \left[(1-\mu)\phi\right] \\ &= \mu(1-\mu)\phi^2. \end{aligned} \]

The denominator becomes

\[ \begin{aligned} (\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1) &= \phi^2(\phi+1). \end{aligned} \]

Hence,

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{ \mu(1-\mu)\phi^2 }{ \phi^2(\phi+1) }. \]

Because \(\phi>0\), we can cancel \(\phi^2\):

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{ \mu(1-\mu) }{ 1+\phi }. \]

Thus, under the mean–precision parameterization,

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y)=\mu, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{1+\phi}. \]

These formulas are central to the rest of the chapter. In a regression setting, \(\mu_i\) determines the conditional mean, while the combination of \(\mu_i\) and \(\phi_i\) determines the conditional variance. This is critical in two places later in our workflow:

  • First, it matters for diagnostics. A fitted Beta regression should reproduce not only the conditional centre of the response but also a plausible amount and pattern of variation around that centre.
  • Second, it matters for probabilistic prediction. A point prediction based on \(\mu_i\) gives only the centre of the predictive distribution. The pair \((\mu_i,\phi_i)\) determines the entire fitted Beta distribution, which is needed for predictive intervals and distribution-based predictive evaluation.

5.8.4 Understanding the Precision Parameter


The word precision describes how tightly a Beta distribution is concentrated around its mean when \(\mu\) is held fixed. Start from

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{ \mu(1-\mu) }{ 1+\phi }. \]

Suppose \(\mu\) is fixed. Then \(\mu(1-\mu)\) is a positive constant because \(0<\mu<1\). Differentiate the variance with respect to \(\phi\):

\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial\phi} \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\phi} \left[ \frac{ \mu(1-\mu) }{ 1+\phi } \right]. \]

Write the denominator using a negative power:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu(1-\mu)(1+\phi)^{-1}. \]

Therefore,

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial\phi} \operatorname{Var}(Y) &= \mu(1-\mu) (-1) (1+\phi)^{-2} \\ &= - \frac{ \mu(1-\mu) }{ (1+\phi)^2 }. \end{aligned} \]

Since

\[ \mu(1-\mu)>0 \]

and

\[ (1+\phi)^2>0, \]

we have

\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial\phi} \operatorname{Var}(Y) <0. \]

Thus, holding the mean fixed:

  • larger \(\phi\) means smaller variance and tighter concentration around \(\mu\);
  • smaller \(\phi\) means larger variance and greater dispersion around \(\mu\).

For example, hold

\[ \mu=0.70. \]

Then

\[ \mu(1-\mu) = (0.70)(0.30) = 0.21. \]

The variance becomes

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{0.21}{1+\phi}. \]

Three precision values illustrate the effect in Table 5.22.

Note that, in Table 5.22, the mean remains exactly \(0.70\) in all three cases. Only the concentration around that mean changes. However, this interpretation has an important qualification.

Heads-up on why constant precision does not mean constant variance!

The precision parameter \(\phi\) is not simply the reciprocal of the response variance. Recall that the variance is

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{ \mu(1-\mu) }{ 1+\phi }, \]

so it depends on both \(\mu\) and \(\phi\).

Suppose precision is common across observations:

\[ \phi_i=\phi. \]

Then

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{ \mu_i(1-\mu_i) }{ 1+\phi }. \]

Even though the denominator is the same for every observation, the numerator can change because \(\mu_i\) changes.

To see the pattern mathematically, hold \(\phi\) fixed and define

\[ V(\mu) = \frac{ \mu(1-\mu) }{ 1+\phi }. \]

Differentiate with respect to \(\mu\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{dV(\mu)}{d\mu} &= \frac{ 1-2\mu }{ 1+\phi }. \end{aligned} \]

Setting the derivative equal to zero gives

\[ 1-2\mu=0, \]

so

\[ \mu=\frac{1}{2}. \]

The second derivative is

\[ \frac{d^2V(\mu)}{d\mu^2} = -\frac{2}{1+\phi} <0, \]

so the variance is maximized at

\[ \mu=0.5. \]

As \(\mu\) moves away from \(0.5\) toward either boundary, \(\mu(1-\mu)\) decreases, and therefore the response-scale variance decreases even though \(\phi\) has not changed.

For example, with the same precision

\[ \phi=20, \]

a Beta distribution with \(\mu=0.50\) has

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{(0.50)(0.50)}{21} = \frac{0.25}{21} \approx 0.01190, \]

whereas a Beta distribution with \(\mu=0.90\) has

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{(0.90)(0.10)}{21} = \frac{0.09}{21} \approx 0.00429. \]

The precision is identical in both cases, but the response variance is not.

This distinction brings us directly back to the training EDA. The study-time categories have substantially different mean grades, and the higher-study-time groups have means closer to the upper boundary. Under a common-precision Beta model, the variance will therefore change automatically as the fitted conditional mean changes.

For the high-mean study-time groups, moving \(\mu_i\) closer to \(1\) reduces

\[ \mu_i(1-\mu_i), \]

which tends to reduce the conditional variance even when \(\phi\) is held constant. Yet the raw training distributions showed broadly comparable amounts of within-group spread across the four study-time categories. That does not prove that precision must vary. Instead, it gives the common-precision model a concrete characteristic to reproduce. Hence, we will begin with the simpler model,

\[ \phi_i=\phi, \]

fit it to the training data, and examine whether its fitted conditional distributions reproduce the observed variation adequately.

If they do, a more complicated precision structure is unnecessary. If they do not, the discrepancy will provide a statistical reason to consider a precision submodel rather than adding one automatically.

This is the key role of \(\phi\) in the modelling workflow:

It gives us a principled way to distinguish changes in the conditional mean from changes in concentration that cannot be explained by the Beta mean–variance relationship alone.

5.9 The Beta Regression Model

The previous section introduced the Beta distribution in its mean-precision parameterization and showed that

\[ \mathbb{E}(Y)=\mu \]

and

\[ \operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{1+\phi}. \]

Beta regression turns this probability distribution into a regression model by allowing the parameters that describe the conditional distribution of the response to depend on observed regressors. Hence, the central idea is to separate two modelling tasks. For observation \(i\):

  • the mean submodel describes how the conditional centre \(\mu_i\) changes with regressors;
  • the precision submodel describes how the conditional concentration \(\phi_i\) changes with regressors.

These two components jointly determine the conditional Beta distribution. In particular, changing \(\mu_i\) can change both the centre and the response-scale variance, whereas changing \(\phi_i\) changes concentration while holding \(\mu_i\) fixed. This distinction is exactly what we need after the training EDA in Section 5.7.4 and the mean–variance discussion in Section 5.8.4.

For notation, \(\mathbf{x}_i\) will denote the regressors used in the mean submodel, while \(\mathbf{z}_i\) will denote regressors used in the precision submodel. The two sets of regressors do not need to be identical. In the running case, the initial mean submodel will use the Study Time indicators defined in Section 5.4.2, whereas the precision submodel will initially contain only an intercept.

Tip on a short history of Beta regression!

Regression modelling with Beta-distributed responses predates the now-standard formulation of Beta regression. For example, Paolino (2001) studied maximum-likelihood regression models with Beta-distributed dependent variables for proportional outcomes in political science. Shortly afterward, Kieschnick and McCullough (2003) compared several approaches for responses observed strictly inside \((0,1)\) and recommended, among the useful alternatives, a parametric regression model based on the Beta distribution.

A particularly influential modern formulation was introduced by Ferrari and Cribari-Neto (2004). Their model reparameterized the Beta distribution in terms of a conditional mean and a precision parameter, related the conditional mean to regressors through a link function, and developed maximum-likelihood estimation, inference, and diagnostic tools. In that formulation, the precision parameter was common across observations.

The framework was subsequently expanded. Smithson and Verkuilen (2006) developed Beta regression models in which location and dispersion could be described by different sets of predictors, making systematic heteroskedasticity part of the model rather than an afterthought. Simas, Barreto-Souza, and Rocha (2010) extended the Ferrari–Cribari-Neto framework to allow regression structures for the precision parameter and nonlinear predictors. Later, Cribari-Neto and Zeileis (2010) provided a widely used implementation of constant- and variable-precision Beta regression through the {betareg} package in R (Kosmidis and Zeileis 2026).

Thus, the model used in this chapter reflects a broader development rather than a single isolated proposal: a Beta likelihood for continuous bounded responses, a regression structure for the conditional mean, and, when the data require it, a second regression structure for precision.

5.9.1 Conditional Beta Distribution

Let \(Y_i\) denote the prepared response for observational unit \(i\). As established in Section 5.5,

\[ 0<Y_i<1. \]

In the general Beta regression formulation, we assume

\[ Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( \mu_i\phi_i,\, (1-\mu_i)\phi_i \right) \]

for

\[ i=1,\ldots,n, \]

where

\[ 0<\mu_i<1 \]

and

\[ \phi_i>0. \]

Thus, observation \(i\) has the two Beta shape parameters

\[ \alpha_i = \mu_i\phi_i \]

and

\[ \beta_i = (1-\mu_i)\phi_i. \]

Their sum is

\[ \begin{aligned} \alpha_i+\beta_i &= \mu_i\phi_i + (1-\mu_i)\phi_i \\ &= \mu_i\phi_i + \phi_i - \mu_i\phi_i \\ &= \phi_i. \end{aligned} \]

Therefore, the mean–precision results from Section 5.8.3 apply observation by observation. The conditional mean is

\[ \mathbb{E} \left( Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \right) = \mu_i, \]

and the conditional variance is

\[ \operatorname{Var} \left( Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \right) = \frac{ \mu_i(1-\mu_i) }{ 1+\phi_i }. \]

These expressions are worth reading together. The conditional mean depends on \(\mu_i\), but the conditional variance depends on both \(\mu_i\) and \(\phi_i\). Consequently, the model does not contain a separate constant response-variance parameter analogous to the \(\sigma^2\) of OLS regression.

For the likelihood-based analysis in this chapter, we additionally assume that observations are conditionally independent given their regressors. In other words, after conditioning on the information represented by \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and \(\mathbf{z}_i\), the model treats the remaining random variation in one student’s response as independent of the remaining random variation in another student’s response. This conditional Beta distribution is the probability component of the model. We now need regression structures that determine \(\mu_i\) and, when required, \(\phi_i\).

5.9.2 Mean Submodel

The mean submodel describes how the conditional mean of the bounded response changes with regressors. Let

\[ \mathbf{x}_i = \left( x_{i,1}, x_{i,2}, \ldots, x_{i,k} \right)^\mathsf{T} \]

denote the \(k\) non-intercept regressors included in a particular mean model. We define the linear predictor

\[ \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i,1} + \beta_2x_{i,2} + \cdots + \beta_kx_{i,k}. \]

The linear predictor can take any real value:

\[ -\infty<\eta_i<\infty. \]

On the other hand, the conditional mean cannot. Because \(Y_i\) follows a Beta distribution,

\[ 0<\mu_i<1. \]

Therefore, we do not generally set \(\mu_i=\eta_i\) directly. Instead, a mean link function \(g(\cdot)\) connects the bounded conditional mean to the unrestricted linear predictor:

\[ g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i,1} + \cdots + \beta_kx_{i,k}. \]

The link maps

\[ g\text{: }(0,1)\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}. \]

Applying its inverse gives

\[ \mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i). \]

Hence, the regression equation is linear on the link scale, not necessarily on the response-mean scale:

\[ \mu_i = g^{-1} \left( \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i,1} + \cdots + \beta_kx_{i,k} \right). \]

This distinction lets us use an ordinary linear predictor while ensuring that the fitted conditional mean remains compatible with the support of the response.

For our running case, the initial mean structure uses the three Study Time indicators already fixed in Section 5.4.2 and Section 5.5.4. With <1 hour as the reference category,

\[ \begin{aligned} x_{i,1} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 1-3 hours}\} \\ x_{i,2} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 3-5 hours}\} \\ x_{i,3} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 5+ hours}\}. \end{aligned} \]

Therefore, the core mean submodel is

\[ g(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i,1} + \beta_2x_{i,2} + \beta_3x_{i,3}. \]

A student in the <1 hour reference category has

\[ x_{i,1}=x_{i,2}=x_{i,3}=0, \]

so that student’s linear predictor is simply

\[ \eta_i=\beta_0. \]

The treatment-coded specification does not assume that the four study-time categories are equally spaced. Each non-reference coefficient instead represents a comparison with the common <1 hour baseline on the chosen link scale.

Now, the next question is therefore:

Which link should connect \(\mu_i\) to \(\eta_i\)?

5.9.3 Logit Link for the Conditional Mean

In this chapter, we use the logit link for the conditional mean:

\[ \operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) = \log \left( \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} \right) = \eta_i. \tag{5.5}\]

This transformation is well defined because

\[ 0<\mu_i<1. \]

Hence,

\[ \mu_i>0 \]

and

\[ 1-\mu_i>0, \]

so

\[ \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}>0. \]

The logarithm of this positive ratio can take any real value, which makes it suitable for an unrestricted linear predictor.

To return from the linear predictor to the conditional mean, we solve the link equation step by step. Let us begin with

\[ \eta_i = \log \left( \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} \right). \]

Exponentiating both sides gives

\[ \exp(\eta_i) = \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}. \]

Then, we multiply both sides by \(1-\mu_i\):

\[ \exp(\eta_i)(1-\mu_i) = \mu_i. \]

Expand the left-hand side:

\[ \exp(\eta_i) - \mu_i\exp(\eta_i) = \mu_i. \]

Now, we add \(\mu_i\exp(\eta_i)\) to both sides:

\[ \exp(\eta_i) = \mu_i + \mu_i\exp(\eta_i). \]

Factor out \(\mu_i\) on the right-hand side:

\[ \exp(\eta_i) = \mu_i \left[ 1+\exp(\eta_i) \right]. \]

Finally, divide by \(1+\exp(\eta_i)\):

\[ \mu_i = \frac{ \exp(\eta_i) }{ 1+\exp(\eta_i) }. \]

Dividing the numerator and denominator by \(\exp(\eta_i)\) gives the equivalent form

\[ \mu_i = \frac{1}{ 1+\exp(-\eta_i) }. \]

Because

\[ \exp(\eta_i)>0, \]

the denominator is always larger than the numerator:

\[ 1+\exp(\eta_i) > \exp(\eta_i). \]

Therefore,

\[ 0 < \frac{ \exp(\eta_i) }{ 1+\exp(\eta_i) } < 1, \]

so the inverse-logit transformation automatically keeps the fitted conditional mean inside \((0,1)\).

For the running study-time model,

\[ \operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i,1} + \beta_2x_{i,2} + \beta_3x_{i,3}. \]

The four study-time categories therefore have the link-scale conditional means

\[ \begin{aligned} \eta_{\text{<1 hour}} &= \beta_0, \\ \eta_{\text{1-3 hours}} &= \beta_0+\beta_1, \\ \eta_{\text{3-5 hours}} &= \beta_0+\beta_2, \\ \eta_{\text{5+ hours}} &= \beta_0+\beta_3. \end{aligned} \]

Applying the inverse logit gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \mu_{\text{<1 hour}} &= \frac{ \exp(\beta_0) }{ 1+\exp(\beta_0) }, \\[6pt] \mu_{\text{1-3 hours}} &= \frac{ \exp(\beta_0+\beta_1) }{ 1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1) }, \\[6pt] \mu_{\text{3-5 hours}} &= \frac{ \exp(\beta_0+\beta_2) }{ 1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_2) }, \\[6pt] \mu_{\text{5+ hours}} &= \frac{ \exp(\beta_0+\beta_3) }{ 1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_3) }. \end{aligned} \]

Thus, the coefficients are estimated on the logit scale, while the inverse link returns fitted conditional means to the proportion scale on which the response is modelled. Later, we will also return these means to the original percentage scale for substantive interpretation.

Heads-up on the logit link in Beta and Binary Logistic regression!

The logit function is the same mathematical transformation used in Binary Logistic regression, but it operates on a different quantity. In Binary Logistic regression,

\[ \operatorname{logit}(\pi_i) = \log \left( \frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i} \right), \]

where \(\pi_i\) is the conditional probability of a binary event.

On the other hand, in Beta regression,

\[ \operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) = \log \left( \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} \right), \]

where

\[ \mu_i = \mathbb{E} \left( Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \right) \]

is the conditional mean of a continuous bounded response.

Therefore, the two models use the same link function without modelling the same type of response.

For example, under the running treatment-coded mean model,

\[ \begin{aligned} \beta_1 &= \operatorname{logit} \left( \mu_{\text{1-3 hours}} \right) - \operatorname{logit} \left( \mu_{\text{<1 hour}} \right) \\ &= \log \left[ \frac{ \mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}/(1-\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}) }{ \mu_{\text{<1 hour}}/(1-\mu_{\text{<1 hour}}) } \right]. \end{aligned} \]

Exponentiating gives

\[ \exp(\beta_1) = \frac{ \mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}/(1-\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}) }{ \mu_{\text{<1 hour}}/(1-\mu_{\text{<1 hour}}) }. \]

This is a ratio of odds formed from conditional means. It is not an event odds ratio, because \(Y_i\) is not a binary event indicator. For this reason, our substantive interpretation later in the chapter will emphasize fitted conditional means and percentage-point contrasts rather than importing Binary Logistic regression language mechanically.

5.9.4 Precision Submodel

The mean submodel controls \(\mu_i\). Beta regression can also allow the precision parameter \(\phi_i\) to change systematically across observations. Thus, in general, let

\[ \mathbf{z}_i = \left( z_{i,1}, z_{i,2}, \ldots, z_{i,m} \right)^\mathsf{T} \]

denote the non-intercept regressors used in the precision submodel. These regressors can be the same as those in the mean submodel, a subset of them, a different set, or absent entirely beyond an intercept.

We introduce a precision linear predictor

\[ \zeta_i = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1z_{i,1} + \gamma_2z_{i,2} + \cdots + \gamma_mz_{i,m}. \]

Because

\[ \phi_i>0, \]

we again need a link function that respects the parameter space. In general,

\[ h(\phi_i) = \zeta_i = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1z_{i,1} + \cdots + \gamma_mz_{i,m}. \]

For the models fitted in this chapter, we use the log link:

\[ \log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1z_{i,1} + \cdots + \gamma_mz_{i,m}. \tag{5.6}\]

To obtain \(\phi_i\), exponentiate both sides:

\[ \exp \left[ \log(\phi_i) \right] = \exp(\zeta_i). \]

Since \(\exp[\log(\phi_i)]=\phi_i\) for \(\phi_i>0\),

\[ \phi_i = \exp(\zeta_i) = \exp \left( \gamma_0 + \gamma_1z_{i,1} + \cdots + \gamma_mz_{i,m} \right). \tag{5.7}\]

Because

\[ \exp(\zeta_i)>0 \]

for every real \(\zeta_i\), the log link guarantees that every fitted precision is positive.

A constant-precision Beta regression is the special case in which the precision submodel contains only an intercept:

\[ \log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0. \]

Exponentiating gives

\[ \phi_i = \exp(\gamma_0). \]

Because the right-hand side does not depend on \(i\),

\[ \phi_1 = \phi_2 = \cdots = \phi_n = \phi, \]

where

\[ \phi = \exp(\gamma_0). \]

Thus, constant precision is not a different probability model. It is the intercept-only special case of the general precision submodel.

When precision regressors are included, their coefficients have a multiplicative interpretation on the precision scale. Suppose two observations differ by one unit in \(z_{i,j}\) while all other precision regressors remain fixed. Their precision linear predictors differ by

\[ \gamma_j. \]

Hence, the ratio of their fitted precisions is

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\phi_{\text{new}}}{\phi_{\text{old}}} &= \frac{ \exp(\zeta+\gamma_j) }{ \exp(\zeta) } \\ &= \exp(\gamma_j). \end{aligned} \]

Therefore,

\[ \exp(\gamma_j) \]

is the multiplicative change in fitted precision associated with a one-unit increase in \(z_j\), holding the other precision regressors fixed.

Note that this does not translate directly into the reciprocal of a response-variance ratio. As established in Section 5.8.4,

\[ \operatorname{Var} \left( Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \right) = \frac{ \mu_i(1-\mu_i) }{ 1+\phi_i }, \]

so response-scale variance depends jointly on the mean and precision.

For the running case, we will deliberately begin with the simpler constant-precision specification,

\[ \log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0. \]

This choice follows the modelling strategy motivated by the EDA: first, determine whether one common precision can reproduce the conditional variation observed across study-time groups whose fitted means differ substantially. Only if the training-stage model checks show a meaningful lack of fit in the conditional spread will we introduce additional structure into the precision submodel.

Thus, the more flexible precision model is available because the probability model permits it, but it will be used only if the data provide a modelling reason for that additional complexity.

5.9.5 Is Beta Regression a GLM?

Beta regression has a structure that should look familiar from generalized linear models (GLMs). It has:

  1. a probability model for the response conditional on regressors;
  2. a linear predictor;
  3. a link function connecting a conditional mean to that linear predictor.

For the mean component,

\[ g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_0 + \beta_1x_{i,1} + \beta_2x_{i,2} + \cdots + \beta_kx_{i,k}, \]

which is exactly the kind of mean-link-linear-predictor structure encountered in a GLM.

For this reason, Beta regression is often described as GLM-like or as using the modelling architecture of a GLM (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto 2004; Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010). Nevertheless, standard Beta regression is not simply another ordinary GLM family.

The distinction lies in the probability model. Classical GLMs use response distributions from the exponential dispersion family, whose probability structure has a particular relationship among the mean, variance, and dispersion parameter. Although the Beta distribution can be represented as a two-parameter exponential-family distribution, the standard Beta likelihood does not have the exponential-dispersion form required for an ordinary GLM. This is crucial because Beta regression is built from its own specialized likelihood,

\[ Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( \mu_i\phi_i,\, (1-\mu_i)\phi_i \right), \]

with

\[ \operatorname{Var} \left( Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \right) = \frac{ \mu_i(1-\mu_i) }{ 1+\phi_i }. \]

Moreover, the model can contain a second linked regression structure for precision,

\[ h(\phi_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1z_{i,1} + \gamma_2z_{i,2} + \cdots + \gamma_mz_{i,m}, \]

which is not part of the basic one-mean-submodel formulation students usually encounter when first learning GLMs.

Heads-up on calling Beta regression a GLM!

It is useful to recognize the strong family resemblance between Beta regression and GLMs, but we should not let that similarity erase an important distinction. A concise way to remember it is:

Beta regression uses a GLM-like mean structure, but it is fitted with a specialized Beta likelihood and may also contain its own precision submodel.

Accordingly, in R foe example, we should not think of standard Beta regression as merely another family passed to the ordinary glm() function. In this chapter, the model will be fitted with fitting functions designed specifically for the Beta likelihood and its mean–precision structure.

This distinction also helps organize the remainder of our case study. The mean submodel tells us how the centre of the bounded response distribution changes; the precision submodel tells us whether its concentration requires additional systematic structure; and the Beta likelihood combines both pieces into one conditional probability distribution. Therefore, the next modelling steps will fit the simpler study-time mean model with common precision first and then evaluate, using the training data, whether either component needs to become more complex.

5.10 Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Beta Regression

The previous section specified the Beta regression model by combining a conditional Beta distribution with separate mean and precision submodels. Now, we need to estimate the unknown coefficients in those submodels from the observed training data. That said, Beta regression is estimated by maximum likelihood. The basic principle is the same as in other likelihood-based regression models: among the candidate parameter values allowed by the model, we seek those that make the observed responses most compatible with the assumed conditional probability distribution.

For compactness in this section, we augment the mean and precision regressor vectors to include their intercepts:

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i = \begin{pmatrix} 1\\ x_{i,1}\\ \vdots\\ x_{i,k} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i = \begin{pmatrix} 1\\ z_{i,1}\\ \vdots\\ z_{i,m} \end{pmatrix}. \tag{5.8}\]

Likewise, collect the corresponding coefficients into

\[ \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0\\ \beta_1\\ \vdots\\ \beta_k \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\gamma} = \begin{pmatrix} \gamma_0\\ \gamma_1\\ \vdots\\ \gamma_m \end{pmatrix}. \]

Under the logit mean link and log precision link used in this chapter,

\[ \eta_i = \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\beta}, \qquad \mu_i = \frac{\exp(\eta_i)} {1+\exp(\eta_i)}, \]

and

\[ \zeta_i = \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\gamma}, \qquad \phi_i = \exp(\zeta_i). \]

Thus, the coefficients do not enter the Beta density directly. They first determine the two linear predictors, which determine \(\mu_i\) and \(\phi_i\), which in turn determine the two Beta shape parameters. Maximum likelihood estimates the coefficients by following this entire chain.

5.10.1 Conditional Probability Density Function

For observational unit \(i\), recall from Section 5.9.1 that

\[ Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( \mu_i\phi_i,\, (1-\mu_i)\phi_i \right). \]

Define the observation-specific shape parameters

\[ a_i = \mu_i\phi_i \tag{5.9}\]

and

\[ b_i = (1-\mu_i)\phi_i. \tag{5.10}\]

Because

\[ a_i+b_i = \mu_i\phi_i + (1-\mu_i)\phi_i = \phi_i, \]

the conditional probability density function is

\[ f_Y \left( y_i;\mu_i,\phi_i \right) = \frac{ \Gamma(\phi_i) }{ \Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i) \Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right] } y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1} (1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1}, \]

for \(0<y_i<1\). The notation

\[ f_Y \left( y_i;\mu_i,\phi_i \right) \]

emphasizes that \(y_i\) is the observed response value, whereas \(\mu_i\) and \(\phi_i\) are parameters of its conditional Beta distribution.

Those two parameters are themselves determined by the regression coefficients:

\[ \mu_i = \frac{ \exp \left( \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\beta} \right) }{ 1+ \exp \left( \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\beta} \right) } \]

and

\[ \phi_i = \exp \left( \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\gamma} \right). \]

Hence, changing a coefficient in \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) changes the conditional mean and therefore changes the Beta density. Changing a coefficient in \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\) changes the precision and also changes the Beta density. Therefore, the likelihood must estimate the two coefficient blocks jointly.

For the initial running model, the precision submodel contains only an intercept. In that special case,

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i = 1 \]

for every observation and

\[ \phi_i = \exp(\gamma_0) = \phi. \]

Thus, all training observations share the same precision, while their conditional means can still differ across study time categories.

5.10.2 Likelihood

Suppose the \(n\) responses are conditionally independent given the regressors, as assumed in Section 5.9.1. Then, the joint conditional density is the product of the observation-specific Beta densities. Therefore, the likelihood for the parameter vectors is

\[ \mathcal{L} \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \mathbf{y} \right) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} f_Y \left( y_i; \mu_i,\phi_i \right). \]

where

\[ \mathbf{y} = (y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top \]

is the vector of observed training responses.

Substituting the Beta density gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L} \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \mathbf{y} \right) &= \prod_{i=1}^{n} \Bigg[ \frac{ \Gamma(\phi_i) }{ \Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i) \Gamma((1-\mu_i)\phi_i) } \times \\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1} (1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1} \Bigg]. \end{aligned} \tag{5.11}\]

Although the density in Equation 5.11 is written in terms of \(\mu_i\) and \(\phi_i\), the likelihood is ultimately a function of the regression coefficients because

\[ \mu_i = g^{-1} \left( \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\beta} \right) \]

and

\[ \phi_i = h^{-1} \left( \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\gamma} \right). \]

For the links used in this chapter,

\[ g^{-1}(\eta_i) = \frac{\exp(\eta_i)} {1+\exp(\eta_i)} \]

and

\[ h^{-1}(\zeta_i) = \exp(\zeta_i). \]

The maximum likelihood estimators are therefore defined by

\[ \left( \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \right) = \underset{ \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma} }{ \operatorname{arg\,max} } \; \mathcal{L} \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \mathbf{y} \right). \]

For the initial constant-precision model, the precision parameter vector reduces to the single parameter \(\gamma_0\). Hence,

\[ \left( \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \widehat{\gamma}_0 \right) = \underset{ \boldsymbol{\beta}, \gamma_0 }{ \operatorname{arg\,max} } \; \mathcal{L} \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \gamma_0; \mathbf{y} \right), \]

where

\[ \phi = \exp(\gamma_0). \]

This formulation is crucial for later model refinement. Allowing precision to depend on study time does not replace the likelihood with a different type of likelihood. It enlarges \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}\) and therefore allows \(\phi_i\) to vary systematically across observations.

5.10.3 Log-likelihood

Products of many probability densities can be inconvenient numerically. Maximum-likelihood software therefore works with the log-likelihood,

\[ \ell \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \mathbf{y} \right) = \log\left[ \mathcal{L} \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \gamma_0; \mathbf{y} \right)\right]. \]

Because the logarithm of a product is a sum,

\[ \log \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i \right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(a_i), \]

we obtain

\[ \ell \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \mathbf{y} \right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell_i \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; y_i \right), \]

where \(\ell_i(\cdot)\) is the contribution of observation \(i\).

We start from the conditional density:

\[ f_Y \left( y_i;\mu_i,\phi_i \right) = \frac{ \Gamma(\phi_i) }{ \Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i) \Gamma((1-\mu_i)\phi_i) } y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1} (1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1}. \]

Taking the logarithm gives

\[ \begin{aligned} \ell_i \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; y_i \right) &= \log \left\{ \frac{ \Gamma(\phi_i) }{ \Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i) \Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right] } \right\} + \\ &\qquad \log \left( y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1} \right) + \\ &\qquad \quad \log \left[ (1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1} \right]. \end{aligned} \]

Use

\[ \log\left(\frac{a}{bc}\right) = \log(a)-\log(b)-\log(c) \]

and

\[ \log(a^r) = r\log(a). \]

Then

\[ \begin{aligned} \ell_i \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; y_i \right) &= \log\left[\Gamma(\phi_i)\right] - \log\left[\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)\right] - \\ & \qquad \log\left\{\Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]\right\} + \\ &\qquad \quad (\mu_i\phi_i-1)\log(y_i) + \\ &\qquad \quad \quad [(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1] \log(1-y_i). \end{aligned} \tag{5.12}\]

Summing over all observations yields

\[ \begin{aligned} \ell \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \mathbf{y} \right) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell_i \left( \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; y_i \right) \\ &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big\{ \log\left[\Gamma(\phi_i)\right] - \log\left[\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)\right] - \log\left\{\Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]\right\} + \\ &\qquad (\mu_i\phi_i-1)\log(y_i) + \\ &\qquad \quad [(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1] \log(1-y_i) \Big\}. \end{aligned} \]

The dependence on the regression coefficients can be summarized as

\[ \boldsymbol{\beta} \longrightarrow \eta_i = \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T} \boldsymbol{\beta} \longrightarrow \mu_i = \frac{\exp(\eta_i)} {1+\exp(\eta_i)}, \]

and
