Figure 5.17 (or Figure 5.18) makes the effect of the variable-precision specification more concrete. For <1 hour, the observed and model-implied within-group SDs are 5.00 and 4.99 percentage points, respectively; for 1–3 hours, they are 5.01 and 5.00. Thus, the paired bars for the first two study-time categories nearly coincide. The agreement is less exact for the two higher-study-time categories. For 3–5 hours, the model-implied SD is 5.87 percentage points compared with an observed SD of 4.92; for 5+ hours, the corresponding values are 5.83 and 4.60. The fitted conditional distributions are therefore somewhat broader than the raw within-group spread in these two categories. Nevertheless, this adjustment is in the direction required to correct the much stronger under-dispersion imposed by the constant-precision model (see Figure 5.11), and it is consistent with the nearly unit quantile-residual SDs obtained after the refinement.

The fitted precision values themselves should not be interpreted as targets that must reproduce each raw group SD exactly. They are maximum-likelihood estimates chosen jointly with the mean parameters to represent the entire conditional Beta distribution. Holding the fitted mean fixed, a larger \(\phi_g\) corresponds to a more concentrated conditional distribution and a smaller \(\phi_g\) to a broader one. In the present model, the substantial decline in fitted precision across the study-time categories supplies the additional dispersion needed near the upper response boundary. These differences are features of the fitted conditional distribution; they should not be interpreted as evidence that study time causally changes the variability of student performance.

5.14.5 Influence and Leverage

We finish the adequacy screen by repeating the targeted case-deletion analysis for the revised model. Because Study Time supplies the same four-category design basis to both the mean and precision submodels, the ordinary design leverage remains simple. The more informative question is whether one of the largest quantile-residual cases materially changes either the four fitted means or the four fitted category-specific precisions.

As before, this is a sensitivity screen, not a hypothesis test or an automatic deletion rule.

  • R
  • Python
beta_variable_mean_design <- model.matrix(~ `Study Time`, data = training_data)
beta_variable_design_leverage <- rowSums(
  (beta_variable_mean_design %*% solve(crossprod(beta_variable_mean_design))) *
    beta_variable_mean_design)
beta_variable_screen_positions <- head(
  order(abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

beta_variable_reference <- beta_variable_residual_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(fitted_mean = first(fitted_mean_beta),
    fitted_precision = first(fitted_precision), .groups = "drop")

beta_variable_influence_screen <- bind_rows(lapply(
  beta_variable_screen_positions, function(position) {
    beta_variable_reduced_data <- training_data[-position, , drop = FALSE]
    beta_variable_reduced_model <- update(
      beta_variable_model, data = beta_variable_reduced_data)
    beta_variable_reduced_mean <- predict(
      beta_variable_reduced_model, type = "response")
    beta_variable_reduced_precision <- predict(
      beta_variable_reduced_model, type = "precision")
    beta_variable_reduced_reference <- beta_variable_reduced_data |>
      mutate(fitted_mean = beta_variable_reduced_mean,
        fitted_precision = beta_variable_reduced_precision) |>
      group_by(`Study Time`) |>
      summarise(fitted_mean = first(fitted_mean),
        fitted_precision = first(fitted_precision), .groups = "drop")

    tibble(`Training row` = position,
      `Study Time` = as.character(training_data$`Study Time`[position]),
      `Final grade (%)` = training_data$`Final Grade (%)`[position],
      `|Quantile residual|` = abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals[position]),
      `Design leverage` = beta_variable_design_leverage[position],
      `Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)` = beta_grade_scale_factor *
        max(abs(beta_variable_reduced_reference$fitted_mean -
          beta_variable_reference$fitted_mean)),
      `Max absolute relative precision change (%)` = 100 * max(abs(
        beta_variable_reduced_reference$fitted_precision /
          beta_variable_reference$fitted_precision - 1)))
  }))

beta_variable_max_design_leverage <- max(beta_variable_design_leverage)
beta_variable_max_mean_sensitivity <- max(
  beta_variable_influence_screen[["Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)"]])
beta_variable_max_phi_sensitivity <- max(
  beta_variable_influence_screen[["Max absolute relative precision change (%)"]])

beta_variable_influence_screen |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
beta_variable_mean_design = beta_variable_model.model.exog
beta_variable_design_leverage = np.einsum(
    "ij,jk,ik->i", beta_variable_mean_design,
    np.linalg.inv(beta_variable_mean_design.T @ beta_variable_mean_design),
    beta_variable_mean_design)
beta_variable_screen_positions = np.argsort(
    np.abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals))[-5:][::-1]

beta_variable_reference = beta_variable_residual_data.groupby(
    "Study Time", observed=True).agg(
        fitted_mean=("fitted_mean_beta", "first"),
        fitted_precision=("fitted_precision", "first")).reindex(study_time_levels)

beta_variable_influence_rows = []
for position in beta_variable_screen_positions:
    beta_variable_reduced_data = training_data.drop(training_data.index[position])
    beta_variable_reduced_model = BetaModel.from_formula(
        'grade_beta ~ C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
        data=beta_variable_reduced_data,
        exog_precision_formula=
            'C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
        link=sm.families.links.Logit(), link_precision=sm.families.links.Log(),
    ).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=1000, disp=False)
    beta_variable_reduced_mean = beta_variable_reduced_model.model.predict(
        beta_variable_reduced_model.params, which="mean")
    beta_variable_reduced_precision = beta_variable_reduced_model.model.predict(
        beta_variable_reduced_model.params, which="precision")
    beta_variable_reduced_reference = beta_variable_reduced_data[
        ["Study Time"]].copy()
    beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_mean"] = beta_variable_reduced_mean
    beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_precision"] = (
        beta_variable_reduced_precision)
    beta_variable_reduced_reference = beta_variable_reduced_reference.groupby(
        "Study Time", observed=True).agg(
            fitted_mean=("fitted_mean", "first"),
            fitted_precision=("fitted_precision", "first")).reindex(study_time_levels)

    beta_variable_influence_rows.append({
        "Training row": int(position + 1),
        "Study Time": str(training_data.iloc[position]["Study Time"]),
        "Final grade (%)": training_data.iloc[position]["Final Grade (%)"],
        "|Quantile residual|": abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals[position]),
        "Design leverage": beta_variable_design_leverage[position],
        "Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)": beta_grade_scale_factor *
            np.max(np.abs(beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_mean"]
                - beta_variable_reference["fitted_mean"])),
        "Max absolute relative precision change (%)": 100 * np.max(np.abs(
            beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_precision"]
            / beta_variable_reference["fitted_precision"] - 1)),
    })

beta_variable_influence_screen = pd.DataFrame(beta_variable_influence_rows)
beta_variable_max_design_leverage = beta_variable_design_leverage.max()
beta_variable_max_mean_sensitivity = beta_variable_influence_screen[
    "Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)"].max()
beta_variable_max_phi_sensitivity = beta_variable_influence_screen[
    "Max absolute relative precision change (%)"].max()
beta_variable_influence_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_variable_influence_screen, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")

The ordinary mean-design leverage remains uniformly low. Its largest value is only 0.0062, which is expected because the retained model uses the same four well-represented Study Time categories in both submodels. Hence, in Table 5.48, none of the five screened observations is unusual because of its regressor configuration. Instead, they are selected because their responses are unusual relative to their fitted conditional Beta distributions.

The case-deletion results show a clear difference between the stability of the conditional means and the stability of the precision parameters. Deleting any one of the five observations changes the four fitted mean grades by at most 0.133 percentage points, so the fitted mean structure is extremely stable. The largest sensitivity occurs for the 3–5 hours observation with the most extreme positive quantile residual: removing that single case changes at least one fitted category-specific precision by as much as 35.48%. The remaining screened cases produce appreciably smaller precision changes.

Note that this distinction is substantively important. The revised model’s mean component is not being driven by a handful of unusual observations, but the precision component is understandably more responsive to observations near the upper response boundary because it governs the concentration of the conditional distribution. In particular, the largest precision sensitivity is associated with an observation receiving a final grade of 100% in a category where such a response lies far into the fitted upper tail. This is consistent with the localized upper-tail departure that remained visible in the variable-precision Q-Q plot (see Figure 5.15).

These sensitivity values do not have universal cutoff thresholds, and a comparatively large relative change in one fitted precision is not, by itself, a reason to delete the corresponding observation. More importantly, the broader diagnostic evidence does not disappear because of this case: the fitted means remain stable, the group-specific quantile-residual SDs are now approximately equal, and the systematic increase in residual dispersion seen under constant precision has been substantially removed. Thus, we retain all observations and interpret the case-deletion result as evidence of localized precision sensitivity, not as evidence that the overall variable-precision refinement is being driven by a single case.

5.14.6 Variable-precision Model Practical Adequacy Summary

The repeated training-stage diagnostics now assess the focused Study Time mean + Study Time precision model selected in Section 5.13.4 and retained after the parsimony check in Section 5.13.5. The summarized diagnostic conclusions are shown in Table 5.50.

Taken together, the diagnostics show that the targeted precision refinement addresses the main structural inadequacy of the initial model without introducing unsupported complexity into the mean submodel. The conditional means remain well represented, and the group-specific quantile-residual SDs are now essentially equal across the four Study Time categories. This is a substantial improvement over the constant-precision model, where residual dispersion increased systematically with the fitted conditional mean.

The revised model is not diagnostically perfect. The Q-Q plot, from Figure 5.15, still shows several localized upper-tail departures, and the response-scale precision diagnostic shows that the fitted distributions for 3–5 hours and 5+ hours are somewhat broader than their raw within-group grade spread. In addition, the case-deletion screen identifies one extreme observation for which a fitted precision is noticeably sensitive. These remaining features are important to report, but they do not reproduce the systematic across-group failure that motivated the refinement: the fitted means remain highly stable, the residual spreads are now approximately comparable, and the overall dispersion pattern is no longer driven by the constant-precision restriction.

The likelihood-ratio test in Section 5.13.4 provides formal training-stage evidence in favour of allowing precision to depend on Study Time, while the separate mean-complexity test in Section 5.13.5 does not support retaining the additional 18 mean coefficients. The diagnostic evidence is therefore coherent with the model-development decisions: retain the focused Study Time mean structure, retain Study Time-dependent precision, and do not reopen the larger mean model.

No finite collection of diagnostics can establish that a fitted model is literally correct. The practical question is whether any remaining departure is sufficiently large, systematic, or structurally interpretable to justify another round of model development before examining the testing outcomes. Here, the remaining issues are localized rather than systematic, and no comparably strong unresolved pattern emerges that would motivate another specification change.

Thus, we judge the Study Time mean + Study Time precision Beta regression to be adequate enough to freeze as the final specification. From this point onward, the response transformation, mean and precision structures, links, treatment coding, and prediction targets should remain fixed. The frozen model can now be carried forward to the final inferential analysis and the held-out predictive evaluation without using the testing outcomes to alter the specification.

5.15 Freezing the Final Specification

At this point, the training-stage model-development process is complete. The variable-precision model addressed the main distributional inadequacy of the initial constant-precision fit, while the separate complexity check did not support expanding the mean submodel beyond Study Time. Thus, we freeze the complete analysis specification before examining the testing outcomes.

Freezing applies to more than the regression formula. It also fixes the response definition, links, category coding, predictive baseline, evaluation scales, predictive metrics, interval level, and distributional calibration diagnostic. The testing responses may later be used to evaluate the pre-specified inferential and predictive questions, but they cannot be used to revise any of these choices.

The distinction between the modelling scale and the reporting scale is critical. The Beta likelihood, NLPD, and PIT calculations use the transformed response grade_beta, because this is the response on \((0,1)\) for which the fitted Beta distribution is defined. By contrast, conditional-mean point predictions and predictive-interval endpoints will be translated back to the original grade-percentage scale for interpretation. Because the boundary transformation was fixed before the split, neither the final model nor the baseline may use a different transformation after the testing outcomes are examined.

5.15.1 Pre-specified Point-Prediction Assessment

For a held-out student \(i\), let \(g_i\) denote the observed final grade in percentage points and let \(\widehat{g}_i\) denote the conditional-mean prediction obtained from the training-fitted variable-precision model after reversing the fixed boundary transformation. If

\[ e_i = g_i-\widehat{g}_i, \]

then the point-prediction metrics are

\[ \operatorname{ME} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}}e_i, \tag{5.26}\]

\[ \operatorname{MAE} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}}|e_i|, \tag{5.27}\]

and

\[ \operatorname{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}}e_i^2 }. \tag{5.28}\]

All three quantities are evaluated on the original grade-percentage scale. With the sign convention in Equation 5.26, a positive ME indicates average underprediction, whereas a negative ME indicates average overprediction. MAE describes the typical absolute size of the prediction error, while RMSE gives comparatively greater weight to larger errors. MAE and RMSE therefore assess the accuracy of the predicted conditional mean; they do not assess whether the fitted Beta distribution represents predictive dispersion appropriately.

The inverse transformation used to recover the percentage-scale point prediction is also frozen. If \(\widehat{\mu}_i\) is the predicted conditional mean on the transformed Beta scale and \(n\) is the full-sample value fixed in Section 5.5.3, then

\[ \widehat{g}_i = 100 \left( \frac{n\widehat{\mu}_i-0.5}{n-1} \right). \tag{5.29}\]

5.15.2 Pre-specified Probabilistic Predictive Assessment

Beta regression provides an entire fitted conditional distribution, not only \(\widehat{\mu}_i\). For each held-out student, the frozen training model will produce

\[ \widehat{\mu}_i, \qquad \widehat{\phi}_i, \]

and therefore the fitted Beta shape parameters

\[ \widehat{\alpha}_i = \widehat{\mu}_i\widehat{\phi}_i, \qquad \widehat{\beta}_i = (1-\widehat{\mu}_i)\widehat{\phi}_i. \]

Definition of plug-in predictive distribution

A plug-in predictive distribution uses parameter estimates obtained from the training data and then treats those fitted values as fixed when predicting or evaluating new observations. Here, the training-fitted values \(\widehat{\mu}_i\) and \(\widehat{\phi}_i\) determine a Beta distribution for each held-out student.

This distribution represents conditional response variability under the fitted model, but it does not integrate over uncertainty in the estimated regression coefficients or precision parameters. Hence, it is different from a Bayesian posterior predictive distribution, which averages over parameter uncertainty.

Our primary probabilistic score will be NLPD. For the transformed held-out response \(y_i=\texttt{grade\_beta}_i\),

\[ \operatorname{NLPD}_i = -\log f_{\operatorname{Beta}} \left( y_i; \widehat{\alpha}_i, \widehat{\beta}_i \right), \tag{5.30}\]

and the testing-set summary is

\[ \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}} = -\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} \log f_{\operatorname{Beta}} \left( y_i; \widehat{\alpha}_i, \widehat{\beta}_i \right). \tag{5.31}\]

Unlike MAE and RMSE, NLPD evaluates the entire fitted conditional Beta distribution through the predictive density assigned to the response that actually occurs. More precisely, the observation-specific quantity in Equation 5.30 is the negative of the logarithmic score. For a predictive density \(p(\cdot)\) and realized outcome \(\omega\), Gneiting and Raftery (2007) define the logarithmic score as \(\operatorname{LogS}(p,\omega)=\log p(\omega)\) and show that it is strictly proper. Strict propriety means that, in expectation, the score is optimized by issuing the predictive distribution that corresponds to the data-generating distribution rather than a different one.

In our loss-oriented formulation, NLPD changes the sign of the logarithmic score, so smaller values are better. Consequently, a fitted Beta distribution receives a larger penalty when it assigns little density to a response that actually occurs. This can happen because its conditional mean is poorly located or because its dispersion is poorly represented: an overly concentrated distribution may assign very little density to even a modest departure from its fitted mean, whereas an unnecessarily diffuse distribution spreads its density more broadly.

In our frequentist setting, we apply NLPD to the plug-in held-out predictive distributions produced by the frozen training model. Thus, the fitted parameters are estimated from the training data and then treated as fixed when the testing responses are evaluated. When competing models are assessed on the same held-out observations, response definition, and transformation, a smaller mean NLPD indicates better probabilistic predictive performance.

Heads-up on interpreting NLPD!

A negative NLPD is possible because NLPD uses a probability density, not a probability. Let us recall that a probability must lie between \(0\) and \(1\). However, a PDF is a height of a density curve and can be greater than \(1\). What must equal \(1\) is the total area under the PDF curve, not its maximum height. This is especially easy to encounter for distributions defined on a short interval such as the Beta distribution on \((0,1)\). For example, suppose the fitted Beta distribution assigns density

\[ f_{\operatorname{Beta}}(y_i;\widehat{\alpha}_i,\widehat{\beta}_i)=3 \]

to an observed held-out response. Then

\[ \operatorname{NLPD}_i = -\log(3) \approx -1.10. \]

The negative value does not mean that the model assigned a negative probability. It means that the observed response occurred at a location where the fitted continuous density was relatively high. Conversely, if the fitted density at the observed response were only \(0.01\), then

\[ -\log(0.01)\approx 4.61, \]

which is much larger and indicates that the model assigned very little predictive density to what actually occurred.

Thus, NLPD is not bounded below by \(0\) for continuous responses, and a negative observation-specific or mean NLPD is not a computational error. This follows because NLPD is the negative logarithm of a density, and a continuous density can exceed \(1\).

The key interpretation is comparative:

Smaller NLPD is better when models are evaluated on the same held-out observations, using the same response definition and transformation.

Gneiting and Raftery (2007) define the logarithmic score for predictive densities as \(\operatorname{LogS}(p,\omega)=\log p(\omega)\) and show that it is strictly proper; they also emphasize that average scores for competing forecasting procedures are directly comparable when they refer to the same set of forecast situations.

Finally, testing NLPD should not be confused with the negative training log-likelihood used to estimate the model. Their mathematical forms are similar, but the training likelihood is evaluated on observations used for estimation, whereas held-out NLPD evaluates new responses using the already-frozen training-derived model. Gneiting and Raftery’s discussion of plug-in maximum-likelihood scoring and cross-validation provides the corresponding predictive-scoring framework (Gneiting and Raftery 2007).

The full model will be compared with the pre-specified intercept-only Beta baseline. Both models will be fitted using the training data only and evaluated on exactly the same testing observations. The baseline has no Study Time terms in either submodel, so it provides one training-derived conditional mean and one training-derived precision. It therefore supplies a deliberately simple reference for both point prediction and full-distribution prediction.

5.15.3 Pre-specified Predictive Intervals and Calibration

NLPD is complemented by a direct assessment of predictive uncertainty. For each held-out student, the frozen model will produce the equal-tailed 90% plug-in predictive interval

\[ \left[ F_{\operatorname{Beta}}^{-1} \left( 0.05; \widehat{\alpha}_i, \widehat{\beta}_i \right), \, F_{\operatorname{Beta}}^{-1} \left( 0.95; \widehat{\alpha}_i, \widehat{\beta}_i \right) \right]. \tag{5.32}\]

The endpoints will be transformed back to the original grade-percentage scale for reporting. We will summarize the intervals using empirical coverage, the proportion of held-out grades falling inside their intervals, and average interval width, reported in percentage points. Coverage and width must be interpreted together: very wide intervals can attain high coverage while still providing weak predictive resolution.

Finally, predictive calibration will be assessed using the PIT. For a continuous random variable with CDF \(F(\cdot)\), evaluating the CDF at a realization from that distribution produces a \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) random variable. Rosenblatt (1952) formalized a multivariate extension of this transformation, mapping an absolutely continuous multivariate distribution to a Uniform distribution on the unit hypercube. In predictive-distribution evaluation, Diebold, Gunther, and Tay used the PIT as the basis of a general framework for assessing density forecasts (Diebold, Gunther, and Tay 1998), and Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery subsequently placed PIT diagnostics within a broader framework for assessing probabilistic calibration (Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery 2007).

For each held-out observation,

\[ \operatorname{PIT}_i = F_{\operatorname{Beta}} \left( y_i; \widehat{\alpha}_i, \widehat{\beta}_i \right). \tag{5.33}\]

If the frozen conditional predictive distributions represent the held-out responses well, their PIT values should be approximately \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\). Diebold, Gunther, and Tay show that correctly specified continuous conditional density forecasts generate Uniform PIT values, while Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery relate PIT Uniformity directly to probabilistic calibration (Diebold, Gunther, and Tay 1998; Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery 2007).

Departures from Uniformity can therefore reveal aspects of predictive-distribution miscalibration. The shape of the PIT histogram can also be informative about the nature of those departures. However, PIT Uniformity should not be treated as a standalone model-acceptance criterion: a Uniform PIT distribution is a necessary but not sufficient condition for an ideal probabilistic forecast, and apparently Uniform PIT histograms can occur even for defective forecasting procedures (Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery 2007). Accordingly, we interpret the PIT histogram as one diagnostic component of the broader held-out predictive assessment rather than converting it into a single accept-or-reject test (Diebold, Gunther, and Tay 1998).

We pre-specify a PIT histogram with ten equal-width bins on \([0,1]\) as the main held-out calibration diagnostic. Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery (2007) note that 10 or 20 bins generally provide an adequate display for PIT histograms. Our use of ten bins is therefore a pre-specified visualization choice, not a claim that ten is a theoretically optimal number of bins.

Table 5.52 summarizes the complementary roles of the frozen predictive criteria.

The freeze is now complete. Testing outcomes cannot be used to change the response transformation, model terms, links, reference category, baseline, point metrics, probabilistic score, predictive-interval level, or calibration diagnostic. For prediction, the current training-fitted variable-precision model will remain fixed when the testing regressors are supplied. For inference, the same frozen model specification may later be refitted to the testing data for the protected inferential analysis, but those results will not reopen model development.

5.16 Interpreting Beta Regression Coefficients

The final Beta regression specification is now frozen, but its coefficients still require careful interpretation. In particular, the logit link used for the conditional mean creates algebra that resembles Binary Logistic regression while referring to a fundamentally different quantity. Here,

\[ \mu_i = \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i) \]

is the conditional mean of a continuous response on \((0,1)\); it is not the probability of a binary event.

The frozen model contains Study Time in both submodels. This section focuses on the mean-submodel coefficients \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_3\), because the chapter’s inferential inquiry concerns differences in conditional mean final grade. The precision coefficients \(\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_3\) retain the distributional interpretation established in Section 5.13.2: after exponentiation, they describe multiplicative differences in fitted precision, not changes in the conditional mean.

To keep the split workflow intact, the numerical examples below use the already fitted training model beta_variable_model. They illustrate how to read the frozen specification; they are not the chapter’s final inferential estimates. As established in Section 5.6.4, the protected coefficient estimates, model-based SEs, CIs, and original-scale inferential contrasts will later come from the same frozen specification refitted to the testing data.

5.16.1 Logit-mean Scale

For the frozen mean submodel,

\[ \operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) = \log\left( \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} \right) = \beta_0+\beta_1x_{i,1}+\beta_2x_{i,2}+\beta_3x_{i,3}, \tag{5.34}\]

where the three indicators represent 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours, with <1 hour as the reference category. Thus,

\[ \beta_0 = \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}), \]

while

\[ \begin{aligned} \beta_1 &= \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{1\text{–}3}) - \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}),\\ \beta_2 &= \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{3\text{–}5}) - \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}),\\ \beta_3 &= \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{5+}) - \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}). \end{aligned} \]

Because Study Time is the only regressor in the frozen mean submodel, these are direct category contrasts. There are no additional mean regressors that need to be held fixed when describing the three comparisons.

Heads-up on interpreting continuous regressors!

Although the running model contains no continuous mean regressor, the same coefficient logic is important more generally. Suppose a Beta-regression mean submodel contains a continuous regressor \(x_j\) linearly and without an interaction or nonlinear transformation:

\[ \operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) = \beta_0+\beta_jx_{i,j}+\cdots. \]

Then, comparing two otherwise model-comparable observations whose values of \(x_j\) differ by \(\Delta\),

\[ \Delta\operatorname{logit}(\mu) = \beta_j\Delta. \]

For a one-unit increase, \(\Delta=1\), so the fitted logit of the conditional mean changes by \(\beta_j\), holding the other included regressors fixed. The meaning of one unit is determined by how the regressor enters the model; if it has been rescaled, the coefficient must be interpreted in those rescaled units.

This interpretation does not automatically carry over when the systematic component is more complicated. If the same continuous regressor also appears through a quadratic term, another nonlinear transformation, or an interaction, its fitted change generally depends on its starting value and/or the value of the interacting regressor. In that setting, a meaningful finite contrast should be constructed from the complete linear predictor rather than interpreting one coefficient in isolation.

5.16.2 Exponentiated Coefficients

Exponentiating Equation 5.34 gives

\[ \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} = \exp\left( \beta_0+\beta_1x_{i,1}+\beta_2x_{i,2}+\beta_3x_{i,3} \right). \tag{5.35}\]

The quantity

\[ \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} \]

is the ratio of the conditional mean proportion to its complement. We will refer to this transformation as the conditional-mean odds for convenience. For a treatment-coded category \(g\) relative to the reference category,

\[ \frac{ \mu_g/(1-\mu_g) }{ \mu_{<1}/(1-\mu_{<1}) } = \exp(\beta_g). \tag{5.36}\]

Therefore, \(\exp(\beta_g)\) is the multiplicative factor relating the two categories on the conditional-mean-odds scale.

The same result applies to a continuous regressor that enters linearly and without interactions. For a change of \(\Delta\) units in \(x_j\),

\[ \frac{ \mu(x_j+\Delta)/[1-\mu(x_j+\Delta)] }{ \mu(x_j)/[1-\mu(x_j)] } = \exp(\beta_j\Delta), \]

holding the other included regressors fixed. A one-unit change therefore multiplies the conditional-mean odds by \(\exp(\beta_j)\).

Heads-up: this is not an event odds ratio!

The algebra in Equation 5.35 resembles Binary Logistic regression, but the object being transformed is different. In Binary Logistic regression, \(\pi_i\) is the probability of an event, so \(\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)\) represents event odds. In this Beta regression,

\[ \mu_i = \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i) \]

is the conditional mean of a continuous grade proportion. Hence,

\[ \frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i} \]

is a transformation of that conditional mean, not the odds of an event.

Consequently, \(\exp(\beta_j)\) should not be described as “the odds ratio of receiving a higher grade”, “the odds of success”, or any similar event-based statement. It is a multiplicative change in \(\mu/(1-\mu)\). For substantive communication, the fitted conditional mean on the original grade-percentage scale will usually be more intuitive.

5.16.3 Study Time Category Contrasts

We can now apply these rules to the frozen training fit. The first four elements of beta_variable_parameters are the mean-submodel coefficients; the remaining four belong to the precision submodel.

  • R
  • Python
beta_mean_parameters <- beta_variable_parameters[1:4]
beta_mean_exponentiated <- exp(beta_mean_parameters)
stopifnot(length(beta_mean_parameters) == 4L)

beta_mean_interpretation <- tibble(
  Term = c("Intercept (<1 hour)", "1–3 hours vs <1 hour",
    "3–5 hours vs <1 hour", "5+ hours vs <1 hour"),
  Estimate = beta_mean_parameters,
  `Exponentiated coefficient` = beta_mean_exponentiated)

beta_mean_interpretation |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = c("c", "c", "c"))
beta_mean_parameters = beta_variable_parameters[:4]
beta_mean_exponentiated = np.exp(beta_mean_parameters)
assert beta_mean_parameters.size == 4

beta_mean_interpretation = pd.DataFrame({
    "Term": [
        "Intercept (<1 hour)", "1–3 hours vs <1 hour",
        "3–5 hours vs <1 hour", "5+ hours vs <1 hour"],
    "Estimate": beta_mean_parameters,
    "Exponentiated coefficient": beta_mean_exponentiated,
})
beta_mean_interpretation_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_mean_interpretation, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")

The intercept in Table 5.53 is the fitted logit of the conditional mean grade proportion for students in the <1 hour reference category. Its exponentiated value is the fitted conditional-mean odds for that category; it is not a comparison with another study-time category. The remaining rows are contrasts with <1 hour. For 1–3 hours, \(\widehat{\beta}_1=\text{0.457}\), so the fitted conditional-mean odds are multiplied by 1.580 relative to <1 hour. For 3–5 hours, the corresponding multiplier is 3.022, and for 5+ hours it is 5.050.

These comparisons require no “holding the other regressors fixed” clause because the frozen mean model contains no other regressor. They are also reference-category comparisons, not statements that moving an individual student from one study-time category to another would cause the stated change in grade. The coefficients describe fitted conditional-mean differences across the categories represented in the model. Changing the treatment-coding reference category would change the individual coefficient values and reverse some comparison directions, but it would not change the fitted conditional means themselves. For example, the contrast from <1 hour to 5+ hours is \(\beta_3\), whereas the reverse contrast is \(-\beta_3\); the corresponding exponentiated values are reciprocals.

5.16.4 Meaningful Conditional-mean Contrasts

The coefficient and exponentiated-coefficient scales (as in Table 5.53) are mathematically useful, but neither is the most natural scale for communicating final-grade differences. Because the logit link is nonlinear, a fixed change in the logit of \(\mu\) does not correspond to a fixed percentage-point change in the conditional mean.

For the <1 hour reference category,

\[ \mu_{<1} = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0), \]

while, for a non-reference study-time category \(g\),

\[ \mu_g = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_g). \tag{5.37}\]

The frozen boundary transformation must then be reversed to express the fitted conditional mean in the original grade-percentage units. Using the full-sample value of \(n\) fixed in Section 5.5.3,

\[ \widehat{g}_g = 100 \times \left( \frac{n\widehat{\mu}_g-0.5}{n-1} \right). \tag{5.38}\]

Heads-up on returning to the original grade scale!

The expression in Equation 5.38 comes directly from reversing the boundary transformation introduced in Section 5.5.3. Recall from Equation 5.2 that the original rescaled grade proportion \(y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}\) was transformed to the Beta-regression modelling scale as

\[ y_i = \frac{ y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1)+0.5 }{ n }. \]

To recover the original proportion, solve this equation for \(y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}\). Multiplying by \(n\) gives

\[ ny_i = y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1)+0.5, \]

so

\[ ny_i-0.5 = y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1), \]

and therefore

\[ y_i^{\mathrm{raw}} = \frac{ny_i-0.5}{n-1}. \]

The fitted quantity \(\widehat{\mu}_g\) is the conditional mean of the transformed Beta-regression response for study-time category \(g\). Because the Smithson–Verkuilen transformation is affine (i.e., a linear rescaling plus a constant shift), the same inverse transformation applies exactly to the conditional mean:

\[ \widehat{\mu}_g^{\mathrm{raw}} = \frac{ n\widehat{\mu}_g-0.5 }{ n-1 }. \]

Finally, \(y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}\) is a proportion, whereas the original final grade is expressed as a percentage. Multiplying by \(100\) gives

\[ \widehat{g}_g = 100 \times \left( \frac{ n\widehat{\mu}_g-0.5 }{ n-1 } \right), \]

which is precisely Equation 5.38.

The same full-sample value of \(n\) fixed before the training/testing split is used here. We do not estimate or recompute a new value of \(n\) when interpreting fitted means or making held-out predictions.

A percentage-point contrast between any two study-time categories \(g\) and \(h\) is therefore

\[ \widehat{\Delta}_{g,h} = \widehat{g}_g-\widehat{g}_h. \tag{5.39}\]

This formulation is not restricted to the treatment-coding reference category. Once the fitted means have been obtained, any scientifically useful pairwise contrast can be formed directly on the original grade scale.

The training-stage fitted means already computed in Section 5.14.2 provide the following interpretation of the frozen model.

  • R
  • Python
beta_mean_fitted <- beta_variable_mean_calibration |>
  transmute(`Study Time`,
    `Fitted conditional mean grade (%)` = `Fitted mean grade (%)`)
beta_mean_reference_grade <- beta_mean_fitted[["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]][1]
beta_mean_fitted <- beta_mean_fitted |>
  mutate(`Difference vs <1 hour (percentage points)` =
    `Fitted conditional mean grade (%)` - beta_mean_reference_grade)

beta_mean_fitted |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = c("c", "c", "c"))
beta_mean_fitted = beta_variable_mean_calibration.loc[
    :, ["Study Time", "Fitted mean grade (%)"]].copy()
beta_mean_fitted = beta_mean_fitted.rename(columns={
    "Fitted mean grade (%)": "Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"})
beta_mean_reference_grade = beta_mean_fitted.loc[
    0, "Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]
beta_mean_fitted["Difference vs <1 hour (percentage points)"] = (
    beta_mean_fitted["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]
    - beta_mean_reference_grade)
beta_mean_fitted_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_mean_fitted, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")

According to Table 5.55, on the original grade scale, the frozen training model estimates conditional mean grades of 65.78% for <1 hour, 75.24% for 1–3 hours, 85.34% for 3–5 hours, and 90.70% for 5+ hours. Then, relative to <1 hour, these correspond to fitted differences of 9.46, 19.56, and 24.91 percentage points for 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours, respectively. These original-scale contrasts are the most direct substantive description of how the fitted conditional mean grade differs across the four study-time categories.

The conditional-mean contrasts should not be mistaken for complete descriptions of the fitted conditional distributions. In the frozen model, Study Time also enters the precision submodel, so categories can differ in both centre and spread. The quantities in Table 5.55 isolate the mean component; predictive-distribution comparisons later in the chapter will use both \(\widehat{\mu}\) and \(\widehat{\phi}\).

For the final inferential analysis, these same original-scale fitted means and percentage-point contrasts will be recomputed from the testing-set refit of the frozen specification and accompanied by model-based CIs where appropriate. Those intervals must propagate the joint uncertainty in the relevant mean-submodel coefficients through the nonlinear inverse-logit transformation. In particular, a CI for an exponentiated coefficient is not a CI for a percentage-point difference. Hence, we reserve the final CIs and inferential claims for the protected testing-stage analysis rather than treating the training-fit values above as final evidence.

5.17 Prediction with Beta Regression

The model-development stage is complete and the specification has been frozen. We can therefore turn to the chapter’s predictive inquiry without reopening any modelling decisions. As established in Section 5.6.4, prediction uses the variable-precision model already fitted to the training data. The testing regressors determine which fitted conditional distribution applies to each held-out student, but the testing responses do not enter the prediction calculations themselves.

Throughout this section, a hat denotes a quantity obtained from that frozen training fit. Thus, \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) and \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\) are the maximum-likelihood parameter estimates obtained from the training data, following the estimation framework in Section 5.10. Quantities such as \(\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}\) and \(\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}\) are then computed from those same fitted coefficients for a new student’s regressor values. We therefore retain the notation established earlier rather than introducing an additional train superscript.

Because the frozen model contains Study Time in both the mean and precision submodels, a prediction consists of more than one number. For a new or held-out student, the model supplies a fitted conditional mean, a fitted precision, and therefore an entire conditional Beta distribution from which predictive quantiles and intervals can be obtained.

5.17.1 What Does Beta Regression Predict?

Let \(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}\) denote the intercept-augmented mean-submodel design vector for a new student. Under the frozen treatment coding,

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1\\ x_{\mathrm{new},1}\\ x_{\mathrm{new},2}\\ x_{\mathrm{new},3} \end{pmatrix}, \]

where the leading \(1\) represents the intercept and \(x_{\mathrm{new},1}\), \(x_{\mathrm{new},2}\), and \(x_{\mathrm{new},3}\) are the indicators for 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours, respectively. Thus,

\[ \begin{aligned} <1\text{ hour:}&\quad \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}} = (1,0,0,0)^\mathsf{T},\\ 1\text{–}3\text{ hours:}&\quad \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}} = (1,1,0,0)^\mathsf{T},\\ 3\text{–}5\text{ hours:}&\quad \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}} = (1,0,1,0)^\mathsf{T},\\ 5+\text{ hours:}&\quad \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}} = (1,0,0,1)^\mathsf{T}. \end{aligned} \]

With

\[ \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \begin{pmatrix} \widehat{\beta}_0\\ \widehat{\beta}_1\\ \widehat{\beta}_2\\ \widehat{\beta}_3 \end{pmatrix}, \]

the fitted mean linear predictor is

\[ \widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}^\mathsf{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \]

and therefore

\[ \widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}} = g^{-1} \left( \widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right) = \operatorname{logit}^{-1} \left( \widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right). \tag{5.40}\]

Following the intercept-augmented notation introduced in Equation 5.8, let \(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}\) denote the precision-submodel design vector for the same new student:

\[ \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1\\ z_{\mathrm{new},1}\\ z_{\mathrm{new},2}\\ z_{\mathrm{new},3} \end{pmatrix}. \]

In the frozen model, the same three Study Time indicators enter both submodels. Hence,

\[ z_{\mathrm{new},j} = x_{\mathrm{new},j}, \qquad j=1,2,3, \]

so \(\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}\) and \(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}\) have the same numerical entries for a given student. We retain separate symbols because they represent design vectors for different submodels.

With

\[ \widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} = \begin{pmatrix} \widehat{\gamma}_0\\ \widehat{\gamma}_1\\ \widehat{\gamma}_2\\ \widehat{\gamma}_3 \end{pmatrix}, \]

the fitted precision linear predictor is

\[ \widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}^\mathsf{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}, \]

and therefore

\[ \widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}} = h^{-1} \left( \widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right) = \exp \left( \widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right). \tag{5.41}\]

Together, \(\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}\) and \(\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}\) determine the fitted conditional Beta distribution. Thus, Beta regression can provide several related predictive quantities as shown in Table 5.57.

The distinction between the point prediction and the realized response is central. The conditional mean answers:

Where is the fitted distribution centred?

On the other hand, the precision and full Beta distribution answer:

How much conditional variation does the fitted model allow around that centre?

Then, predictive quantiles and intervals summarize particular features of that distribution.

5.17.2 Manual Prediction for a New Observation

Consider a new student whose Study Time category is 3–5 hours. Under the treatment coding fixed in Section 5.13.2, this student has

\[ x_{1}=0,\qquad x_{2}=1,\qquad x_{3}=0. \]

Because the same indicators enter the precision submodel, the corresponding precision indicators are also \((0,1,0)\). The fitted mean and precision linear predictors are therefore

\[ \widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_2 \]

and

\[ \widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widehat{\gamma}_0+\widehat{\gamma}_2. \]

The following calculations use only the coefficients already estimated from the training data.

  • R
  • Python
beta_precision_parameters <- beta_variable_parameters[5:8]
beta_manual_eta <- beta_mean_parameters[1] + beta_mean_parameters[3]
beta_manual_mu <- plogis(beta_manual_eta)
beta_manual_zeta <- beta_precision_parameters[1] + beta_precision_parameters[3]
beta_manual_phi <- exp(beta_manual_zeta)
beta_manual_alpha <- beta_manual_mu * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_beta_shape <- (1 - beta_manual_mu) * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_grade <- beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_manual_mu + beta_grade_scale_offset

stopifnot(length(beta_precision_parameters) == 4L, beta_manual_mu > 0,
  beta_manual_mu < 1, beta_manual_phi > 0)
from scipy.special import expit

beta_precision_parameters = beta_variable_parameters[4:8]
beta_manual_eta = beta_mean_parameters[0] + beta_mean_parameters[2]
beta_manual_mu = expit(beta_manual_eta)
beta_manual_zeta = beta_precision_parameters[0] + beta_precision_parameters[2]
beta_manual_phi = np.exp(beta_manual_zeta)
beta_manual_alpha = beta_manual_mu * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_beta_shape = (1 - beta_manual_mu) * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_grade = (
    beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_manual_mu + beta_grade_scale_offset)

assert beta_precision_parameters.size == 4
assert 0 < beta_manual_mu < 1 and beta_manual_phi > 0

For this student, the training-fitted mean linear predictor is

\[ \widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_2 = \text{1.759}, \]

so the inverse-logit transformation gives

\[ \widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}} = \operatorname{logit}^{-1} \left( \widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right) = \text{0.8531}. \]

For precision,

\[ \widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widehat{\gamma}_0+\widehat{\gamma}_2 = \text{3.567}, \]

and the inverse log link gives

\[ \widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}} = \exp\left( \widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right) = \text{35.39}. \]

The implied Beta shape parameters are therefore

\[ \widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}} \widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}} = \text{30.19} \]

and

\[ \widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \left( 1-\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}} \right) \widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}} = \text{5.20}. \]

Finally, applying the inverse boundary transformation already derived in Section 5.16.4 gives the predicted conditional mean on the original grade scale:

\[ \widehat{g}_{\mathrm{new}} = \text{85.34}\%. \]

This final percentage is the conditional-mean point prediction. It summarizes the centre of the fitted distribution, but it does not describe the range of individual grades that the model regards as plausible.

5.17.3 Predictive Distribution

The full plug-in predictive distribution combines the fitted mean and precision from the training-fitted frozen model. Using the augmented-vector notation introduced in Equation 5.8,

\[ Y_{\mathrm{new}} \mid \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}, \widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}; \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( \widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}}, \widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right), \]

where

\[ \widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}} = \widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}} \widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}} = \left( 1-\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}} \right) \widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}. \tag{5.42}\]

For the 3–5 hours example,

\[ Y_{\mathrm{new}} \mid \texttt{Study Time}=\texttt{3–5 hours} \sim \operatorname{Beta} \left( \text{30.19}, \text{5.20} \right). \]

To visualize this distribution on the original grade-percentage scale, we evaluate the fitted density over a fine grid of grades. Because this is a density for the reported grade scale, the Beta density on the modelling scale is transformed through the same affine map discussed in Section 5.16.4.

  • R
  • Python
beta_manual_grade_grid <- seq(0, 100, length.out = 1000)
beta_manual_beta_grid <- (
  beta_manual_grade_grid - beta_grade_scale_offset
) / beta_grade_scale_factor
beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data <- tibble(
  grade = beta_manual_grade_grid,
  density = dbeta(
    beta_manual_beta_grid,
    shape1 = beta_manual_alpha,
    shape2 = beta_manual_beta_shape
  ) / beta_grade_scale_factor
)
beta_manual_density_ymax <- 1.05 * max(
  beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data$density
)

Figure 5.19 (or Figure 5.20) shows the entire plug-in predictive distribution, not just its centre. The orange line marks the predicted conditional mean grade of 85.34%, while the curve height indicates how strongly the fitted model concentrates probability density around different grade values. A taller, narrower curve would correspond to a larger fitted precision, and a flatter, broader curve would correspond to a smaller one.

The point prediction \(\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}\) tells us only the conditional centre. The fitted Beta distribution adds information about conditional dispersion, asymmetry, and tail behaviour. Two predictions can have similar conditional means but very different predictive distributions if their fitted precisions differ. This is precisely why the chapter froze both a mean submodel and a precision submodel, and why the later held-out evaluation includes NLPD, predictive-interval coverage and width, and PIT rather than relying only on MAE or RMSE.

As previously defined, this is a plug-in predictive distribution. The training-estimated coefficients are treated as fixed when the new response is predicted. Hence, the distribution represents conditional response variability under the frozen fitted model; it does not integrate over uncertainty in the estimated coefficients.

5.17.4 Prediction Intervals / Predictive Quantiles

A predictive quantile is obtained directly from the fitted conditional Beta CDF. For probability level \(p\),

\[ \widehat{q}_{p,\mathrm{new}} = F_{\operatorname{Beta}}^{-1} \left( p; \widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}}, \widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}} \right). \tag{5.43}\]

The frozen evaluation plan uses an equal-tailed 90% plug-in predictive interval, so the modelling-scale endpoints are

\[ \left[ \widehat{q}_{0.05,\mathrm{new}}, \widehat{q}_{0.95,\mathrm{new}} \right]. \]

For the manual 3–5 hours example, we now compute those quantiles and display them on the predictive-density plot.

  • R
  • Python

  beta_manual_interval_beta + beta_grade_scale_offset

  mutate(in_interval = dplyr::between(
    grade,
    beta_manual_interval_grade[1],
    beta_manual_interval_grade[2]

The resulting 90% plug-in predictive interval is 74.65% to 93.75% on the original grade scale. In Figure 5.21 (or Figure 5.22), the dashed green lines mark the 5th and 95th predictive quantiles, and the shaded region between them contains 90% of the fitted predictive probability. The orange line remains the predicted conditional mean, making it easy to distinguish the distribution’s centre from its predictive spread. Under the fitted plug-in Beta distribution, 90% of the predictive probability lies between those two conditional quantiles. This is the nominal interval probability under the fitted distribution; empirical coverage will be evaluated later using the frozen testing set. Note that the Beta distribution also respects the bounded \((0,1)\) support of the modelling-scale response, so its predictive quantiles cannot extend outside that interval. We then apply the same fixed inverse boundary transformation to report the quantiles in grade-percentage units.

A predictive interval should not be confused with a CI for the conditional mean as indicated in Table 5.58.

Because the interval used here is plug-in, it treats the fitted coefficients as fixed and therefore does not add parameter-estimation uncertainty to the predictive distribution. The CIs used later for inferential contrasts address a different target and should not be substituted for predictive intervals.

Interval width is also meaningful only together with coverage. A very broad interval may cover many observations simply because it is uninformative, whereas a narrow interval is useful only if its empirical coverage remains compatible with the nominal level. The later predictive evaluation will therefore report both empirical 90% coverage and average 90% interval width, exactly as frozen in Section 5.15.

5.17.5 Held-out Predictions


Now, we generate predictions for the canonical testing observations. No testing response is used to estimate or modify the model. For each study-time category \(g\), let \(\widehat{\mu}_g\) and \(\widehat{\phi}_g\) denote the conditional mean and precision obtained from the frozen training fit. Because both frozen submodels contain only Study Time, every testing student in category \(g\) receives the same \(\widehat{\mu}_g\), \(\widehat{\phi}_g\), Beta shape parameters, and predictive quantiles. Hence, we can compute the four category-specific predictive distributions once and then match them to the testing regressors.

  • R
  • Python
beta_prediction_reference <- tibble(
  `Study Time` = factor(study_time_levels, levels = study_time_levels),
  mean_eta = beta_mean_parameters[1] + c(0, beta_mean_parameters[2:4]),
  precision_eta = beta_precision_parameters[1] +
    c(0, beta_precision_parameters[2:4])) |>
  mutate(predicted_mean_beta = plogis(mean_eta),
    predicted_precision = exp(precision_eta),
    alpha = predicted_mean_beta * predicted_precision,
    beta_shape = (1 - predicted_mean_beta) * predicted_precision,
    lower_90_beta = qbeta(0.05, alpha, beta_shape),
    upper_90_beta = qbeta(0.95, alpha, beta_shape),
    predicted_mean_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * predicted_mean_beta +
      beta_grade_scale_offset,
    lower_90_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * lower_90_beta +
      beta_grade_scale_offset,
    upper_90_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * upper_90_beta +
      beta_grade_scale_offset)

beta_testing_predictions <- testing_data |>
  transmute(`Study Time`) |>
  left_join(beta_prediction_reference, by = "Study Time")

stopifnot(nrow(beta_testing_predictions) == nrow(testing_data),
  all(is.finite(beta_testing_predictions$predicted_mean_grade)))

beta_testing_predictions |>
  transmute(`Study Time`,
    `Predicted conditional mean (%)` = predicted_mean_grade,
    `Lower 90% predictive bound (%)` = lower_90_grade,
    `Upper 90% predictive bound (%)` = upper_90_grade) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c"))
beta_prediction_reference = pd.DataFrame({
    "Study Time": pd.Categorical(
        study_time_levels, categories=study_time_levels, ordered=False),
    "mean_eta": beta_mean_parameters[0]
        + np.r_[0, beta_mean_parameters[1:4]],
    "precision_eta": beta_precision_parameters[0]
        + np.r_[0, beta_precision_parameters[1:4]],
})
beta_prediction_reference["predicted_mean_beta"] = expit(
    beta_prediction_reference["mean_eta"])
beta_prediction_reference["predicted_precision"] = np.exp(
    beta_prediction_reference["precision_eta"])
beta_prediction_reference["alpha"] = (
    beta_prediction_reference["predicted_mean_beta"]
    * beta_prediction_reference["predicted_precision"])
beta_prediction_reference["beta_shape"] = (
    (1 - beta_prediction_reference["predicted_mean_beta"])
    * beta_prediction_reference["predicted_precision"])
beta_prediction_reference["lower_90_beta"] = stats.beta.ppf(
    0.05, beta_prediction_reference["alpha"],
    beta_prediction_reference["beta_shape"])
beta_prediction_reference["upper_90_beta"] = stats.beta.ppf(
    0.95, beta_prediction_reference["alpha"],
    beta_prediction_reference["beta_shape"])
for target, source in [
    ("predicted_mean_grade", "predicted_mean_beta"),
    ("lower_90_grade", "lower_90_beta"),
    ("upper_90_grade", "upper_90_beta"),
]:
    beta_prediction_reference[target] = (
        beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_prediction_reference[source]
        + beta_grade_scale_offset)

beta_testing_predictions = (
    testing_data[["Study Time"]].reset_index(drop=True)
    .merge(beta_prediction_reference, on="Study Time", how="left", sort=False))

assert len(beta_testing_predictions) == len(testing_data)
assert np.isfinite(beta_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"]).all()

beta_testing_predictions_display = beta_testing_predictions[[
    "Study Time", "predicted_mean_grade",
    "lower_90_grade", "upper_90_grade"]].copy()
beta_testing_predictions_display.columns = [
    "Study Time", "Predicted conditional mean (%)",
    "Lower 90% predictive bound (%)", "Upper 90% predictive bound (%)"]
beta_testing_predictions_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_testing_predictions_display.head(8),
    float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")

Table 5.59 contains only quantities determined by the training-fitted frozen model and the testing Study Time values. The testing grade responses remain uninspected at this stage. Therefore, we do not yet compute ME, MAE, RMSE, NLPD, empirical interval coverage, average interval width, or PIT summaries. The object beta_testing_predictions stores only the frozen held-out predictive quantities needed for the pre-specified evaluation that follows. Because the model contains only Study Time, repeated predicted means and interval endpoints within a category are expected rather than evidence of a coding error.

5.18 Results and Statistical Interpretation

The model-development stage is complete, the final specification has been frozen, and the held-out predictive quantities have already been generated. We can now use the protected testing data for the two roles fixed in advance: final inference from a testing-set refit of the frozen specification and held-out predictive evaluation of the frozen training-fitted model.

5.18.1 Returning to the Two Guiding Inquiries

Recall the two guiding inquiries introduced in Section 5.3.2. The inferential inquiry is:

How does the conditional mean final-grade proportion differ across weekly study time categories?

To answer this question, we refit the already frozen Beta regression specification on the testing data, exactly as established in Section 5.6.4. The mean submodel remains Study Time, the precision submodel remains Study Time, the logit and log links remain fixed, and <1 hour remains the treatment-coding reference category. This testing-set refit is used for inference only; its results cannot be used to change the model.

On the other hand, the predictive inquiry is:

How accurately can the developed Beta regression model predict held-out final-grade proportions, and how well does its fitted conditional Beta distribution represent predictive uncertainty?

This inquiry keeps the variable-precision model already fitted on the training data fixed. The testing responses are used only after the predictions have been generated, so they evaluate rather than estimate the predictive model. The final study-time model is compared with the pre-specified intercept-only Beta baseline, also fitted using the training data only.

Table 5.61 summarizes the distinction. Also, note that neither branch reopens model development. In particular, no testing result may be used to add or remove regressors, revise the mean or precision structure, change the links, alter the boundary transformation, or redefine the pre-specified predictive assessment.

5.18.2 Final Inferential Analysis

The inferential branch now uses the testing observations to estimate the fixed model specification selected from the training analysis. This is deliberately different from the predictive branch later in the section: the testing-set fit constructed here will not be used to generate the held-out predictions or predictive scores.

Fixed-specification Testing-set Refit

We refit exactly the frozen specification,

\[ \text{mean}\sim\texttt{Study Time}, \qquad \text{precision}\sim\texttt{Study Time}, \]

using the testing observations. No formula, coding, link, or response transformation is reconsidered.

  • R
  • Python

Before using this refit for the pre-specified inferential analysis, we repeat the numerical-stability checks from Section 5.14.1: optimizer convergence, finite coefficient estimates and model-based SEs, fitted conditional means strictly inside \((0,1)\), and positive fitted precisions.

  • R

beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean <- predict(beta_testing_refit, type = "response")
beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision <- predict(beta_testing_refit, type = "precision")
beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade <- beta_grade_scale_factor *
  beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean + beta_grade_scale_offset

stopifnot(beta_testing_refit_converged,
  all(is.finite(beta_testing_refit_parameters)),
  all(is.finite(beta_testing_refit_standard_errors)),
  all(beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean > 0 & beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean < 1),
  all(beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision > 0))

  Check = c("Optimizer converged", "All coefficient estimates finite",
    "All model-based SEs finite", "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
    "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)", "Minimum fitted precision",

    formatC(max(beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2),
    formatC(min(beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision), format = "f", digits = 3),

    + beta_grade_scale_offset)

assert beta_testing_refit_converged
assert np.isfinite(beta_testing_refit_parameters).all()
assert np.isfinite(beta_testing_refit_standard_errors).all()
assert ((beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean > 0) &
        (beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean < 1)).all()

    "Check": ["Optimizer converged", "All coefficient estimates finite",
        "All model-based SEs finite", "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
        "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)", "Minimum fitted precision",
        "Maximum fitted precision"],
