The baseline deliberately ignores Study Time. Thus, it represents the predictive performance attainable from a single training-derived Beta distribution before asking whether category-specific means and precisions provide useful held-out improvement.

Point-prediction Metrics

We first evaluate the conditional-mean predictions on the original grade-percentage scale, using the ME (Equation 5.26), MAE (Equation 5.27), and RMSE (Equation 5.28) definitions frozen in Section 5.15.1. Recall that the error is observed minus predicted, so positive ME indicates average underprediction and negative ME indicates average overprediction.

  • R
  • Python
beta_testing_predictions <- beta_testing_predictions |>
  mutate(observed_grade_beta = testing_data[["grade_beta"]],
    `Observed testing grade (%)` = testing_data[["Final Grade (%)"]])

beta_study_time_error <- beta_testing_predictions[["Observed testing grade (%)"]] -
  beta_testing_predictions[["predicted_mean_grade"]]
beta_baseline_error <- beta_baseline_testing_predictions[["observed_grade"]] -
  beta_baseline_testing_predictions[["predicted_mean_grade"]]

beta_point_metrics <- tibble(
  Model = beta_model_labels,
  ME = c(mean(beta_study_time_error), mean(beta_baseline_error)),
  MAE = c(mean(abs(beta_study_time_error)), mean(abs(beta_baseline_error))),
  RMSE = c(
    sqrt(mean(beta_study_time_error^2)),
    sqrt(mean(beta_baseline_error^2))
  )
)

beta_point_metrics |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = rep("c", 4))
beta_testing_predictions["observed_grade_beta"] = (
    testing_data["grade_beta"].to_numpy())
beta_testing_predictions["Observed testing grade (%)"] = (
    testing_data["Final Grade (%)"].to_numpy())

beta_study_time_error = (
    beta_testing_predictions["Observed testing grade (%)"].to_numpy()
    - beta_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"].to_numpy())
beta_baseline_error = (
    beta_baseline_testing_predictions["observed_grade"].to_numpy()
    - beta_baseline_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"].to_numpy())

beta_point_metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": beta_model_labels,
    "ME": [
        beta_study_time_error.mean(),
        beta_baseline_error.mean(),
    ],
    "MAE": [
        mean_absolute_error(
            beta_testing_predictions["Observed testing grade (%)"],
            beta_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"]),
        mean_absolute_error(
            beta_baseline_testing_predictions["observed_grade"],
            beta_baseline_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"]),
    ],
    "RMSE": [
        np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(
            beta_testing_predictions["Observed testing grade (%)"],
            beta_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"])),
        np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(
            beta_baseline_testing_predictions["observed_grade"],
            beta_baseline_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"])),
    ],
})
beta_point_metrics_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_point_metrics, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")

The study-time model has a held-out MAE of 4.199 percentage points and an RMSE of 5.134 percentage points. For the intercept-only baseline, the corresponding values are 9.160 percentage points and 10.870 percentage points, respectively. Because these metrics are evaluated on the original grade-percentage scale, their units have a direct practical interpretation. The MAE for the study-time model means that, across the held-out students, the predicted conditional mean grade differs from the observed grade by about 4.199 percentage points on average in absolute value. The intercept-only baseline has an average absolute error of about 9.160 percentage points. Relative to the baseline, the study-time model reduces held-out MAE by approximately 54.2% and RMSE by approximately 52.8%. Thus, the study-time model improves held-out point prediction under both absolute-error and squared-error criteria relative to the intercept-only baseline.

MAE and RMSE summarize prediction error differently. MAE gives each absolute error a contribution proportional to its size,

\[ \operatorname{MAE} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{test}}} \left| e_i \right|, \]

whereas RMSE squares the errors before averaging,

\[ \operatorname{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{test}}} e_i^2 }. \]

Consequently, RMSE gives relatively greater weight to larger prediction errors. The fact that the study-time model has a smaller value for both metrics means that its held-out advantage is not confined to only one of these loss functions: it improves the average absolute discrepancy while also reducing the quadratic penalty associated with larger misses. This does not mean that every individual testing observation is predicted more accurately by the study-time model; these are aggregate summaries across the full held-out sample.

The corresponding ME values are -0.50 percentage points for the study-time model and -0.68 percentage points for the baseline. Recall that we defined

\[ e_i = g_i-\widehat{g}_i, \]

so a positive ME indicates average underprediction and a negative ME indicates average overprediction. Therefore, the study-time model slightly overpredicts grades on average, while the intercept-only baseline also overpredicts grades on average.

The magnitude of ME should be interpreted together with MAE and RMSE. In particular, a mean error close to zero does not imply that predictions are individually accurate: positive and negative errors can cancel when averaged. Here, the study-time model’s absolute ME is 0.50 percentage points, whereas its MAE is 4.199 percentage points. The difference between those quantities illustrates why ME is primarily a measure of directional bias, whereas MAE and RMSE are more useful for comparing overall point-prediction accuracy.

All together, these point-prediction metrics indicate that incorporating Study Time materially improves the held-out prediction of the conditional mean grade relative to a model that assigns every student the same predicted mean. However, point-prediction accuracy answers only part of the predictive inquiry. Beta regression also provides a complete conditional predictive distribution through both \(\widehat{\mu}_i\) and \(\widehat{\phi}_i\). Therefore, we next evaluate whether the study-time model also improves probabilistic prediction, rather than assuming that better MAE and RMSE automatically imply a better fitted predictive distribution.

Probabilistic Predictive Performance

Point metrics evaluate only the predicted conditional means. We now evaluate the entire fitted predictive Beta distributions using mean NLPD. As fixed in Equation 5.31,

\[ \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}} = -\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} \log f_{\operatorname{Beta}} \left( y_i; \widehat{\alpha}_i, \widehat{\beta}_i \right). \]

As in Section 5.17, the hats in this predictive branch denote quantities obtained from the frozen training fit. Lower mean NLPD is better when the models are evaluated on the same held-out observations using the same response definition and transformation.

  • R
  • Python
beta_study_time_log_density <- dbeta(
  beta_testing_predictions[["observed_grade_beta"]],
  beta_testing_predictions[["alpha"]],
  beta_testing_predictions[["beta_shape"]],
  log = TRUE
)
beta_baseline_log_density <- dbeta(
  beta_baseline_testing_predictions[["observed_grade_beta"]],
  beta_baseline_testing_predictions[["alpha"]],
  beta_baseline_testing_predictions[["beta_shape"]],
  log = TRUE
)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(beta_study_time_log_density)),
  all(is.finite(beta_baseline_log_density))
)

beta_probabilistic_metrics <- tibble(
  Model = beta_model_labels,
  `Mean NLPD` = c(
    -mean(beta_study_time_log_density),
    -mean(beta_baseline_log_density)
  )
)

beta_probabilistic_metrics |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = c("c", "c"))
beta_study_time_log_density = stats.beta.logpdf(
    beta_testing_predictions["observed_grade_beta"],
    beta_testing_predictions["alpha"],
    beta_testing_predictions["beta_shape"],
)
beta_baseline_log_density = stats.beta.logpdf(
    beta_baseline_testing_predictions["observed_grade_beta"],
    beta_baseline_testing_predictions["alpha"],
    beta_baseline_testing_predictions["beta_shape"],
)

assert np.isfinite(beta_study_time_log_density).all()
assert np.isfinite(beta_baseline_log_density).all()

beta_probabilistic_metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": beta_model_labels,
    "Mean NLPD": [
        -beta_study_time_log_density.mean(),
        -beta_baseline_log_density.mean(),
    ],
})
beta_probabilistic_metrics_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_probabilistic_metrics,
    float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")

The study-time model has a held-out mean NLPD of -1.519, compared with -0.775 for the intercept-only baseline. Because smaller NLPD is better, the study-time model provides better held-out probabilistic prediction according to the pre-specified logarithmic-score criterion. The difference in mean NLPD is

\[ \Delta_{\mathrm{NLPD}} = \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{baseline}} - \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{Study\text{-}time}}, \]

which here equals 0.744. A positive value favours the study-time model because it means that the baseline incurs a larger average negative log predictive density on the same held-out observations.

The fact that both mean NLPD values are negative is not a computational problem. As discussed earlier in Section 5.15, NLPD is based on a continuous density, and a density can exceed \(1\). When the fitted model assigns density greater than \(1\) near an observed response, its log density is positive and the corresponding negative log density is negative. Thus, the absolute sign of NLPD is not the key interpretation; the comparison between models evaluated on the same held-out responses and the same transformed response scale is what matters.

The NLPD difference also has a useful density-scale interpretation. Since

\[ \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}} = - \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} \log f_i(y_i), \]

we can exponentiate the difference in mean log predictive density:

\[ \exp \left( \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{baseline}} - \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{Study\text{-}time}} \right). \]

Heads-up on why a geometric mean appears here!

The term geometric mean appears because NLPD is built from log predictive densities. For a fitted model \(M\), let

\[ d_i^{(M)} = f_i^{(M)}(y_i) \]

denote the predictive density that the model assigns to the held-out response that actually occurs for observation \(i\). The usual arithmetic mean would average these densities directly:

\[ \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} d_i^{(M)}. \]

NLPD does something different. It first takes the logarithm of each predictive density and then averages those log densities:

\[ -\overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_M = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} \log d_i^{(M)}. \]

Exponentiating this average gives

\[ \exp \left( -\overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_M \right) = \exp \left[ \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} \log d_i^{(M)} \right]. \]

Using the identity

\[ \exp \left( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log d_i \right) = \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n} d_i \right)^{1/n}, \]

we obtain

\[ \exp \left( -\overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_M \right) = \left[ \prod_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} d_i^{(M)} \right]^{1/n_{\mathrm{test}}}. \tag{5.51}\]

In Equation 5.51, the right-hand side is the geometric mean predictive density. Thus, exponentiating the mean log predictive density returns us to the original density scale, but through a geometric rather than arithmetic average. This also explains the model comparison used above, where \(\operatorname{GM}\) indicates geometric mean:

\[ \frac{ \operatorname{GM}_{\mathrm{Study\text{-}time}} }{ \operatorname{GM}_{\mathrm{baseline}} } = \exp \left( \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{baseline}} - \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{Study\text{-}time}} \right). \]

For our held-out data, this ratio is approximately 2.10. Therefore, on the geometric-mean scale, the study-time model assigns about 2.10 times as much predictive density to the responses that actually occurred as the intercept-only baseline.

This quantity is not an average probability. These are continuous predictive densities, which can exceed \(1\). The ratio is meaningful here because both models are evaluated on the same held-out observations and the same transformed response scale. It summarizes their relative multiplicative density assignment across the held-out sample; it does not imply that the study-time model assigns more density than the baseline to every individual observation.

For these held-out data, this quantity is approximately 2.10. In other words, the geometric mean predictive density assigned to the responses that actually occurred is about 2.10 times as large under the study-time model as under the intercept-only baseline. Note that this is a comparison of predictive densities, not a probability ratio and not a statement that every held-out observation receives more density under the study-time model. Some individual observations can still be better represented by the baseline. The mean NLPD summarizes the average log-score performance across the complete held-out sample.

Unlike MAE and RMSE, NLPD evaluates more than the location of the predicted conditional mean. For observation \(i\), the predictive density

\[ f_{\operatorname{Beta}} \left( y_i; \widehat{\alpha}_i, \widehat{\beta}_i \right) \]

depends on both

\[ \widehat{\mu}_i \qquad\text{and}\qquad \widehat{\phi}_i. \]

Therefore, a model can receive a poor NLPD because its conditional mean is badly located, because its predictive distribution is inappropriately concentrated or diffuse, or because both features are misspecified. Conversely, two models with similar point predictions can have quite different NLPD values if one assigns substantially more plausible predictive density around the responses that actually occur.

For this chapter, the direction of the probabilistic result is consistent with the point-prediction results from our previous subsection on point-prediction metrics: the study-time model improves both the location-based prediction metrics and the held-out logarithmic score relative to the intercept-only baseline. This provides evidence that using Study Time improves not only the predicted conditional means but also the overall probabilistic representation of the held-out grades under the fitted Beta distributions.

However, a better mean NLPD does not by itself establish that the predictive distributions are well calibrated. NLPD rewards distributions that assign greater density to realized responses, whereas calibration asks whether the predictive distributions have appropriate frequency properties across the held-out sample. Therefore, we next examine the pre-specified 90% predictive-interval coverage and width together with the PIT diagnostic.

Held-out Predictive-distribution Assessment

We next assess the pre-specified 90% plug-in predictive intervals. For each model, empirical coverage is the proportion of held-out grades falling inside the corresponding interval, and average width is reported in practical percentage-point units.

  • R
  • Python
beta_study_time_covered <- with(
  beta_testing_predictions,
  `Observed testing grade (%)` >= lower_90_grade &
    `Observed testing grade (%)` <= upper_90_grade
)
beta_baseline_covered <- with(
  beta_baseline_testing_predictions,
  observed_grade >= lower_90_grade &
    observed_grade <= upper_90_grade
)

beta_interval_metrics <- tibble(
  Model = beta_model_labels,
  `90% coverage (%)` = 100 * c(
    mean(beta_study_time_covered),
    mean(beta_baseline_covered)
  ),
  `Average 90% interval width (percentage points)` = c(
    mean(beta_testing_predictions[["upper_90_grade"]] -
      beta_testing_predictions[["lower_90_grade"]]),
    mean(beta_baseline_testing_predictions[["upper_90_grade"]] -
      beta_baseline_testing_predictions[["lower_90_grade"]])
  )
)

beta_interval_metrics |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = rep("c", 3))
beta_study_time_covered = (
    (beta_testing_predictions["Observed testing grade (%)"]
     >= beta_testing_predictions["lower_90_grade"])
    & (beta_testing_predictions["Observed testing grade (%)"]
       <= beta_testing_predictions["upper_90_grade"]))
beta_baseline_covered = (
    (beta_baseline_testing_predictions["observed_grade"]
     >= beta_baseline_testing_predictions["lower_90_grade"])
    & (beta_baseline_testing_predictions["observed_grade"]
       <= beta_baseline_testing_predictions["upper_90_grade"]))

beta_interval_metrics = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": beta_model_labels,
    "90% coverage (%)": [
        100 * beta_study_time_covered.mean(),
        100 * beta_baseline_covered.mean(),
    ],
    "Average 90% interval width (percentage points)": [
        (beta_testing_predictions["upper_90_grade"]
         - beta_testing_predictions["lower_90_grade"]).mean(),
        (beta_baseline_testing_predictions["upper_90_grade"]
         - beta_baseline_testing_predictions["lower_90_grade"]).mean(),
    ],
})
beta_interval_metrics_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_interval_metrics,
    float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")

For a nominal 90% predictive interval, the empirical held-out coverage is

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{Coverage}} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} \mathbb{I} \left( L_i \leq g_i \leq U_i \right), \]

where \(L_i\) and \(U_i\) are the lower and upper predictive bounds for held-out observation \(i\), \(g_i\) is its observed grade, and \(\mathbb{I}(\cdot)\) equals \(1\) when the observed grade falls inside the interval and \(0\) otherwise. The corresponding average interval width is

\[ \overline{W} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}} \sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}} \left( U_i-L_i \right). \]

Thus, coverage measures how often the predictive intervals contain the realized held-out grades, whereas width measures how concentrated those intervals are on the original grade-percentage scale.

The study-time model covers 90.67% of the held-out grades. In counts, this corresponds to 272 of 300 held-out observations falling inside their 90% predictive intervals. Its empirical coverage is therefore only 0.67 percentage points away from the nominal 90% level. On the other hand, the intercept-only baseline covers 92.7% of the held-out grades, corresponding to 278 of 300 observations. Its empirical coverage is 2.67 percentage points away from the nominal level.

Nevertheless, coverage alone is not enough to compare predictive intervals. An interval can achieve high empirical coverage simply by being very wide. Hence, we interpret coverage jointly with the practical width of the intervals. For the study-time model, the average 90% predictive-interval width is 17.58 percentage points. For the intercept-only baseline, the corresponding width is 38.02 percentage points. Thus, the study-time model reduces average interval width by approximately 53.8% relative to the baseline. This is a substantial difference in practical terms. The baseline obtains somewhat higher coverage, but it does so using predictive intervals that are much wider. By contrast, the study-time model produces intervals that are considerably narrower while retaining empirical coverage close to the nominal 90% level. In this sense, the study-time model provides a more concentrated (or sharper) held-out predictive distribution without sacrificing much coverage.

It is important not to interpret the nominal 90% level as a requirement that exactly 90% of one finite testing sample must be covered. Even if the predictive distributions were perfectly calibrated, empirical coverage would fluctuate from sample to sample. Therefore, the observed difference between the nominal 90% level and the empirical values above should be interpreted diagnostically rather than as a pass/fail test. The width also should not be interpreted as a fixed \(\pm\) margin around the predicted mean. Because the fitted Beta distributions can be asymmetric, the lower and upper predictive bounds need not lie equally far from the conditional mean. The reported width is simply the average distance \(U_i-L_i\) between those two bounds on the grade-percentage scale.

Having said all this, these results favour the study-time model from an interval-prediction perspective: it achieves empirical coverage close to the pre-specified nominal level while using intervals that are markedly narrower than those of the intercept-only baseline. That is a more informative result than coverage alone, because useful probabilistic predictions should be sufficiently well calibrated without being unnecessarily diffuse.

Still, predictive-interval coverage checks only one aspect of the fitted predictive distributions. A model could obtain reasonable 90% coverage while still allocating probability unevenly within those intervals. Thus, we complement coverage and width with the PIT diagnostic, which examines the predictive distributions across their full probability scale. We compute PIT values from the study-time model’s frozen training-derived Beta distributions and use exactly ten equal-width bins on \([0,1]\), as fixed in Section 5.15.3.

  • R
  • Python
beta_pit_values <- pbeta(
  beta_testing_predictions[["observed_grade_beta"]],
  beta_testing_predictions[["alpha"]],
  beta_testing_predictions[["beta_shape"]]
)
beta_pit_breaks <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)
beta_pit_values_plot <- pmin(
  pmax(beta_pit_values, 0), 1 - .Machine$double.eps)
beta_pit_bins <- cut(
  beta_pit_values_plot, breaks = beta_pit_breaks,
  include.lowest = TRUE, right = FALSE)
beta_pit_counts <- as.numeric(table(beta_pit_bins))
beta_pit_expected_count <- length(beta_pit_values) / 10
beta_pit_y_step <- max(
  1, ceiling(1.15 * max(c(beta_pit_counts, beta_pit_expected_count)) / 5))
beta_pit_y_max <- 5 * beta_pit_y_step
beta_pit_y_breaks <- seq(0, beta_pit_y_max, by = beta_pit_y_step)

beta_pit_plot_data <- tibble(
  midpoint = head(beta_pit_breaks, -1) + 0.05,
  count = beta_pit_counts)

beta_pit_plot <- ggplot(
  beta_pit_plot_data, aes(x = midpoint, y = count)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.092, fill = "#56B4E9", colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = beta_pit_expected_count,
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D55E00") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, beta_pit_y_max),
    breaks = beta_pit_y_breaks[beta_pit_y_breaks != 0],
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.title.y = element_text(
      size = 20, vjust = 0.5, margin = margin(r = 12)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "\n Probability integral transform",
    y = "Held-out observations"
  )

beta_pit_plot
beta_pit_values = stats.beta.cdf(
    beta_testing_predictions["observed_grade_beta"],
    beta_testing_predictions["alpha"],
    beta_testing_predictions["beta_shape"],
)
beta_pit_breaks = np.linspace(0, 1, 11)
beta_pit_values_plot = np.clip(
    beta_pit_values, 0, np.nextafter(1.0, 0.0))
beta_pit_counts, _ = np.histogram(
    beta_pit_values_plot, bins=beta_pit_breaks)
beta_pit_expected_count = len(beta_pit_values) / 10
beta_pit_y_step = max(
    1, int(np.ceil(
        1.15 * max(beta_pit_counts.max(), beta_pit_expected_count) / 5)))
beta_pit_y_max = 5 * beta_pit_y_step
beta_pit_y_breaks = np.arange(
    0, beta_pit_y_max + beta_pit_y_step, beta_pit_y_step)

beta_pit_plot_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "midpoint": beta_pit_breaks[:-1] + 0.05,
    "count": beta_pit_counts,
})

beta_pit_plot, beta_pit_axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8))
_ = beta_pit_axis.bar(
    beta_pit_plot_data["midpoint"],
    beta_pit_plot_data["count"],
    width=0.092,
    color="#56B4E9",
    edgecolor="#0072B2",
)
_ = beta_pit_axis.axhline(
    beta_pit_expected_count,
    linestyle="dashed",
    linewidth=1,
    color="#D55E00",
)
_ = beta_pit_axis.set_xlim(0, 1)
_ = beta_pit_axis.set_ylim(0, beta_pit_y_max)
_ = beta_pit_axis.set_xticks(np.linspace(0, 1, 11))
_ = beta_pit_axis.set_yticks(beta_pit_y_breaks[beta_pit_y_breaks != 0])
_ = beta_pit_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Probability integral transform", fontsize=20)
_ = beta_pit_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Held-out observations", fontsize=20, labelpad=12)
_ = beta_pit_axis.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)
_ = beta_pit_axis.grid(True, which="major", axis="both", alpha=0.3)
_ = beta_pit_axis.grid(False, which="minor")

_ = beta_pit_plot.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Recall that, for held-out observation \(i\),

\[ \operatorname{PIT}_i = F_i(y_i), \]

where \(F_i(\cdot)\) is the fitted conditional Beta CDF supplied by the frozen training-derived model and \(y_i\) is the observed transformed grade. A PIT value near \(0\) means that the observed response falls unusually low in its fitted predictive distribution, a value near \(1\) means that it falls unusually high, and a value near \(0.5\) places it closer to the middle of that distribution.

If the held-out predictive distributions were exactly calibrated, these PIT values would behave approximately as draws from a \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) distribution. With ten equal-width bins, the corresponding expected count is

\[ \frac{n_{\mathrm{test}}}{10} = \text{30.0} \]

observations per bin. The dashed horizontal line in Figure 5.23 (or Figure 5.24) shows this reference. Note that the observed bin heights should not be expected to equal that line exactly. With only 300 held-out observations, ordinary finite-sample variation produces uneven counts even when the underlying PIT distribution is Uniform. Therefore, we look for broad, systematic patterns rather than treating every bin-to-bin difference as evidence of miscalibration.

In our histogram, the PIT values are not perfectly even across \([0,1]\). The most populated bin contains 47 observations, compared with an expected count of 30.0. More broadly, 174 of 300 observations (or 58.0%) have PIT values below \(0.5\), compared with 50% under an exact Uniform reference. Thus, the histogram shows somewhat greater mass in the lower half of the PIT distribution than in the upper half.

That direction has a useful predictive interpretation. An excess of relatively small PIT values means that held-out grades occur toward the lower portions of their fitted predictive distributions more often than a perfectly Uniform PIT pattern would suggest. In practical terms, this is consistent with a mild tendency for the fitted distributions to be positioned somewhat high relative to some observed grades. This direction is also broadly consistent with the negative held-out ME reported in Table 5.72, which indicated slight average overprediction of the conditional mean.

However, our histogram does not show an extreme accumulation at \(0\) or \(1\), nor is its main feature a pronounced symmetric U-shape or sharply concentrated central hump. Those kinds of shapes would suggest stronger and more systematic problems with predictive spread. Instead, the departure here appears more like an asymmetric unevenness toward lower PIT values, superimposed on the sampling variability expected from a testing set of this size.

This interpretation also complements the predictive-interval results. The study-time model achieved empirical 90% coverage close to the nominal level while using substantially narrower intervals than the baseline. The PIT histogram adds information that interval coverage alone cannot provide: even when the overall proportion of covered observations is reasonable, the responses need not be distributed perfectly evenly throughout their fitted predictive distributions.

Consistent with the caution in Section 5.15.3, we therefore interpret the PIT histogram as a diagnostic rather than a standalone model-acceptance test (Diebold, Gunther, and Tay 1998; Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery 2007). A finite-sample histogram need not look perfectly flat, and PIT Uniformity would not by itself be sufficient to establish that a predictive model is ideal. Taken together with the held-out NLPD, interval coverage, and interval width, the histogram suggests that the study-time model provides a substantially improved and reasonably informative predictive distribution relative to the intercept-only baseline, while still leaving some evidence of localized predictive-distribution miscalibration.

Predictive Performance Summary


We can now place the pre-specified held-out predictive criteria side by side. No new metric or decision rule is introduced here; the purpose is to synthesize the complementary evidence already examined for point prediction, probabilistic prediction, predictive intervals, and distributional calibration.

  • R
  • Python
beta_predictive_summary <- beta_point_metrics |>
  left_join(beta_probabilistic_metrics, by = "Model") |>
  left_join(beta_interval_metrics, by = "Model")

beta_predictive_summary |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = rep("c", 7))
beta_predictive_summary = (
    beta_point_metrics
    .merge(beta_probabilistic_metrics, on="Model")
    .merge(beta_interval_metrics, on="Model")
)
beta_predictive_summary_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_predictive_summary,
    float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")

For point prediction, the study-time model has a held-out MAE of 4.199 percentage points and an RMSE of 5.134 percentage points, compared with 9.160 and 10.870 percentage points for the intercept-only baseline. Relative to that baseline, this corresponds to reductions of approximately 54.2% in MAE and 52.8% in RMSE. Thus, incorporating Study Time substantially improves the held-out prediction of the conditional mean grade under both the absolute-error and squared-error criteria.

The ME values provide a different piece of information. They are -0.500 percentage points for the study-time model and -0.680 percentage points for the baseline. Because our error is defined as observed minus predicted, the negative values indicate slight average overprediction. Their small magnitudes relative to the corresponding MAEs also reinforce an important distinction: little average signed bias does not imply small individual prediction errors, because positive and negative errors can cancel.

For probabilistic prediction, the conclusion points in the same direction. The study-time model has mean NLPD -1.519, compared with -0.775 for the baseline. Since smaller NLPD is better, the difference

\[ \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{baseline}} - \overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}_{\mathrm{Study\text{-}time}} \]

is 0.744 in favour of the study-time model. On the geometric-mean predictive-density scale developed earlier in this section, this corresponds to a ratio of approximately 2.10. Hence, the improvement is not limited to locating the conditional means more accurately: the category-specific means and precisions also assign substantially more predictive density, on average on the log-score scale, to the held-out grades that actually occur.

The predictive-interval evidence adds an important qualification. The study-time model attains 90.67% empirical coverage, only 0.67 percentage points from the nominal 90% level. Its average interval width is 17.58 percentage points. The baseline attains 92.67% coverage, but with an average width of 38.02 percentage points. Consequently, the study-time model’s intervals are approximately 53.8% narrower on average than the baseline intervals while still retaining coverage close to the nominal target. The baseline’s somewhat higher empirical coverage should therefore not be interpreted automatically as superior interval prediction: it is achieved with a much less concentrated predictive distribution. Considering coverage and width together, the study-time model provides substantially sharper intervals without an obvious loss of nominal-level coverage.

The PIT histogram in Figure 5.23 (or Figure 5.24) provides a further view of the full predictive distributions. Under exact \(\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\) behaviour, each of the ten bins would contain 30.0 observations on average. In the observed testing sample, 174 of 300 PIT values (or 58.0%) fall below \(0.5\). Hence, the histogram shows some asymmetric unevenness toward the lower part of the predictive distributions, consistent with the slight average overprediction seen in ME. At the same time, it does not display an extreme boundary accumulation or another dramatic shape suggesting severe global predictive-distribution failure.

All this means that the calibration conclusion should remain deliberately nuanced. The study-time model’s 90% interval coverage is close to its nominal target, and its intervals are much narrower than the baseline’s, but the PIT histogram still shows some localized departure from ideal Uniform behaviour. We therefore do not reduce calibration to a single pass/fail label. Coverage, width, and PIT describe different aspects of the predictive distributions and are most informative when interpreted together.

Taken as a whole, the held-out evidence answers the chapter’s predictive inquiry consistently. Adding Study Time improves point prediction, improves the logarithmic predictive score, and yields substantially sharper predictive intervals while maintaining coverage close to 90% relative to an intercept-only Beta benchmark. Thus, the model gains predictive value from allowing both the conditional mean and precision to vary across study-time categories, rather than assigning every student the same training-derived Beta distribution.

At the same time, this is not evidence that the predictive model is complete or ideal. The predictive distributions are plug-in distributions, so they represent conditional response variability while treating the training-estimated coefficients as fixed and do not incorporate parameter-estimation uncertainty. The testing sample is finite, PIT Uniformity is neither expected exactly in a finite sample nor sufficient by itself to establish ideal forecasting, and the frozen model uses only Study Time to distinguish students. Other student-level information and sources of variation in final grades remain outside this model.

Accordingly, the predictive conclusion is appropriately narrower: for these protected held-out observations, the frozen study-time variable-precision Beta regression provides substantially better predictive performance than the pre-specified intercept-only Beta baseline, while the calibration diagnostics also identify some remaining predictive-distribution structure that the model does not fully capture.

5.19 Synthesizing Inference and Prediction

The inferential and predictive branches of this case study now point in a consistent direction, but they answer different statistical questions. Keeping those questions separate is essential:

  • The inferential analysis asks how the conditional mean final grade differs across study-time categories under the frozen model specification.
  • The predictive analysis asks whether the training-fitted model predicts new held-out grades and their predictive distributions better than a pre-specified intercept-only Beta baseline.

The testing-set inferential analysis provides strong evidence of an association between Study Time and the conditional mean grade. The joint likelihood-ratio test produced an LR statistic of 297.268 with 3 degrees of freedom and a \(p\)-value <0.001. On the original grade scale, the fitted conditional mean increases from 65.12% for <1 hour to 89.91% for 5+ hours. Relative to <1 hour, the three fitted differences are 9.85, 20.11, and 24.80 percentage points for 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours, respectively. Their 95% model-based CIs all lie above \(0\), so the coefficient-level and original-scale results agree with the joint test.

This is the chapter’s inferential conclusion:

In this synthetic dataset, Study Time is strongly associated with the conditional mean final grade under the frozen Beta regression specification.

The word associated is crucial. Nothing in the data-generating description or analysis supplies a randomized intervention, a causal identification strategy, or an adjustment set designed to remove confounding. Therefore, a fitted difference of, for example, 24.80 percentage points between 5+ hours and <1 hour should not be read as the amount by which an individual student’s grade would increase if that student were made to study longer.

The held-out predictive results answer a separate question and also favour the study-time model. For point prediction, its MAE and RMSE are 4.199 and 5.134 percentage points, compared with 9.160 and 10.870 for the intercept-only baseline. This corresponds to reductions of approximately 54.2% in MAE and 52.8% in RMSE. Thus, Study Time provides materially useful information for predicting the centre of the held-out grade distribution rather than merely describing an in-sample association. Furthermore, the conclusion is also favourable for probabilistic prediction, where the entire fitted Beta distribution matters. The study-time model has a mean NLPD of -1.519, compared with -0.775 for the baseline. The corresponding geometric-mean predictive-density ratio is approximately 2.10 in favour of the study-time model. Hence, the predictive gain extends beyond locating the conditional mean: the final model also assigns substantially more predictive density, on average on the log-score scale, to the held-out responses that actually occur.

The predictive-interval and PIT results add an important qualification to the positive predictive result. The study-time model obtains 90.67% empirical coverage for its nominal 90% intervals, with an average width of 17.58 percentage points. Its intervals are approximately 53.8% narrower than those of the intercept-only baseline while retaining coverage close to the nominal target. At the same time, the PIT histogram shows some asymmetric unevenness toward lower PIT values. The final predictive assessment is therefore positive but not absolute:

The model is markedly more informative than the baseline, while some localized predictive-distribution miscalibration remains.

The role of the variable-precision structure should also be interpreted carefully. During model development, the constant-precision model showed a systematic dispersion problem, and the training-stage diagnostics in Section 5.14 showed that allowing precision to vary by Study Time substantially improved distributional adequacy. That refinement was selected before the testing outcomes were examined. The resulting frozen variable-precision model then delivered the held-out probabilistic improvements summarized above. However, the held-out benchmark comparison is between the final study-time variable-precision model as a whole and an intercept-only Beta baseline. Hence, this comparison does not isolate the predictive contribution of the precision submodel from that of the mean submodel. The training-stage diagnostics justified allowing precision to vary with Study Time, while the held-out results show that the resulting final model, taken as a whole, provides substantially better probabilistic prediction than the intercept-only baseline.

The distinction among the main conclusions can be summarized in Table 5.80.

A useful final distinction is that statistical association, point prediction, and probabilistic prediction are not interchangeable achievements. The inferential branch quantifies how the conditional mean differs across categories. Point prediction evaluates how close predicted conditional means are to individual held-out outcomes. Probabilistic prediction evaluates whether the full fitted conditional distributions (including their precision) place appropriate density and uncertainty around those outcomes. A model can perform well in one of these roles without necessarily performing equally well in the others.

In this case, the evidence happens to align: Study Time is strongly associated with the conditional mean in the protected inferential analysis, and including it in the frozen variable-precision Beta model materially improves both point and probabilistic prediction on held-out data. That coherence strengthens the practical case for Study Time as a useful modelling variable in this synthetic example. It still does not turn the association into a causal effect. Predictive usefulness answers whether Study Time helps us anticipate grades under the observed data-generating pattern; causal inference would require a different design and a different set of modelling assumptions.

5.20 Storytelling

A statistical analysis is not finished when the model has been fitted and the diagnostics have been checked. The final step is to communicate what the analysis says in language that preserves the magnitude of the results, their uncertainty, the predictive evidence, and the limits of the study design. For this case study, the central message is:

In this synthetic student dataset, higher study-time categories are strongly associated with higher conditional mean final grades, and using Study Time materially improves held-out prediction relative to an intercept-only Beta baseline. These results are associational and predictive, not causal.

The inferential results make the association clear. The protected testing-set analysis provides strong evidence that the conditional mean grade differs across the four study-time categories, with a joint likelihood-ratio test yielding a \(p\)-value <0.001. More importantly for communication, the fitted conditional mean grades on the original percentage scale are 65.12%, 74.97%, 85.22%, and 89.91% for <1 hour, 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours, respectively.

Relative to the <1 hour category, the fitted differences are 9.85 percentage points for 1–3 hours, 20.11 percentage points for 3–5 hours, and 24.80 percentage points for 5+ hours. Their corresponding 95% model-based CIs are [8.31, 11.39], [18.43, 21.78], and [22.79, 26.80] percentage points. Reporting these contrasts is more informative to a non-technical audience than reporting only logit-scale coefficients: they describe both the size of the association and the uncertainty around it in the same units as the original grades.

The predictive results tell a complementary story. When the frozen training-fitted study-time model is evaluated on held-out students, its MAE is 4.20 percentage points and its RMSE is 5.13 percentage points. The intercept-only Beta baseline, which assigns every held-out student the same training-derived conditional mean and predictive distribution, has an MAE of 9.16 percentage points and an RMSE of 10.87 percentage points. In practical terms, incorporating Study Time reduces MAE by about 54.2% and RMSE by about 52.8% relative to that simple benchmark.

That improvement concerns point prediction: the fitted conditional means are closer to the held-out grades. Beta regression also lets us ask a richer predictive question because it supplies an entire conditional distribution. By the pre-specified logarithmic-score criterion, the study-time model has a mean NLPD of -1.519, compared with -0.775 for the baseline. On the geometric-mean predictive-density scale developed earlier, this corresponds to about a 2.10-fold advantage for the study-time model. Thus, the predictive benefit is not limited to getting the centre of the grade distribution closer to the observed outcomes; the fitted distributions also place substantially more predictive density, on average on the log-score scale, around the grades that actually occur.

The predictive intervals describe the remaining uncertainty in more familiar units. The study-time model’s nominal 90% predictive intervals cover 90.7% of the held-out grades and have an average width of 17.58 percentage points. The baseline reaches 92.7% coverage, but its intervals average 38.02 percentage points wide. The study-time model therefore produces intervals about 53.8% narrower while retaining empirical coverage close to the nominal target. The PIT diagnostic adds some caution: its histogram shows localized unevenness toward lower PIT values, so the predictive distributions should not be described as perfectly calibrated.

This is where the Beta model adds something that a mean-only story would miss. The model separates the conditional mean, which describes where the grade distribution is centred, from the precision, which describes how concentrated the distribution is around that centre. Training-stage diagnostics showed that a common precision was too restrictive, so the final specification allowed precision to vary with Study Time. That refinement improved the distributional adequacy of the fitted model before the testing outcomes were examined. In the final held-out analysis, the resulting variable-precision model then performed substantially better than the intercept-only Beta baseline as a complete predictive model.

For an applied audience, the appropriate takeaway is therefore not simply that “more study time means a higher grade.” A more faithful statement is:

Within this synthetic dataset, study-time category is informative about both the conditional mean final grade and the predictive distribution of final grades. The fitted model shows sizeable mean-grade differences across categories and materially better held-out prediction than a covariate-blind Beta baseline, while still leaving meaningful uncertainty around individual outcomes.

This type of model is useful when the response is continuous and bounded, when the scientific or practical question concerns differences in its conditional mean, and when representing the conditional spread or a full predictive distribution is also important. The analysis should still be supported by model diagnostics, and held-out predictive claims should be based on data not used to fit the predictive model.

Finally, the running dataset is synthetic. It was designed to provide a clear teaching example for the Beta-regression workflow, not to support claims about real students, courses, or institutions. The numerical contrasts and predictive results should therefore not be translated into recommendations for study policies, advising practices, grading systems, or institutional interventions.

5.21 Limitations and Extensions

The analysis in this chapter is deliberately focused: it develops a complete Beta-regression workflow while keeping the running model interpretable enough to examine mean structure, precision structure, inference, and prediction in detail. That focus also places clear limits on what the fitted model and its results can support:

  1. The dataset is synthetic. The fitted associations, uncertainty intervals, predictive errors, and calibration diagnostics are useful for learning the modelling workflow, but they do not describe a real student population and should not be generalized to a particular course, program, or institution.
  2. Standard Beta regression requires the modelling response to lie strictly inside \((0,1)\) (Ferrari and Cribari-Neto 2004; Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010). Our dataset contains exact grades of \(100\%\), so Section 5.5.3 applies the fixed Smithson–Verkuilen transformation before model fitting (Smithson and Verkuilen 2006). This was a deliberate and pre-specified choice, but it is not the only possible way to handle genuine boundary observations. Because the transformation changes the modelling-scale response for every observation, a different boundary-handling convention could lead to somewhat different fitted quantities. This concern is particularly relevant for the precision parameters and density-based quantities such as log-likelihood and NLPD. We did not conduct a sensitivity analysis over alternative boundary adjustments, so the robustness of those quantities to the chosen convention remains an open question.
  3. The final mean submodel contains only Study Time. The larger training-stage mean model did not provide evidence, through the pre-specified joint likelihood-ratio comparison, that its additional mean terms improved the fitted model enough to retain them. This does not imply that study time is the only feature related to final grades, nor that every omitted variable is individually irrelevant. It means only that the chapter retained the simpler study-time mean structure under the model-development strategy used here. The remaining held-out prediction errors and PIT departures also remind us that substantial outcome variation remains unexplained by this single categorical regressor.
  4. The constant-precision specification was inadequate for the training data. The diagnostics showed systematic differences in residual dispersion across Study Time, and Section 5.14 showed that allowing precision to vary substantially improved that aspect of model adequacy. Hence, conclusions from the initial constant-precision model should not be treated as interchangeable with those from the final variable-precision specification. More generally, Beta regression requires attention to both the conditional mean and conditional precision rather than assuming automatically that a common precision is sufficient (Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010).
  5. The predictive analysis is held-out but not necessarily prospective. The random training/testing split demonstrates performance on observations that were not used to fit the predictive model, but the synthetic dataset does not document a real operational timeline for when Study Time would become available relative to the final grade. Therefore, this chapter establishes retrospective held-out predictive performance. A genuinely prospective use would require confirming that every regressor used for prediction is available at the intended prediction time and is measured in the same way for future observations.
  6. The likelihood developed in this chapter treats observations as statistically independent. That assumption would be questionable for repeated measurements on the same student, students nested within classes or instructors, longitudinal observations, or other clustered data structures. Dependence changes both the probability model and the uncertainty calculation, so ordinary independent-observation Beta regression should not simply be carried over to such settings.
  7. The response must be meaningfully treated as a continuous bounded quantity. A percentage scale by itself does not guarantee that Beta regression is appropriate. A binary outcome, a success count with a known denominator, an ordinal score, or a response with substantively distinct boundary masses has a different data-generating structure and may require a different model. This distinction was emphasized at the beginning of the chapter and remains a limitation on how broadly the fitted model can be applied.
  8. Study Time is represented by the four observed categories <1 hour, 1–3 hours, 3–5 hours, and 5+ hours. Hence, the model estimates category-specific contrasts; it does not learn a continuous curve in hours. Extrapolation beyond these categories is not meaningful. For example, the fitted model cannot tell us what should happen at seven versus ten hours per week simply because both values fall within or beyond one of the coarse categories.
  9. The substantive comparisons remain observational and associational. Statistical significance and held-out predictive improvement do not identify the causal effect of changing a student’s study time.

A few natural extensions are worth knowing about, but each represents a new modelling decision rather than an automatic upgrade to the analysis:

  • Alternative mean links. The logit link is convenient and interpretable, but Beta regression can use other suitable link functions when their shape is better aligned with the conditional-mean relationship (Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010). Choosing among them should be motivated by the scientific question, interpretability, and model adequacy rather than by trying many links until one gives the most favourable result.
  • Different precision regressors. The mean and precision submodels need not contain the same variables. A different set of regressors can be used for precision when there is substantive or diagnostic evidence that conditional dispersion changes with those features (Cribari-Neto and Zeileis 2010). In this chapter, using Study Time in both components was a focused response to the training-stage dispersion pattern, not a general requirement of Beta regression.
  • Boundary-aware Beta models. When exact \(0\)s or \(1\)s are genuine outcomes rather than values that can reasonably be moved into the interior, an explicitly boundary-aware model can avoid relying on an interior transformation. Extended-support Beta regression provides one such approach for responses on \([0,1]\) (Kosmidis and Zeileis 2026). Whether this is preferable depends on what the boundaries mean in the application.
  • Dependence-aware or mixed-effects Beta models. If bounded responses are clustered, repeated, or longitudinal, extensions that model the dependence structure directly are more appropriate than assuming independent observations. Mixed and mixture Beta-regression approaches provide examples of how bounded-response models can be extended to dependent data (Verkuilen and Smithson 2012).
  • Resampling-based predictive assessment. A single protected testing split is easy to explain and preserves a clean separation between development and final evaluation, but its numerical results depend partly on the particular split. When the goal is broader predictive-performance estimation or model comparison, repeated resampling or cross-validation can provide information across multiple training/validation partitions (Arlot and Celisse 2010). Such procedures would need to preserve the full preprocessing and model-development workflow within each resample to avoid information leakage.

These extensions are best viewed as directions for a later analysis rather than additional steps that must be appended to every Beta regression. The central workflow remains the same: match the probability model to the response-generating structure, specify both mean and precision thoughtfully, diagnose inadequacies before refining the model, separate model development from final evaluation, and keep inferential, predictive, and causal claims distinct.

5.22 Chapter Summary

This chapter developed Beta regression as a modelling framework for continuous bounded responses whose conditional mean, conditional spread, and full predictive distribution are all of interest. The student final-grade case study also illustrated a broader regression principle: fitting a model is only one part of the workflow. Response preparation, distributional assumptions, diagnostics, model refinement, specification freezing, inference, and prediction each answer a different question.

The main ideas from the chapter are:

  • Standard Beta regression models continuous responses on the open unit interval \((0,1)\). A response expressed as a percentage or proportion is not automatically appropriate for Beta regression: its data-generating structure is still critical. Binary responses, grouped success counts, and bounded continuous responses with genuine endpoint masses require different probability-model considerations.
  • Exact boundary values require an explicit modelling decision. In the running dataset, exact \(100\%\) grades map to \(1\) after ordinary percentage-to-proportion rescaling, whereas a standard Beta distribution assigns support only to values strictly between \(0\) and \(1\). For this synthetic teaching case, we fixed the Smithson–Verkuilen transformation (see Section 5.5.3) before splitting the data, \[ y_i=\frac{y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1)+0.5}{n}, \] using the full-sample value of \(n\) throughout the workflow. The original grade percentage was retained separately for later interpretation. This boundary-handling convention is part of the model specification rather than a consequence of the Beta distribution itself.
  • The mean–precision parameterization makes Beta regression especially useful for regression modelling. Writing \[ Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i \sim \operatorname{Beta}\!\left( \mu_i\phi_i,\, (1-\mu_i)\phi_i \right), \] gives \[ \mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)=\mu_i, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i) = \frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi_i}. \] Thus, the conditional variance depends on both the conditional mean and the precision. In this chapter, the mean submodel used the logit link, \[ \operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)= \widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \] while the precision submodel used the log link, \[ \log(\phi_i)=\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol{\gamma}. \] The regressors in these two submodels need not generally be identical, although the final case-study specification used Study Time in both.
  • Beta regression is fitted by maximum likelihood. The mean and precision coefficients are estimated jointly through the Beta likelihood. The chapter used the resulting model-based covariance matrix to obtain model-based SEs, Wald tests, and CIs. These uncertainty statements depend on the fitted model and its regularity assumptions; they do not make model adequacy automatic.
  • Diagnostics can reveal inadequacy that is not visible from fitted means alone. The initial model represented the study-time group centres well but imposed a common precision parameter. Training-stage quantile-residual and response-scale dispersion checks showed a systematic across-group mismatch under that restriction. Allowing precision to depend on Study Time substantially reduced that pattern, while a separate mean-complexity check did not support expanding the focused Study Time mean submodel. The variable-precision model therefore addressed the principal diagnostic failure without adding unsupported complexity to the mean structure.
  • Model development ended before the protected testing outcomes were used. Once the variable-precision specification was judged practically adequate, the response transformation, mean and precision structures, links, treatment coding, predictive baseline, prediction target, metrics, interval level, and PIT diagnostic were frozen. This prevented the testing results from feeding back into another round of model selection.
  • Inference and prediction used the protected testing data differently. For the inferential inquiry, the already frozen specification was refitted on the testing data, and that fixed-specification refit supplied the final joint Study Time test, coefficient-level model-based inference, and original-grade-scale mean contrasts. For the predictive inquiry, the model fitted on the training data remained fixed: testing regressors were used to generate held-out predictions first, and the testing responses were used only afterward for evaluation. The inferential analysis established a strong association between Study Time and conditional mean grade in this synthetic dataset; it did not establish a causal effect.
  • Point prediction uses only the fitted conditional mean, whereas probabilistic prediction uses the full fitted Beta distribution. For a held-out observation, the frozen training-fitted model supplies \(\widehat{\mu}_i\) and \(\widehat{\phi}_i\), and therefore the complete predictive distribution \[ Y_i\mid\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i,\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i; \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\sim\operatorname{Beta}\!\left(\widehat{\mu}_i\widehat{\phi}_i,\, (1-\widehat{\mu}_i)\widehat{\phi}_i \right). \] Conditional-mean predictions and predictive-interval endpoints were translated back to the original grade-percentage scale for interpretation.
  • Held-out prediction was evaluated against a pre-specified intercept-only Beta baseline. ME, MAE, and RMSE assessed conditional-mean point prediction. Mean negative log predictive density (NLPD) assessed how much density the entire fitted Beta distribution assigned to the held-out responses, with smaller values preferred when models are compared on the same observations and response scale. Equal-tailed 90% plug-in predictive intervals were summarized using empirical coverage and average width, and a ten-bin PIT histogram assessed the held-out predictive distributions more broadly. Coverage, interval width, and PIT behaviour were interpreted together rather than reduced to a single pass/fail calibration rule.
  • The final study-time model improved both point and probabilistic prediction relative to the intercept-only baseline, but predictive success does not remove uncertainty or imply causality. The final model produced smaller held-out point-prediction errors, better mean NLPD, and substantially sharper predictive intervals while retaining empirical coverage close to the nominal level. The PIT histogram still showed some localized departure from ideal Uniform behaviour, so the predictive distribution was not described as perfect.

The case study also has important limits. The data are synthetic, the boundary transformation is one modelling convention whose choice can affect especially precision- and likelihood-based quantities, the final mean model uses only a coarse categorical Study Time regressor, the likelihood assumes independent observations, and the response must genuinely be suitable for continuous bounded modelling. The random split provides retrospective held-out predictive evidence but does not by itself establish prospective deployment conditions. Extrapolation beyond the observed study-time categories is not meaningful, and neither statistical significance nor predictive improvement identifies the causal effect of changing study time.

Hence, the central workflow lesson is broader than this particular dataset:

Match the probability model to the response, model both the conditional mean and conditional distribution carefully, diagnose before interpreting, freeze the specification before final evaluation, and keep inference, prediction, and causation conceptually distinct.

Having said all this, what makes Beta regression particularly interesting is that it pushes us beyond the version of regression that is most often introduced first: a model for how the conditional mean changes with regressors. Here, the support of the response is crucial, the mean and variance are structurally connected, the precision can itself be modelled, and prediction naturally produces an entire conditional distribution rather than only a fitted value. A seemingly simple response (i.e., a proportion between \(0\) and \(1\)) therefore leads us to think carefully about the probability model, the boundary behaviour, the sources of conditional variation, and what we actually want a regression model to tell us.

Beta regression is also less commonly encountered in standard regression sequences, which often devote most of their attention to Gaussian linear regression and a small number of more familiar GLMs. Yet bounded continuous responses arise naturally in many applications: rates, indices, fractions, scores, and percentages can all create modelling questions for which ordinary linear regression is not an especially natural probabilistic description. Beta regression is valuable not because it should replace those familiar tools, but because it illustrates how much becomes possible once the model is chosen to reflect the structure of the response.

Perhaps the broader lesson is that regression is not a single technique with a collection of minor variations. It is a way of building conditional models, and different data-generating situations can require different distributions, links, dispersion structures, diagnostics, and predictive summaries. Thus, the ideas developed in this chapter (support, likelihood, conditional mean, precision, uncertainty, diagnostics, and prediction) are not isolated features of Beta regression. They are part of a larger statistical language that lets us adapt regression reasoning to increasingly varied problems.

Fun fact!

Beet-a you didn’t know! The beet plant belongs to the genus Beta (Beta vulgaris, to be precise). So the next time you run a Beta regression, remember that somewhere in a field, a humble root vegetable is quietly sharing your model’s name.
